text: Where to find support and learn from others running experiments: established research groups that can provide outside technical support alongside EuroCOMP Lab, practical resources for setting up your own evaluation, peers already running experiments, and related initiatives across the European Commission.

title: Partners and related initiatives
text:
International research partners
Established labs and research groups already running rigorous impact evaluations. Many of them also publish free guidance and training you can use directly.


J-PAL
The Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab specialises in impact evaluation design.
Go further

Research resources: detailed, step-by-step resources for setting up a research programme, from design to data collection and analysis.
MicroMasters in Data, Economics and Design of Policy: an online programme from MIT and J-PAL for those who want to learn more.



IPA
Innovations for Poverty Action designs and rigorously evaluates solutions to poverty.


World Bank DIME
The World Bank’s Development Impact Evaluation group.
Go further

DIME Wiki: a collaborative, open-source resource with guidelines that are easy to understand and apply for users of varying levels of expertise.



International Initiative for Impact Evaluation (3ie)
A global non-profit research organisation working with governments, foundations, non-governmental organisations, and development and research organisations worldwide.
Go further

3ie resources: support for policymakers, researchers and practitioners making evidence-based decisions.



Innovation Growth Lab (IGL)
A global partnership that supports governments to test and evaluate innovation, entrepreneurship and growth policies.
Go further

IGL resources: guides, toolkits and evidence for running policy experiments.



Inter-American Development Bank (IDB)
The IDB’s impact evaluation work, which measures the effects of the projects it finances and shares the methods and lessons learned.
Go further

Impact Evaluation in Practice: a free handbook from the World Bank and the IDB on designing and running impact evaluations.

title: Glossary
text: Plain-language definitions of the evaluation terms used throughout this site.

title: Glossary
text:
A

Activities

The concrete actions taken to deliver an intervention, such as running grant calls, disbursing subsidies or delivering advisory services. What an intervention does.

Additionality

The share of an intervention’s results that would not have happened without it. Firms that would have invested anyway generate little that is truly additional per euro of public money spent.

Assumptions

In a Theory of Change, the conditions that must hold for one step in an intervention’s causal chain to lead to the next. If an assumption does not hold, for example that firms face a genuine financing constraint, an intervention can produce outputs without producing the intended results.

Attrition

Participants dropping out of a study, or no longer responding to follow-up data collection. It becomes a risk when dropout is not random: if struggling firms are the ones most likely to disappear, the firms still measured make an intervention look better than it is.

title: Glossary
text:
B

Balance

How similar the treatment and comparison groups look on observable characteristics before an intervention starts. A successful random assignment should produce balance; large, systematic differences are a warning sign that something went wrong with the draw.

Baseline data

Data collected from participants before an intervention begins, used as the starting point against which later change is measured.

Bin-ranking design

A randomised controlled trial (RCT) design in which applicants are scored and sorted into bins: the highest scorers are funded automatically, the lowest are rejected, and only the middle bin, where expected returns are least certain, is randomised between a treatment and a comparison group. Also called a cutoff design; effective when eligibility criteria are clear and resources are limited.

title: Glossary
text:
C

Cohesion policy

The EU’s main investment policy for reducing economic and social disparities between regions, delivered through the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF), the European Social Fund Plus (ESF+), the Cohesion Fund (CF) and the Just Transition Fund (JTF).

Common output indicator

A standardised output measure that managing authorities report to the European Commission. For the ERDF, the Cohesion Fund and the JTF, common output indicators carry an RCO code, for example RCO01 (enterprises supported). Programmes can also use programme-specific output indicators.

Common result indicator

A standardised result measure that managing authorities report to the European Commission, capturing the change for direct beneficiaries. For the ERDF, the Cohesion Fund and the JTF, common result indicators carry an RCR code. Programmes can also use programme-specific result indicators. In a Theory of Change, results correspond closely to medium-term outcomes.

Community Innovation Survey (CIS)

A recurring EU survey of firm-level innovation activity. One of several validated frameworks managing authorities can draw on when defining evaluation indicators.

Comparison / control group

The group not receiving the intervention, used as a benchmark for what would have happened to the treatment group without it.

Confidence level

How certain an evaluation needs to be that a measured effect is not simply due to chance. One of the inputs to a power calculation.

Confounding factors

External characteristics (variables) that can distort the perceived relationship between a policy intervention and its results, leading to incorrect conclusions about the policy’s effectiveness.

Contamination

The often unintended exposure of participants in the comparison group to the randomly assigned intervention, which can compromise the comparison between the two groups and affect the study’s validity.

Cost-benefit analysis

Weighing an intervention’s measured impact against its cost, to judge whether it was a good use of public money and to compare it with alternative investments.

Counterfactual

What would have happened without the newly introduced change (treatment, intervention, implementation approach, investment). It cannot be observed directly, so impact evaluation estimates it, for example with a comparison group.

title: Glossary
text:
D

Deadweight

Support that pays for activity a beneficiary would have carried out anyway. High deadweight, the mirror image of low additionality, means public money is substituting for spending the beneficiary would have made regardless.

Difference-in-differences (DiD)

A quasi-experimental method that compares the change over time in a treatment group with the change over the same period in a comparison group that had a similar prior trend. Relies on the parallel trends assumption, that both groups would have followed the same trajectory without the intervention, which cannot be tested directly.

Digital Economy and Society Index (DESI)

A European Commission index tracking digital performance and adoption. Used in the North-East Romania example to track firms’ digital adoption.

title: Glossary
text:
E

Encouragement design

Randomising who receives extra outreach to take up an intervention that cannot be denied to anyone, then comparing the whole encouraged group with the whole non-encouraged group. Used when take-up, not access, is the problem.

Endline data

Data collected once an intervention has run long enough for effects to plausibly appear, used to measure the gap between the treatment and comparison groups.

European Regional Development Fund (ERDF)

An EU cohesion policy fund that co-finances regional programmes, including many of the business-support and innovation interventions evaluated on this site.

European Social Fund Plus (ESF+)

An EU cohesion policy fund that co-finances programmes on employment, skills and social inclusion.

title: Glossary
text:
G

Goals

In a Theory of Change, the long-term aspirations behind a policy, such as a more innovative regional economy or greater resilience to economic shocks. Goals typically take years to materialise.

title: Glossary
text:
I

Impact evaluation

An assessment of whether, and by how much, an intervention caused the changes observed, by comparing participants’ results with a credible counterfactual. It serves two purposes: policy learning (what works, for whom, and under what conditions) and accountability (both financial and performance).

Implementation problems

A risk to an RCT’s validity where the intervention itself is delivered unevenly across participants, making the treatment experienced by the treatment group less consistent than intended.

Innovation activity

All developmental, financial and commercial activities undertaken by a firm that are intended to result in an innovation.

Inputs

In a Theory of Change, the resources invested in a policy: financing, personnel, equipment and training. For ERDF programmes, inputs typically include EU and national co-financing and the administrative capacity of the managing authority.

Intention-to-treat (ITT) effect

The effect estimated by comparing groups exactly as originally assigned by randomisation, regardless of whether participants assigned to treatment actually took it up. It stays unbiased because assignment was random, but it understates the effect on those who actually took part.

Intervention logic

The account, already required for cohesion policy programmes, of how an intervention is expected to produce its intended effects: from needs and objectives, through inputs and activities, to outputs, results and impacts. A Theory of Change builds on this by adding explicit assumptions and showing which links in the chain are strong or uncertain.

title: Glossary
text:
L

Local average treatment effect (LATE)

The impact estimate produced by a regression discontinuity design. Valid only for units close to the eligibility cut-off, not for the full population of participants.

Lottery

An RCT design that randomly selects who receives an intervention, by public or private draw, among applicants that already qualify. Works best when eligibility is clear and the intervention is oversubscribed.

title: Glossary
text:
M

Managing authority

The national or regional body responsible for managing a cohesion policy programme, including reporting to the European Commission and, where an impact evaluation is planned, integrating randomisation into the design of an intervention from the outset.

Matching

A quasi-experimental method that pairs participants with non-participants who share similar observable characteristics, to mimic an RCT. Assumes there are no unobserved differences between matched participants that also affect the results.

Medium-term outcomes

In a Theory of Change, the broader changes that accumulate from short-term outcomes, such as gains in firm-level productivity, tracked through result indicators (common or programme-specific). Impact evaluation aims to show that an intervention actually caused these changes, not just that they occurred.

Micro-, small- and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs)

Micro-sized enterprise commonly refers to an enterprise with fewer than 10 employees, small-sized enterprise to an enterprise with fewer than 50 employees and medium-sized enterprise to an enterprise with fewer than 250 employees.

Monitoring

The regular collection of data on inputs, outputs, results and participants to track whether an intervention is implemented as planned and to support day-to-day management. Unlike impact evaluation, monitoring does not show whether the changes observed were caused by the intervention.

Multiple treatment arms

Randomly assigning different versions of an intervention, with or without a control group, to learn which design works best rather than only whether the intervention works at all.

title: Glossary
text:
O

Oslo Manual

The OECD/Eurostat standard that defines innovation for statistical purposes, including the product innovation and process innovation definitions used on this site.

Outputs

The direct, countable deliverables of an intervention’s activities, such as the number of firms supported or grants awarded. What an intervention produces, tracked through output indicators (common or programme-specific).

title: Glossary
text:
P

Power calculation

A calculation, made before an intervention launches, that combines the expected effect size, the variation between participants, the desired confidence level and the desired statistical power into the minimum sample size an evaluation needs.

Pre-post (before-after) design

A quasi-experimental method that compares participants before and after an intervention. It assumes nothing else affected the results over the same period, an assumption that rarely holds in practice.

Primary data

Information collected directly from firms, individuals or organisations, through surveys or interviews conducted specifically for an evaluation. Gives more control over what is measured than secondary data, but costs more and takes longer to collect.

Process innovation

A new or improved business process for one or more business functions that differs significantly from the firm’s previous business processes and has been implemented within the firm.

Product innovation

A new or improved good or service that differs significantly from the firm’s previous goods or services and has been implemented on the market. Includes significant changes to the design of a good and digital goods or services; excludes the simple re-sale of new goods and changes of a solely aesthetic nature.

title: Glossary
text:
Q

Quasi-experimental methods

Methods that estimate the counterfactual without random assignment, by comparing participants with non-participants selected in another way. They can be planned in advance or applied after an intervention has been rolled out. They rely on assumptions, some of which cannot be tested, so the credibility of the evaluation depends on the credibility of those assumptions.

title: Glossary
text:
R

Random assignment

A key element of beneficiary selection when RCTs are implemented, creating comparable groups before the intervention starts. It differs from random selection in surveys.

Randomised controlled trial (RCT)

An impact evaluation design that randomly assigns eligible participants to a treatment group, which receives the intervention, and a control group, which does not. Because randomisation makes the two groups alike on average, the control group’s results show what would have happened without the intervention, without needing further assumptions about how results would have evolved.

Randomised intensities

Randomly varying how much of an intervention each participant receives, for example 100%, 50% or 0% of eligible employees, to study spillovers within or between firms.

Randomised phase-in

A design in which everyone eventually receives an intervention, in a randomly assigned order; participants still waiting act as the comparison group. Best when budget or capacity cannot cover everyone at once, though it limits how long the comparison can be observed.

Regression discontinuity design (RDD)

A quasi-experimental method that compares participants just above an eligibility cut-off with those just below it. Because unobservable characteristics are unlikely to differ sharply at the cut-off, it needs weaker assumptions than other quasi-experimental methods, but it only estimates impact for participants near the cut-off, a local average treatment effect.

Research and Development (R&D)

Creative and systematic work undertaken to increase the stock of knowledge, including knowledge of humankind, culture and society, and to devise new applications of available knowledge.

title: Glossary
text:
S

Secondary data

Information that already exists in administrative records, such as business registries, tax data or a programme’s own management information system. Cheaper and covers larger samples than primary data, but may not cover the specific result indicators an evaluation needs.

Selection bias

Occurs when assignment to treatment is not random, likely creating systematic differences between treatment and comparison groups. For example, firms with higher innovation levels may self-select into an intervention offering innovation vouchers, so observed differences may stem from pre-existing characteristics rather than the intervention itself. RCTs mitigate this by randomising participants, so later differences in results can be attributed to the intervention.

Short-term outcomes

In a Theory of Change, the immediate changes that follow directly from an intervention’s outputs, typically within one to two years, such as a firm adopting a new technology or a researcher filing a patent application.

Simple difference

A quasi-experimental method that compares participants with non-participants. It assumes the only difference between the two groups is participation in the intervention, which is often untrue since those who choose to participate may differ systematically from those who do not.

SMART indicators

Five characteristics of a well-defined evaluation indicator: Specific, Measurable, Attributable, Realistic and Targeted.

Smart Specialisation Strategy

A regional or national strategy that sets innovation priorities based on a region’s specific strengths, used to guide where cohesion policy innovation funding is targeted.

SMEs

Small- and medium-sized enterprises. Small-sized enterprise commonly refers to an enterprise with fewer than 50 employees and medium-sized enterprise to an enterprise with fewer than 250 employees.

Spillover effects

Indirect exposure of the comparison group to an intervention’s benefits, for example when know-how spreads by word of mouth to non-participating firms. Related to contamination: it understates an intervention’s measured impact by improving results for those who were not meant to receive support.

Statistical power

The likelihood that an evaluation will detect a real effect of the intervention if one actually exists. Higher power requires a larger sample, especially when the expected effect is small or participants vary widely.

title: Glossary
text:
T

Technology Readiness Level (TRL)

A 9-point scale used to measure the maturity of a technology from an initial basic idea to a fully functioning system. The TRL scale was originally developed by NASA and adapted by the European Commission for use across all Horizon Europe and ERDF R&D instruments. TRL 1–3 corresponds to basic and applied research; TRL 4–6 to technology development and validation; TRL 7–9 to demonstration and market deployment.

Theory of Change (ToC)

A structured account of how a policy’s activities are expected to lead, step by step, to its intended results, including the assumptions that must hold at each step. It builds on the intervention logic and shows what to measure and where the causal chain is most likely to break.

Treatment group

The group receiving the intervention.

title: Glossary
text:
W

World Bank Enterprise Surveys

A World Bank survey programme covering firm-level performance and business conditions. Another validated source of internationally comparable indicators for evaluation design.

title: Outcome indicators: energy efficiency
text:
Indicator repository
Matching survey questions: energy efficiency

Total energy consumption

Definition: total energy used by the firm across all sources (electricity, gas, oil, solid fuels, and renewables) in the reference year
Metric: total energy consumption in kWh; % change from baseline to endline


Total energy cost

Definition: total expenditure on energy across all sources in the reference year
Metric: total energy cost in €; energy cost as % of total turnover; % change from baseline to endline


Grid electricity consumption

Definition: total electricity consumed from the public grid in the reference year, excluding on-site generation
Metric: total grid electricity consumption in kWh or MWh; % change from baseline to endline


Energy source mix

Definition: the range of energy sources used by the firm, capturing the degree of diversification and shift towards non-fossil fuels
Metric: binary indicator per energy source (natural gas / oil / solid fuels / solar photovoltaic (PV) / other renewables / grid only); number of energy sources used


On-site renewable energy production

Definition: whether the firm generates electricity from on-site renewable sources (primarily solar PV), and the scale of that generation
Metric: binary indicator for solar PV installation (yes/no); installed capacity in kilowatt-peak (kWp); total renewable electricity generated in kWh; % of total energy consumption met by on-site renewables


Energy monitoring

Definition: whether the firm systematically tracks its own energy consumption as part of its management practices
Metric: binary indicator (yes/no)


Formal energy reduction goals

Definition: whether the firm has adopted explicit, documented targets for reducing energy consumption
Metric: binary indicator (yes/no)


External energy audit

Definition: whether the firm underwent an independent external assessment of its energy use and efficiency in the reference year
Metric: binary indicator (yes/no)


Dedicated energy management

Definition: whether the firm has assigned a specific person responsible for managing energy consumption and efficiency
Metric: binary indicator (yes/no)


Energy certification

Definition: whether the firm holds a recognised energy-related certification or label, such as ISO 50001 or an EU Energy Label
Metric: binary indicator (yes/no); type of certification held


Energy efficiency investment

Definition: whether the firm invested in activities aimed at reducing energy consumption or improving energy efficiency in the reference year, and the type and scale of those investments
Metric: binary indicator (yes/no); total expenditure on energy efficiency investments in €; binary indicator per investment type (renewables / storage / lighting / heating, ventilation and cooling (HVAC) / building fabric / smart controls / electric vehicles (EVs) / machinery / equipment / audit / training); number of investment types undertaken


Planned energy efficiency investment

Definition: whether the firm intends to invest in energy efficiency improvements in the coming year
Metric: binary indicator (yes/no)


Energy consumption reduction

Definition: the percentage reduction in total energy consumption achieved by the firm relative to the previous year or a comparable reference period
Metric: % reduction in total energy consumption; binary indicator for positive reduction (yes/no)

title: Outcome indicators: business support and training
text:
Indicator repository
Matching survey questions: business support and training

Application for business support programmes

Definition: whether the firm applied for any business support programme in the reference year
Metric: binary indicator (yes/no)


Participation in business support programmes

Definition: whether the firm participated in any business support programme in the reference year
Metric: binary indicator (yes/no)


Type of business support programme

Definition: specific type(s) of business support programme in which the firm participated, covering incubation, acceleration, mentoring, coaching, networking, and matchmaking
Metric: binary indicator per programme type (yes/no); number of programme types participated in


Formal employee training

Definition: whether the firm operated formal training programmes for its permanent full-time workers in the reference year
Metric: binary indicator (yes/no)

title: Outcome indicators: employment and human capital
text:
Indicator repository
Matching survey questions: company financial performance, business support and training

Employment

Definition: total number of people employed by the firm at a given point in time, reflecting the firm’s size and capacity
Metric: Number of full-time equivalent (FTE) employees (absolute level)


Employment growth

Definition: net change in the number of people employed by the firm
Metric: % change in FTE employment from baseline to endline; log of employment


High-skilled employment

Definition: whether the firm increased the share of high-skilled or knowledge-intensive workers
Metric: share of employees with tertiary education (%); share of STEM employees (%); number of researchers hired


Training provision

Definition: whether the firm provided formal training to employees
Metric: binary indicator; number of employees trained; training hours per employee; training expenditure ([currency])


Wages

Definition: wages, reflecting improved worker productivity or firm profitability
Metric: [currency], % change in average gross wage per employee from baseline to endline

title: Outcome indicators: digitalisation and technology
text:
Indicator repository
Matching survey questions: digitalisation and technology adoption

Digital technology adoption

Definition: whether and which digital technologies the firm uses (cloud, artificial intelligence, Internet of Things, big data, etc.)
Metric: number of digital technologies in use; binary indicators per technology type


Online sales share

Definition: share of total sales conducted through digital channels
Metric: % of total turnover from online sales


Digital investment

Definition: spending on digital technologies and software
Metric: total digital investment in €


Digital skills of the workforce

Definition: improvement in the digital capabilities of the firm’s employees
Metric: share of employees with intermediate or advanced digital skills (%); binary indicator for digital training provision


Digital maturity score

Definition: overall level of digitalisation across the firm’s strategy, processes, skills, and security
Metric: composite index score based on standardised questions


Technology adoption rate

Definition: whether the firm has adopted new technologies during the evaluation period
Metric: binary indicator (yes/no); number of new technologies adopted; type of technology


Technology spending

Definition: investment in purchasing or licensing hardware and software
Metric: total technology investment in €


Technology sophistication

Definition: complexity and frontier-proximity of the technologies adopted by the firm
Metric: categorical scale from basic to advanced technology types; self-reported


DESI digital technology integration score

Definition: level of digital technology integration across the firm’s operations, measured against the European Commission’s Digital Economy and Society Index (DESI) business digitalisation criteria - covering electronic information sharing, cloud computing, big data analytics, social media, IoT, AI, e-invoicing, and e-commerce
Metric: number of DESI criteria met (out of 12); composite DESI integration sub-score; binary indicator for reaching a defined threshold (e.g. at least 7 of 12 criteria)

title: Outcome indicators: innovation and IP
text:
Indicator repository
Matching survey questions: innovation, R&D and intellectual property, technology readiness level

Innovation activity

Definition: whether the firm engaged in any innovation activity during the evaluation period, including product, process, or organisational innovation
Metric: binary indicator (yes/no)


Product innovation

Definition: introduction of a new or significantly improved good or service
Metric: binary indicator (yes/no); number of new products introduced; share of turnover from new products (%)


Process innovation

Definition: introduction of a new or significantly improved production, delivery, or supporting process
Metric: binary indicator (yes/no); type of process innovation introduced


Organisational innovation

Definition: introduction of new organisational methods in business practices, workplace organisation, or external relations
Metric: binary indicator (yes/no)


Novelty of innovation

Definition: whether innovations are new only to the firm, new to the market, or new to the world – a measure of innovation ambition
Metric: categorical (firm-level / market-level / world-level novelty)


Share of turnover from new products

Definition: the proportion of sales generated by products or services introduced in the last three years – captures commercial success of innovation
Metric: % of total turnover attributable to new or significantly improved products


Innovation expenditure

Definition: total spending on innovation-related activities (R&D, design, training, market introduction, etc.)
Metric: total innovation expenditure in €; share of turnover spent on innovation (%)


Technology Readiness Level (TRL)

Definition: the maturity of the firm’s main technology or product under development, assessed against the European Commission’s nine-point TRL scale, from basic principles observed (TRL 1) to a fully proven operational system (TRL 9)
Metric: current TRL score (1–9); TRL advancement (number of levels gained from baseline to endline)


Patent applications

Definition: whether the firm filed for or obtained patents
Metric: number of patent applications; number of patents granted; binary indicator


Trademark and design registration

Definition: whether the firm registered trademarks or designs to protect its market position
Metric: number of trademarks or registered designs; binary indicator


Technology licensing

Definition: whether the firm licenses technology to or from other companies – a measure of knowledge commercialisation
Metric: binary indicator (licensor / licensee); value of licensing agreements (€)

title: Indicator repository
text: Indicators rarely need to be built from scratch. Managing authorities should draw on existing, well-tested measures from comparable evaluations before designing new ones. This repository provides a curated list of indicators, organised by topic, each with a plain-language definition and a metric that says how to operationalise and measure it.

title: Indicator repository
text:
Topics


Firm performance and growth
Turnover, profits, value added, productivity, wages, exports and firm survival.
Example: the TIDES of Change report (World Bank, 2025)


Innovation and intellectual property
Types and novelty of innovation, sales from new products, innovation spending, technology readiness, patents, trademarks and licensing.
Example: the returns to innovation subsidies in Romania (South-Muntenia)


R&D activity
Whether the firm does R&D, how much it spends and how many staff work on it.
Example: financial support to innovate in Spain (Extremadura)


Digitalisation and technology adoption
Technology adoption and spending, online sales, digital investment and skills, and digital maturity.
Example: financial support to digitalise in Romania (North-East)


Collaboration and knowledge transfer
Collaboration, partner diversity, links with universities and researchers, and cluster or network membership.
Example: matching businesses with scientists in Croatia


Employment and human capital
Jobs, job growth, high-skilled staff, training and wages.
Example: financial support to digitalise in Romania (North-East)


Business finance
Access to equity, debt and public finance, and its use for R&D and innovation.
Example: making firms investment-ready in the Western Balkans (2018)


Business support and training
Applications to, participation in and type of business support, and formal employee training.
Example: scaling up management consulting in Colombia


Management practices
An overall management index and its eight dimensions, from problem solving to dealing with underperformance.
Example: how management practices differ in the EU-27 (2025)


Energy efficiency
Energy use, cost and mix, on-site renewables, energy management, audits, investment and savings.
Example: grants for SME energy efficiency in Europe

title: Indicator repository
text:
How to use the indicators
The indicators are suggestions and a starting point, not a complete or prescribed set: they do not cover every indicator an evaluation may need, and not all of them will suit every evaluation.

Open the topic that matches the intervention you are evaluating.
Select the indicators that match the causal chain in your Theory of Change.
Adapt the definitions and metrics to your intervention and context.
Find tested questions to measure them in the survey question repository.

The reports and manuals below give more detail and further indicators, so it is worth consulting them directly when an indicator is central to your evaluation.

title: Indicator repository
text:
Sources
The selection of indicators and their definitions in this repository was informed by the EuroCOMP Lab evaluations (see Examples), policy reports such as the World Bank’s TIDES report, and established indicator manuals such as the OECD Oslo Manual for innovation and the OECD Frascati Manual for research and development. Drawing on these sources improves the quality of your data and makes findings easier to compare with evidence from other interventions and regions.

title: Survey questions: management practices
text:
Survey question repository
Matching indicators: management practices

ASK IF MANUFACTURING: over [year], what best describes what happened at this establishment when a problem in the production process arose?
ASK IF SERVICES: over [year], what best describes what happened at this establishment when a problem in the provision of services arose?

We fixed it but did not take further action
We fixed it and took action to make sure it did not happen again
We fixed it and took action to make sure that it did not happen again, and had a continuous improvement process to anticipate problems like these in advance
No action was taken


Over [year], did this establishment monitor any performance indicators?

Yes
No


How many performance indicators were monitored?

1-2 indicators
3-9 indicators

title: Step 8: ensure high-quality data
text:
Step 1Step 2Step 3Step 4Step 5Step 6Step 7Step 8
Data quality is not something that can be fixed after the fact. Problems that go undetected during fieldwork (inconsistent answers, enumerator errors, item non-response, or systematic biases in who responds) cannot be fully corrected at the analysis stage. The purpose of this step is to put in place the checks that catch these problems early, while there is still time to act on them.
Quality assurance in a randomised controlled trial (RCT) operates at three levels: before fieldwork begins, during fieldwork, and after data collection is complete. Each level requires different tools and different responsibilities.

title: Step 8: ensure high-quality data
text:
Summary
This page covers quality controls before fieldwork, real-time monitoring during fieldwork, and post-collection steps: cleaning, balance checks, attrition assessment, and validation against administrative data.

title: Step 8: ensure high-quality data
section: Before fieldwork: build quality in from the start
text:
Before fieldwork: build quality in from the start
The most effective quality controls are the ones built into the data collection instrument and process before a single interview takes place.
Build validation rules into the digital form. Every digital survey should include:

mandatory fields for key variables
range checks, flagging implausible values such as negative employment or turnover greater than a plausible ceiling
logical consistency checks (for example, research and development (R&D) expenditure cannot exceed total costs)
skip logic that prevents respondents from reaching questions that do not apply to them

These rules catch errors at the point of entry, before they enter the dataset.
Pilot the questionnaire. As described in Step 7, no questionnaire should go to the field untested. The pilot should specifically assess whether questions produce consistent, interpretable answers, not just whether they are understood. For example: if two respondents from similar firms give very different answers to the same question, the wording may be ambiguous even if both respondents felt they understood it.
Train enumerators thoroughly. For Computer-Assisted Telephone Interviews (CATI) and Computer-Assisted Personal Interviews (CAPI) surveys, enumerator quality is one of the strongest predictors of data quality. Training should cover not only how to administer each question but also how to handle refusals, clarify without leading, and record partial responses. Enumerators should complete mock interviews before fieldwork begins.
Pre-specify the analysis plan. Before any data is collected, the main result indicator, the estimator, and the subgroup analyses should be publicly pre-registered. This prevents selective reporting (the practice of reporting only the findings that look good) and provides a clear audit trail from design to findings. Pre-registration is covered under Step 5, but its data quality implications deserve emphasis here: it disciplines both data collection and analysis.

title: Step 8: ensure high-quality data
section: During fieldwork: monitor in real time
text:
During fieldwork: monitor in real time
Once fieldwork begins, the evaluation team should monitor progress continuously rather than waiting for a complete dataset to arrive.
Track response rates by group. Response rates should be monitored separately for the treatment and control groups throughout fieldwork. If response rates diverge significantly (for example, if control units are less willing to respond), this is an early warning of differential attrition that can bias the findings.
Conduct back-checks. A back-check involves re-contacting a random subset of completed interviews (typically 10%) to verify a selection of answers. Significant discrepancies between the original interview and the back-check indicate either enumerator error or data fabrication, both of which require immediate investigation. Back-checks are standard practice in telephone (CATI) and face-to-face (CAPI) surveys and should be a contractual requirement for any data collection firm.
Monitor enumerator performance. Each enumerator’s response patterns should be reviewed regularly for signs of data fabrication: unusually short interview durations, identical or near-identical responses across interviews, or suspiciously high completion rates. Any enumerator showing these patterns should be flagged and their recent interviews back-checked at a higher rate.
Flag implausible values immediately. The survey platform should be configured to generate automatic alerts for out-of-range values or logical inconsistencies. These should be reviewed by the field supervisor within 24 hours and, where possible, resolved by calling the respondent back.

title: Step 8: ensure high-quality data
section: After data collection: clean, document, and validate
text:
After data collection: clean, document, and validate
Once fieldwork is complete, the dataset must be cleaned and validated before analysis begins. This process should be systematic and fully documented so that it can be reproduced and audited.
Check balance between treatment and control groups. The first analytical task after baseline data collection is to verify that randomisation produced comparable treatment and control groups. Run balance checks across all key baseline characteristics (for firms, typically size, age, sector and turnover), including the main result indicator measured at baseline. A significant imbalance on any of these variables should be investigated: it may indicate a flaw in the randomisation procedure, or it may be a chance occurrence that needs to be controlled for in the analysis.
Document all cleaning decisions. Every decision made during data cleaning (how missing values are handled, how outliers are treated, how variables are recoded) must be recorded in a cleaning log. This log is part of the evaluation’s audit trail and should be shared with the managing authority alongside the final dataset.
Validate against external sources. Where possible, key variables from the primary survey should be cross-checked against administrative data. For example, self-reported employment figures can be compared against social security records; self-reported turnover can be compared against VAT declarations. Large discrepancies between survey and administrative data are a signal of measurement error that needs to be understood before it affects the analysis.
Assess and report attrition. Compare the characteristics of participants who completed the endline survey with those who did not. If those who dropped out differ systematically from those who remained (for example, in size, sector, or the baseline values of the result indicators), attrition is selective and may bias the findings. Report attrition rates and the results of these comparisons transparently in the evaluation report, and apply appropriate analytical corrections (such as inverse probability weighting) where differential attrition is detected.

title: Step 8: ensure high-quality data
section: A note on administrative data quality
text:
A note on administrative data quality
The quality assurance steps above apply primarily to primary survey data. Administrative data comes with its own quality challenges that require a different approach.
Before using administrative data to measure results, the evaluation team should assess:

whether variable definitions have changed over the data period
whether there are systematic gaps in coverage (for example, firms below a VAT registration threshold)
whether reporting lags mean that the data will be available in time for the evaluation
whether the data has been used in comparable evaluations and, if so, what quality issues were encountered

Where administrative data quality is uncertain, the evaluation should include a validation exercise. It compares a subset of administrative records with survey-reported values from the same participants, before the data become the main source for the result indicators.

title: Writing terms of reference for an RCT
text:
Step 1Step 2Step 3Step 4Step 5Step 6Step 7Step 8
Managing authorities bring deep knowledge of their interventions to the table; the technical expertise needed to evaluate them rigorously can be contracted in. While this website provides the tools and guidance to get started, implementing randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comes with many specificities and challenges, and having the right expert team on board makes all the difference. What managing authorities need is a well-crafted ToR: the document that attracts the right teams, sets the methodological bar, and defines the conditions for a credible, policy-relevant evaluation. A strong ToR is therefore not a procurement formality: it is an important contribution of the managing authority to the quality of the evaluation.
In principle, a ToR can cover the entire evaluation, including evaluation design, Theory of Change (ToC) development, and selection of the methodological approach, leaving these decisions to the consultant. However, since this website focuses specifically on RCTs as the evaluation design of choice, it assumes that managing authorities have already completed the preparatory steps covered on the previous pages. The ToC is in place, the evaluation questions and indicators are defined, the feasibility of an RCT has been confirmed, the randomisation design has been chosen, and the available data sources have been mapped.
The ToR therefore focuses on two specific functions: preparing and implementing data collection, and conducting the statistical analysis. These can be covered by a single ToR commissioning one consultant or team, or split across two separate ToRs: one for an evaluation consultant responsible for analysis, and one for the data collection firm responsible for fieldwork.

title: Writing terms of reference for an RCT
text:
Summary
This page sets out how to write Expression of Interests (EoI) and what the Terms of Reference (ToR) must contain: intervention background, learning questions, scope of work, methodology, deliverables, budget, data access, required qualifications, and common mistakes to avoid.

title: Writing terms of reference for an RCT
text:
Part 1: the procurement process

Step 1: issue an EoI
For technically complex evaluations, it is strongly recommended to begin with an EoI rather than going directly to a full ToR. An EoI is a short, non-binding call that invites qualified organisations to signal their interest and demonstrate their eligibility before the full competition begins.
The EoI serves three purposes. First, it maps the market: the pool of RCT-capable evaluation teams is narrower than the general consulting market, and an EoI quickly identifies who is actually available and qualified. Second, it allows the managing authority to shortlist candidates who are then invited to submit full proposals in a restricted procedure, which is more efficient for both sides. Third, EoI responses often reveal market realities (realistic timelines, typical costs, data access constraints) that can be incorporated into the final ToR.
An EoI should contain:

A brief description of the intervention and the intended evaluation approach
The estimated budget range and timeline
Shortlisting criteria: relevant experience, team qualifications, organisational capacity
What to submit: a short letter (maximum 3-5 pages), CVs of key staff, two to three examples of comparable prior evaluations
Submission deadline and contact point

The EoI should be open for a minimum of two to three weeks and published through the national procurement portal and the managing authority’s website. Shortlisted candidates, typically three to six, are then invited to submit full proposals in response to the complete ToR.


Step 2: issue the ToR and evaluate proposals
With shortlisted candidates identified, the managing authority issues the full ToR. Proposals are evaluated against pre-defined, published criteria. For an RCT evaluation, technical quality should be weighted heavily:



Criterion

15%



A low-bid selection for a technically complex evaluation is a false economy. The proposal panel should include at least one member with methodological knowledge of RCTs, or an external technical reviewer where this expertise is not available internally.
Before making a final selection, shortlisted candidates should be invited to a clarification interview. Useful questions include: how would you handle lower-than-projected take-up? At what level of attrition would you consider the evaluation compromised?


Step 3: contract signature and inception
Once the contract is signed, the evaluation begins. The first milestone is the inception report, in which the consultant refines the ToC, finalises the evaluation design, confirms the sampling and randomisation strategy, and presents survey instruments for review. This is the last point at which fundamental design decisions can be changed without significant cost or delay.
Key questions to assess at inception review:

Is the power analysis based on realistic assumptions about take-up, response rates, and effect sizes?
Is the randomisation strategy robust to the specific implementation context?
Has the evaluation been pre-registered, or is it about to be?
Are all data access arrangements confirmed?

title: Writing terms of reference for an RCT
section: Part 2: what the ToR must contain
text:
Part 2: what the ToR must contain

1. Background, intervention description, and ToC
This section gives the consultant the context needed to design the data collection instruments and analysis plan. Include:

Name and objectives of the intervention and funding instrument
Description of the intervention: what participants receive, how much, under what conditions
Eligibility criteria and selection methodology
Total budget, value of individual awards, and number of expected beneficiaries
Implementation timeline and any prior rounds
Relevant regulatory obligations (e.g. applicable state aid rules)

Include the completed ToC, covering inputs, activities, outputs, short- and medium-term results, impacts, and assumptions. The ToC has been developed by the managing authority and is provided to the consultant as a fixed reference point for designing the measurement framework and survey instruments.


2. Learning questions
List the primary and secondary learning questions explicitly. These have been defined by the managing authority and are provided to the consultant as the analytical framework that the data collection and analysis must address. State the intended use of the findings.


3. Scope of work
The consultant’s responsibilities cover two functions: data collection and analysis. Specify clearly which tasks fall under each and, where a separate data collection firm is contracted, which tasks are covered elsewhere.
Data collection:

Finalise baseline and endline survey instruments based on the ToC and evaluation questions provided
Pilot the questionnaire and propose revisions
Oversee or coordinate fieldwork; supervise the data collection firm where one is separately contracted
Implement randomisation and produce a balance report confirming comparability of treatment and control groups
Design and maintain a monitoring framework tracking take-up, compliance, contamination, and attrition

Analysis:

Clean and merge survey and administrative data
Conduct impact analysis and heterogeneity analysis
Produce draft and final evaluation reports and a non-technical documents (e.g. a policy brief)
Present findings to the managing authority and relevant stakeholders



4. Methodology
The methodology section is the technical core of the ToR. It should specify the evaluation design clearly enough that a qualified evaluator can assess whether the approach is appropriate, without being so prescriptive that it prevents the consultant from bringing their own expertise to bear.
Design: Specify that the evaluation will use an RCT, and define the unit of randomisation (for business support, typically the firm), the level of randomisation (individual or cluster), and whether there are multiple treatment arms.
Sample size and power: Require a formal power analysis during the inception phase. The consultant must specify and justify the minimum detectable effect, required statistical power, significance level, expected take-up and attrition rates, and baseline variance of the main result indicator.
Estimation: The main analysis should compare all units offered the support with all units in the comparison group, whether or not the units offered actually took the support up. This keeps the comparison fair and shows the effect of offering the intervention. If some of them did not take it up, the consultant should also estimate the effect on those that actually received it.
Pre-registration: Require pre-registration on a recognised public registry, such as the American Economic Association (AEA) RCT Registry, before any data is collected. The pre-registration record must include the research question, randomisation procedure, main and secondary result indicators, and analysis plan.
Data sources: Specify which administrative datasets will be provided by the managing authority and which the consultant must access independently. If primary survey data is needed, clarify whether survey fieldwork is in scope or covered by a separate data collection contract.


5. Deliverables and timeline







Deliverable
Review period




Inception report: refined ToC, evaluation design, power calculations, survey instruments
15 working days


Baseline report: survey data, balance checks, randomisation confirmation
15 working days


Monitoring reports: take-up, compliance, attrition
10 working days


Draft endline report: impact analysis, heterogeneity analysis
20 working days


Final evaluation report
10 working days


Policy brief: 4–6 page non-technical summary
10 working days


Presentation of findings
As agreed





6. Budget
Why a precise estimate is difficult. The cost of an RCT depends on many design choices specific to each intervention. The table below shows the main variables that define the budget and how each one affects it.







Variable
How it affects the budget




Sample size
More participants mean higher survey costs, because each additional interview adds fieldwork cost.


Design complexity
Each additional treatment arm or planned subgroup comparison requires more participants. Randomising in clusters, such as regions or sectors, rather than individual units also requires a larger sample to detect the same effect.


Number of survey rounds
Each round adds a full fieldwork cycle: updating the questionnaire, training enumerators, conducting interviews, and cleaning data. Because data collection is usually the largest cost item, adding a midline or a second follow-up raises the total considerably.


Data collection mode
Web surveys are the cheapest per interview, telephone interviews (CATI) cost more because of interviewer time, and face-to-face interviews (CAPI) cost the most because of travel and enumerator time. Cheaper modes may need extra follow-up to keep response rates up.


Questionnaire length and languages
Longer questionnaires increase interviewer time per interview for CATI and CAPI, and can lower response rates. Each additional language adds translation, back-translation, and piloting costs.


Geographic spread
A widely dispersed sample increases travel time and costs for face-to-face interviews. It makes little difference for web or telephone surveys.


Use of administrative data
Lowers costs where tax, registry, or social security records can replace survey rounds, especially the follow-up. Some costs remain for negotiating access, data-sharing agreements, linking and cleaning the data, and sometimes access fees.


Duration of the evaluation
A longer evaluation means more months of research team time and project management, and more effort to keep track of participants between rounds. RCTs often run several years from design to final report.


Team composition and national labour costs
Senior researchers cost more per day than junior staff, and fees for enumerators and consultants vary widely across countries.


Reporting and dissemination
Workshops, translated reports, policy briefs, and presentations add relatively modest costs, mainly staff time and travel.



Indicative orders of magnitude. International benchmarks give a sense of scale. In a sample of impact evaluations supported by the World Bank’s Strategic Impact Evaluation Fund, costs ranged from about USD 130,000 to USD 2.8 million, with an average of around USD 1 million. A review of 89 impact evaluations funded by 3ie found an average budget of about USD 344,000, and about USD 374,000 for RCTs. In both cases, new data collection was the largest single cost, typically 60–65% of the total. Most of these evaluations took place in low- and middle-income countries. Fieldwork and staff costs in the EU are generally higher, although good administrative data can reduce the need for primary surveys.
As a rough guide for EU competitiveness interventions:

Indicative range

€100,000 – €250,000

€250,000 – €600,000

€600,000 – €1,000,000 or more



These ranges are indicative only. Use the responses to the EoI (Part 1) to check them against current market prices before setting the envelope. The budget should be set before the ToR is issued, not derived from what remains after other costs. The ToR should state explicitly whether fieldwork costs are included in the evaluation budget or procured separately.
Budget structure. Ask applicants to break down their financial proposal by task: inception and design; baseline data collection; monitoring; endline data collection; analysis; reporting and dissemination; travel; and contingency (typically 5–10%).
Payment schedule. Payments should be tied to approved deliverables, not to the passage of time:

Specify clearly whether the budget is inclusive or exclusive of Value Added Tax, and whether travel and data access costs are included or reimbursable separately.


7. Data access and GDPR
Specify which datasets the managing authority will provide, in what format and timeline. The ToR must address General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) compliance (lawful basis for processing, pseudonymisation, data security requirements, and retention obligations) and require a data processing agreement to be signed before any data transfer.


8. Qualifications required
For a full RCT evaluation, require:

an advanced degree in economics, statistics, or a related quantitative field
demonstrated experience designing and implementing experimental impact evaluations (with publicly available outputs as evidence)
experience with data on the target population (for business support, firm-level data)
familiarity with EU cohesion policy and state aid rules

Where a team is required, specify the expected composition and qualifications for each role.


9. Governance and proposal requirements
Describe the reporting line, frequency of progress meetings, and the composition of any evaluation steering committee. Specify the escalation procedure for methodological disagreements. State what applicants must submit (technical proposal length, CV format, number of reference evaluations, financial proposal format) and the submission deadline.

Common mistakes to avoid

Starting too late. An RCT must be designed before beneficiaries are selected. Procurement should begin at least six to twelve months before the first grant is awarded.
Leaving the design entirely to the consultant. The ToR must include a preliminary ToC and evaluation questions: a consultant who receives no guidance will measure what is easy, not what matters.
Setting an unrealistic budget. A ToR with an insufficient budget envelope will either attract low-quality proposals or result in a scope reduction that compromises the evaluation.

With the Theory of Change (ToC), learning questions and indicators in place, the feasibility of the randomised controlled trial (RCT) confirmed and the randomisation designed, the next question is where the data will come from. This is a strategic decision that must be made before the intervention launches, not an operational detail to be worked out later. Getting it wrong wastes resources, delays the evaluation, or produces data that cannot support the intended analysis.

title: Step 6: identify available data sources
text:
Summary
This page covers the choice between primary and secondary data, how to assess what administrative sources already exist and whether they cover the right indicators, where to find secondary (firm-level) data, and how to set up data-sharing agreements.

title: Step 6: identify available data sources
section: The fundamental decision: primary, secondary, or both?
text:
The fundamental decision: primary, secondary, or both?
For each indicator in your evaluation framework, you must decide whether to rely on primary data collected specifically for the evaluation, secondary data that already exists in administrative records, or a combination of both.
Primary data is information collected directly from target units (e.g. firms, individuals, organisations) through surveys or interviews. It gives you control over exactly what is measured and can capture results and mechanisms that administrative records do not contain. The trade-off is cost, time, and respondent burden.
Secondary data draws on records that already exist: censuses on the household level, national business registries, tax authority data, social security and employment records, customs records, patent office databases, or the intervention’s own project management system on the firm level. It is generally cheaper, covers larger samples, and often provides years of pre-intervention history that is invaluable for establishing baselines. The trade-off is that it may not contain the specific indicators you would like to measure, and access can take time to negotiate.
Where administrative data sources are well established and reliable, as is generally the case for firm-level administrative data (e.g. national business registries) across the European Union, combining both sources is often the most effective approach. Secondary data provides broad coverage and pre-intervention history, while primary survey data captures the results and mechanisms that administrative records cannot.

North‑East Romania: data sources
North-East Romania used a combination of primary and secondary data: self-reported survey data was collected using a structured questionnaire that complements administrative data sources.

title: Step 6: identify available data sources
text:
Assess what you already have
Before commissioning a new survey, take stock of the administrative data you already hold or can access. Project management systems typically record beneficiary characteristics, grant amounts, payment dates, and reported output indicators. For firms, national statistical offices, tax authorities, business registries, and customs agencies hold data on turnover, employment, exports, costs, expenditures and tax payments, often going back many years, which is particularly valuable for establishing pre-intervention baselines. For people, social security, public employment service and education records can play the same role.
Two questions determine whether administrative sources can be useful for an evaluation.
First, do they cover the right indicators? Administrative records capture variables that may or may not align with the results the evaluation is designed to measure. An innovation intervention that wants to measure research and development (R&D) expenditure or product novelty will find that some business registries simply do not record these. Before relying on administrative data, map each indicator in your evaluation framework against what each source actually contains, and identify the gaps.
Second, can the administrative data be linked to the participants in the evaluation? If official identification numbers are collected at application stage, they can serve as a linking key to match intervention records against tax, registry, social security or customs data. For firms, that means the VAT or national registration number; for people, the national identification number, where national law allows its use. This makes it possible to measure results without any additional burden on participants. Where no common identifier exists, linkage may still be possible through name and address matching, but this requires more effort and introduces matching errors.

title: Step 6: identify available data sources
text:
Data-sharing agreements
Access to administrative data rarely happens automatically. Relevant microdata are typically held by separate government bodies and subject to their own access rules. Negotiating access takes time (in some countries, many months) and must be initiated well before the evaluation begins.
Preparing the request.

Send an official letter. An official request from the managing authority, signed at an appropriate level of seniority, often carries more weight with a data-holding body than informal contact. It also creates a record of the request.
Be specific about which data you need. List the variables, the units (for example, all firms in the evaluation sample), the years, and the level of detail. Requests for “all available data” are hard to approve and tend to be slowed down or refused.
Explain why you need it. Link each requested item to an indicator in your Theory of Change and to the evaluation question it helps answer. This shows that the request is limited to what is necessary and helps the data holder justify its decision.
Plan for several rounds of negotiation. Expect questions, requests for clarification, and revisions to the scope, the access conditions, or the legal basis. Build this time into the evaluation timeline, and involve your Data Protection Officer and, where helpful, legal advisers from the start.

What the agreement should cover. A data-sharing agreement between the managing authority and the data-holding body sets out the rights and responsibilities of each side. Good practice is to include the following, with the technical details in annexes that can be updated without rewriting the agreement:

Parties and roles. Who provides the data, who receives it, and who is responsible for decisions on how it is used. Name a contact person on each side.
Purpose and legal basis. The specific evaluation purpose for which the data may be used, and the legal basis for sharing it. The data should not be used for any other purpose without written agreement.
Description of the data. The datasets, variables, time period, and units covered, the format, and the identifiers used to link records (for example, a tax or registration number). Specify whether the data is pseudonymised or anonymised.
Access arrangements. How the data will be provided: transferred to the evaluation team, or accessed in a secure environment. State how often it will be updated, which matters if you need data for several years after the intervention.
Authorised users and confidentiality. Only named members of the evaluation team may access identifiable data, on a need-to-know basis, and all of them are bound by confidentiality. Re-identifying individuals or firms, and linking the data to other sources for unrelated purposes, should be prohibited.
Data security. Minimum safeguards such as encryption, pseudonymisation, multi-factor authentication, restricted access with access logs, secure storage, and regular backups. The data holder may ask for the right to verify that these safeguards are in place.
Third parties and transfers. Whether consultants, data collection firms, or research partners may receive the data. This should require prior approval by the data holder and the same obligations as the original recipient. Any transfer outside the EU, for example to an international research partner, should be stated and covered by an appropriate legal mechanism.
Requests from individuals. What happens if a person or firm asks to see, correct, or delete their data: who is notified, and how quickly.
Security incidents. The recipient must notify the data holder promptly, within a defined time limit, of any loss, unauthorised access, or disclosure, and cooperate in the response.
Duration, retention, and deletion. The period for which the agreement and access are valid, which should cover the full evaluation including follow-up rounds. At the end, the data must be returned or securely destroyed, with written confirmation. Confidentiality and security obligations should continue after the agreement ends.
Publication and outputs. Results must be published only in aggregate or anonymised form. The data holder may ask to review outputs before publication, to check that no unit can be identified.
Termination and changes. The conditions under which either side may end the agreement, for example in the event of a breach, and how amendments are agreed in writing.

General Data Protection Regulation compliance must be addressed explicitly in the agreement. Draft the agreement together with the data holder’s own legal and data protection teams, as many institutions have their own templates and requirements.

title: Step 5: how to randomise
text:
Step 1Step 2Step 3Step 4Step 5Step 6Step 7Step 8
With the feasibility conditions confirmed in Step 4, the next decision is how to randomise: which design fits the intervention, how the draw is run, and how to protect the comparison once it has been made.

title: Step 5: how to randomise
text:
Summary
This page covers five randomisation designs and when to use each, and whether to run the draw in public or in private. It also explains how to check that the groups are comparable, the most common problems after the lottery, and how to pre-register the design.

title: Step 5: how to randomise
section: Five ways to randomise your intervention
text:
Five ways to randomise your intervention
Not every intervention fits the same shape. The right design depends on your intervention’s structure, budget, and the learning questions you would like to answer. Here are five approaches in common use.

  
    Lottery
    How: randomly select which eligible units receive the intervention, by a documented public or private draw.
    Best when: eligibility is clear, the intervention is oversubscribed, and a single treatment is being tested.
  
  
    Multiple treatment arms
    How: randomly assign units to different versions of the intervention (for example, grant only vs. grant plus advisory support), with or without a comparison group receiving nothing.
    Best when: you want to know which design element drives results, not just whether the intervention works at all.
  
  
    Randomised phase-in
    How: everyone receives the intervention eventually, but in a randomly assigned order. Units still waiting serve as the comparison group in the meantime.
    Best when: budget or capacity limits mean you cannot reach all eligible units at once, and withholding support permanently would be unacceptable.
  
  
    Randomised intensities
    How: vary the dose of the intervention across units: for example, 100%, 50%, or 0% of eligible employees receive training.
    Best when: you suspect that knowledge or behaviour spreads between treated and untreated members within the same unit, and you want to measure that spread.
  
  
    Encouragement design
    How: randomise who receives extra outreach or information encouraging take-up, rather than randomising access to the intervention itself.
    Best when: the intervention cannot legally be denied to anyone who qualifies (for example, an open voucher scheme), but take-up is voluntary and varies.
  


North‑East Romania used a lottery
North-East Romania used a simple lottery. The 1,038 eligible firms were split into two equal groups of 519 by a random draw. The treatment group was invited to apply for a grant of between €15,000 and €100,000 to invest in equipment, software, or services. The firms in the comparison group were not invited to apply and thus, received no grant. Both groups were surveyed in the same way throughout the evaluation period.

Note: randomised controlled trial (RCT) design used in North-East Romania to measure impacts of digitalisation grants.

title: Step 5: how to randomise
text:
Public or private lottery?
Once you have decided to use a lottery, a second design choice arises: should the draw be conducted publicly or behind the scenes?



Public lottery


The draw takes place in front of an audience: for example, pulling applicants’ names from a hat at a public event, or livestreaming the computerised draw.
Advantage: maximises transparency and public trust. Units can see for themselves that the process was fair.
Disadvantage: once comparison units know they did not receive support, they may change their behaviour (working harder to find alternative funding, for example), which can reduce the measured difference between the groups.




Private lottery


The draw is conducted internally by the evaluation team, with full documentation but without public observation.
Advantage: comparison units do not immediately learn that they were not selected, which reduces the risk of behavioural reactions that narrow the gap between groups.
Disadvantage: the process is less visibly fair, which can make it harder to defend if challenged.




In practice, most RCT evaluations run the draw as a secure, documented, computerised procedure with a verifiable audit trail. This combines the rigour of a private draw with the accountability of one that can be independently checked afterwards.

title: Step 5: how to randomise
section: Randomising only part of the pool: a lottery around a cutoff
text:
Randomising only part of the pool: a lottery around a cutoff
In some interventions, it is not practical or desirable to randomise the entire eligible pool. A common alternative is to score all applicants on eligibility criteria, fund the top scorers outright, and reject the clear non-qualifiers outright. Only the units in the middle are randomised: those whose scores are close enough together that the difference is not meaningful.
This approach reduces the pool that is randomised, focuses the evaluation on the units where the decision is genuinely uncertain, and is easier to justify publicly than a lottery across the full range of applicants.

Keep the scoring process rules-based. Subjective assessment, even by expert panels, has been shown to introduce systematic bias. A structured scoring rubric, applied consistently, is fairer and more defensible than discretionary judgment.

title: Step 5: how to randomise
section: Testing intervention versions: multiple treatment arms
text:
Testing intervention versions: multiple treatment arms
A standard RCT compares one version of the intervention against a comparison group. But sometimes the real question is not whether the intervention works, but which design works best: grant only versus grant plus mentoring, for example, or light-touch advisory versus intensive coaching.
Multiple treatment arms allow you to test these versions against each other and against a comparison group in a single evaluation. Each group of units is randomly assigned to a different version, and results are compared across all groups at endline.
The trade-off is sample size: more arms means more groups, and the available pool must be large enough to power comparisons between each pair.

text:
When you cannot fund everyone at once: randomised phase-in
In many interventions, budget or implementation capacity means it is not possible to reach all eligible units in a single wave. A randomised phase-in turns this constraint into an advantage: units are randomly assigned to waves, and those still waiting to receive the intervention serve as the comparison group for the units already being treated.
The key advantage is that everyone eventually receives support, which makes the approach easier to justify politically and ethically. The key limitation is that there is no comparison group once the last wave has been treated, which means long-term impacts (those that take several years to emerge) cannot be measured.

Varying the dose: randomised intensities
Rather than randomising which units receive the intervention, you can randomise how much of it they receive. For example, some firms might have all eligible employees participate in a training intervention, while others have only half, and others none. Comparing results across these groups reveals not just whether the intervention works but how much of it is needed, and whether the benefits spill over to employees who were not directly treated.
