title: Step 5: how to randomise
section: When take-up is low: encouragement design
text:
When take-up is low: encouragement design
Some interventions cannot be denied to anyone who qualifies: an open advisory service or a voucher scheme, for example. In these cases, it is not possible to assign units to a comparison group that is formally excluded from support. The encouragement design offers an alternative: rather than randomising access, randomise who receives extra outreach, information, or a targeted invitation to use the intervention.
Units who receive the encouragement are then compared with those who do not. Because encouraged units are more likely to take up the intervention than non-encouraged units, the comparison still produces an estimate of the intervention’s effect, even if both groups technically had access.
The main limitation is that the estimate reflects the effect of the encouragement itself as much as the intervention. If untargeted outreach (a news story, a social media post) reaches both groups, the comparison is diluted.

Compliance is rarely perfect in either direction: some encouraged units will never take up the intervention, and some non-encouraged units will find it and engage anyway. The right approach is to compare the whole encouraged group with the whole non-encouraged group, regardless of what individual units actually did. Your evaluation team will handle this in the analysis.

title: Step 5: how to randomise
section: Did randomisation lead to comparable treatment and comparison groups?
text:
Did randomisation lead to comparable treatment and comparison groups?
Once the lottery has been conducted and the baseline survey fielded, the first analytical task is to check whether the draw actually produced two comparable groups. Even a well-designed lottery can, by chance, produce a treatment group that differs from the comparison group (e.g. on firm age, size, sector, or prior performance). A balance check compares the two groups on a set of baseline characteristics and tests whether any differences are larger than chance would produce. If the groups look similar before the intervention starts, the evaluation is on solid ground. If they do not, the analysis will need to account for the imbalance. More details on balance checks and what to do if groups are not comparable

title: Step 5: how to randomise
text:
What are potential challenges?
Even a well-designed RCT must survive contact with reality. These are the four most common problems, and what can be done about each.
Attrition. Units drop out between the baseline and the endline, e.g. because firms closed, relocated, or simply refused to participate in a survey again. If drop-out is higher in one group than the other, the two groups are no longer comparable and the impact estimate may be biased. Prevention is far easier than correction: collect multiple contact details at baseline, keep them updated during the intervention, and keep the endline survey as short as possible.
Spillovers. Comparison units benefit from the intervention indirectly: a treated supplier passes on improved products, or a treated neighbour shares what they learned in a training session. When this happens, the gap between the groups narrows and the evaluation underestimates the true effect. Spillovers are most likely in concentrated sectors or geographically tight clusters. Where the risk is high, randomising at a higher level (by region or sector cohort rather than by individual units) can contain it. If spillovers are expected, the RCT can be designed to measure them.

Romania (South-Muntenia): designing for spillovers South-Muntenia built spillovers into the design. About 900 applicant small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are grouped into roughly 100 geographic or sector clusters. Each cluster is randomly assigned a funding intensity of 0%, 33%, 66% or 100%, and firms within each cluster are then randomly selected for funding up to that share. Comparing funded and unfunded firms within a cluster measures each firm’s own return; comparing clusters with different intensities measures the spillover onto neighbours and competitors. Read the full example.

Low take-up. Some units assigned to the treatment group never use the support: they decline the grant, fail to meet the conditions, or disengage early. Low take-up dilutes the estimated effect: if only half the treatment group actually received the intervention, the impact estimate reflects a half-dose. Monitoring take-up actively during implementation, and understanding why units do not engage, is essential for interpreting what the evaluation ultimately shows.
Uneven implementation. The intervention is delivered inconsistently across units, e.g. some firms receive more advisory time, faster disbursements, or better quality support than others. This introduces noise into the treatment and makes the evaluation harder to interpret. Clear delivery protocols, regular monitoring, and a close relationship between the managing authority and the delivery team reduce this risk.

None of these problems make an RCT impossible, but all of them must be anticipated at the design stage, not discovered after the endline survey.


North‑East Romania: the intervention did not achieve full take-up
Of the 519 firms selected by lottery, only 393 (75.7%) went on to submit a full funding proposal, and 333 (64.2%) were eventually contracted.
Because of limited take-up, it is safer to report the intention-to-treat effect, comparing everyone as originally assigned, even though it understates the effect on the firms that actually took up the grant.

title: Step 5: how to randomise
section: Pre-register the RCT design before the intervention begins
text:
Pre-register the RCT design before the intervention begins
Before the intervention begins (and at the latest before any data analysis begins), the RCT design must be publicly committed to on a recognised registry. This is called pre-registration, and it is one of the most important quality controls in a rigorous RCT.
Pre-registration means publishing, in advance, the main result indicator (registries call it the primary outcome), the evaluation questions, the randomisation procedure, and the analysis plan. Once that record is time-stamped and publicly visible, no one can claim after the fact that a different learning question or indicator was always the main focus. Nor can anyone claim that a subgroup analysis was planned from the beginning when it was actually prompted by the findings. The evaluation team should lead this process, but the managing authority should confirm it has been done before approving the inception report.
For a managing authority, pre-registration also serves a protective function. It shields the evaluation team from pressure to adjust the analysis once the findings are known. And it strengthens the credibility of the findings: when a null result or an inconvenient conclusion is published, pre-registration demonstrates that it reflects reality rather than selective reporting.


AEA RCT Registry
The most widely used registry for economic and policy evaluations. Free to register. socialscienceregistry.org


RIDIE
Registry for International Development Impact Evaluations, hosted by 3ie. ridie.3ieimpact.org

text:
Step 1Step 2Step 3Step 4Step 5Step 6Step 7Step 8
A power calculation sounds technical. In practice it answers one practical question: do you have enough units to detect whether the intervention works? This page explains what drives that number, how to think about it without needing to do the maths yourself, and what to do if the answer turns out to be no.

title: Power calculations: how many units you need
text:
Summary
This page explains what a power calculation is, what goes into it, and what a managing authority needs to know to have a useful conversation with an evaluator about sample size.

title: Power calculations: how many units you need
section: The core problem: too few units and you may miss the truth
text:
The core problem: too few units and you may miss the truth
Imagine an intervention that genuinely improves firm productivity by 8% (the same logic applies to any result, such as employment or school attendance). If your evaluation includes only thirty firms, the natural variation between those firms (some were already growing fast, some were already struggling) may easily produce an 8% difference between treatment and comparison groups by chance alone. You cannot tell whether the intervention caused the difference or whether chance did. The intervention may work, but your evaluation cannot prove it.
Add more firms and the picture becomes clearer. With enough observations, the average results in the two groups settle down and genuine differences become visible. The variation that masks the signal shrinks relative to the size of the groups.



Too few units










Real impacts may go undetected: ordinary differences between units drown out the intervention’s effect.




Enough units










Real impacts become measurable: averages settle and the difference stands out.




More units do not make the lottery fairer. They make its answer visible.

title: Power calculations: how many units you need
section: What drives the required sample size?
text:
What drives the required sample size?
The number of units you need depends on two things that pull in opposite directions.



The size of the effect you want to detect


An intervention that doubles firm turnover is easy to spot even in a small group. An intervention that increases turnover by 5% requires a much larger group to detect reliably.
Small expected effect → more units needed. Large expected effect → fewer units needed.




How much units vary from each other


If all units in the target population are very similar in characteristics (e.g. same firm size, same sector, similar starting performance), a small sample is enough to pick up a difference. If units vary enormously, you need more of them to be confident that a difference reflects the intervention rather than the mix of units you happened to include.
High variation → more units needed. Low variation → fewer units needed.




Think of trying to hear a quiet voice in a noisy room. A louder voice needs no particular conditions to be heard. A quieter voice needs a quieter room, or more people listening carefully. More units are the equivalent of reducing the noise.

title: Power calculations: how many units you need
section: The four ingredients a power calculation combines
text:
The four ingredients a power calculation combines
A power calculation takes four inputs and returns a single number: the minimum sample size the evaluation needs. The evaluator handles the calculation; the managing authority needs to understand what the inputs mean so that the conversation about sample size is grounded in the intervention’s actual context.


  
  Expected effect
  
  Variation
  (standard deviation)
  
  Confidence level
  
  Statistical power
  
  
  POWER CALCULATION
  standard software does the maths
  
  
  Required sample size
  the minimum number of units
  the study needs


Here is what each ingredient means in plain language:
Expected effect. What is the smallest improvement in your main result indicator that would be meaningful enough to be worth detecting? This is a policy judgement, not a statistical one. If a 5% increase in firm research and development (R&D) spending would be considered a success, that is your expected effect. If only a 25% increase would change how the intervention is designed in the next round, use that. Evidence from similar interventions in other regions or member states can help anchor this number. The smaller the effect you want to reliably detect, the more units you will need.
Variation between units. How much do units in your target population differ from each other on the main result indicator, even before the intervention starts? This is usually estimated from existing data: a prior round of the intervention, national statistics, or a comparable survey. The evaluator will handle this, but it is worth knowing that the more heterogeneous your target population, the larger the required sample.
Confidence level. How willing are you to risk concluding that the intervention worked when it actually did not? The standard is a 5% risk, meaning the evaluation is designed so that a false positive would only arise by chance in 1 out of 20 identical studies. This does not normally need to be changed.
Statistical power. How willing are you to risk missing a real effect? The standard is 80%, meaning the evaluation has an 80% chance of detecting a genuine effect if one exists, and a 20% chance of missing it. For evaluations where a null result would have major consequences (for example, if it would be used to cancel an intervention), 90% power is preferable, but requires a larger sample.

North‑East Romania: Was 1,038 companies enough for North‑East Romania? Once the power calculation is run, you compare the required sample with the size of your eligible pool. If your pool exceeds the required sample, you are ready to randomise. If it falls short, you need to grow the pool before the draw.
In North-East Romania, the evaluation team ran the power calculation before the draw and confirmed that the pool of 1,038 firms was large enough to detect the effects they expected. This is why the draw proceeded with 519 firms in each group.

title: Power calculations: how many units you need
section: Always randomise more units than you need at endline
text:
Always randomise more units than you need at endline
The power calculation tells you how many units you need to observe at the end of the evaluation, at the endline survey. But not every unit randomised at baseline will still be reachable by then. For example, firms will have closed, relocated, or simply stopped responding. This is called attrition, and it is one of the most common threats to the validity of a randomised controlled trial (RCT).
The practical implication is straightforward: always recruit more units into the randomised pool than the power calculation requires, to leave a buffer for expected drop-out. If you need 400 units at endline and expect that roughly one in five will be unreachable by then, you need to randomise at least 500 units. The evaluation team will advise on the right buffer based on comparable studies, the expected follow-up period, and the availability of administrative data. In the EU, administrative data can often be used to keep observing units that stop responding to surveys, for example firms through tax records and business registries.

Attrition is not just a power problem. If units drop out at different rates in the treatment and comparison groups, the two groups stop being comparable and the impact estimate becomes biased. This happens, for example, if struggling firms in the comparison group are more likely to close. Step 8 covers how to detect and address this.

title: Power calculations: how many units you need
section: What if there are not enough units?
text:
What if there are not enough units?
If the power calculation reveals that your eligible pool is too small, there are six practical fixes. The right combination depends on what is driving the shortfall.

  
    Increase outreach
    More applicants mean a larger eligible pool. North-East Romania ran outreach events in more than 20 cities before the application window opened, specifically to ensure the pool would be large enough.
  
  
    Expand eligibility
    Lowering the eligibility threshold adds more units to the pool. Be careful not to expand so broadly that the evaluation no longer answers the original question: the expanded population should still be the one the intervention is designed to serve.
  
  
    Combine regions or cohorts
    If a single region or intervention round does not produce enough units, pooling two regions running similar interventions (or two consecutive cohorts) into a single evaluation can reach the required sample without changing the design.
  
  
    Run a phase-in
    Rather than running the intervention to all eligible units at once, stagger rollout across waves. Each wave that is still waiting acts as the comparison group for the waves already receiving support, doubling the effective sample without needing more units overall.
  
  
    Focus on where effects are largest
    If the expected effect is larger among a specific subgroup (e.g. younger firms, firms in a particular sector, firms with no prior R&D experience), narrowing the focus raises the detectable effect and reduces the required sample. This only makes sense if the narrowed population remains policy-relevant.
  
  
    Invest in a strong baseline
    Collecting good baseline data on the main result indicator before the intervention, and using it in the analysis, significantly reduces the sample size needed. The evaluator can explain how much this helps in your specific context; the reduction is often substantial.

title: Power calculations: how many units you need
section: A practical note for managing authorities
text:
A practical note for managing authorities
The power calculation is usually the evaluator’s job, not the managing authority’s. But the managing authority is the only party that can answer the policy question that drives the most important input: what effect would be large enough to matter?
A managing authority that can say “we would consider the intervention successful if it increased firm R&D spending by at least 15%” gives the evaluator something concrete to work with. A managing authority that leaves that question open will get a power calculation based on assumptions it may not recognise or agree with. It may end up with a required sample that is either impossibly large or so small that meaningful effects cannot be detected.

The conversation about sample size is one of the most important early conversations between the managing authority and the evaluation team. Have it before the intervention design is finalised, not after the eligible pool is already fixed.

text:
Tools for power calculations
The evaluator will run the power calculation, but free tools are available if you want to explore the numbers yourself or check the evaluator’s assumptions.

title: Step 3: determine relevant indicators
text:
Step 1Step 2Step 3Step 4Step 5Step 6Step 7Step 8
Once the ToC is in place, it becomes the blueprint for selecting indicators. Every element of the ToC (inputs, activities, outputs, short- and medium-term outcomes, goals, and assumptions) needs at least one measurable indicator to track whether things are moving as expected.
For managing authorities, some of this work is already done. Some cohesion policy programmes operate within a mandatory performance framework that includes output and result indicators set by the European Commission. These provide a useful starting point, but they are generally not sufficient for an RCT. These indicators are designed for monitoring: they show what was delivered and what changed for beneficiaries, but not whether the intervention caused that change. An evaluation therefore measures change in a way that allows comparison with a counterfactual (what would have happened without the intervention).
Indicators for evaluation purposes therefore need to go beyond the mandatory monitoring set and capture the intermediate and long-term changes described in the ToC.
The indicator that measures the result named in the primary question (Step 2) is the main result indicator (evaluators and trial registries usually call it the primary outcome). The sample size, the data collection and the analysis plan are built around it.

title: Step 3: determine relevant indicators
text:
Summary
This page covers how to move from the Theory of Change (ToC) to measurable indicators, what makes a good indicator using the SMART criteria, and where to find validated measures for a randomised controlled trial (RCT), including the indicator repository.

title: Step 3: determine relevant indicators
text:
Well-defined indicators
Good indicators share five characteristics, often summarised as SMART:







Criterion
Description




Specific
The indicator measures exactly the construct it is supposed to measure, not a proxy that is merely convenient


Measurable
The information can be reliably obtained, ideally in a numerical form that allows for comparison over time and across groups


Attributable
The indicator is sensitive to the intervention’s efforts and not so heavily influenced by external factors that changes cannot be attributed to the intervention


Realistic
The data can be obtained within the available time and budget, at a frequency that matches the evaluation timeline


Targeted
The indicator reflects results for the specific population the intervention is designed to serve

title: Step 3: determine relevant indicators
text:
Choosing indicators: where to start
Indicators rarely need to be built from scratch. Managing authorities should draw on existing, well-tested measures from comparable evaluations before designing new ones. The indicator repository draws on the EuroCOMP Lab evaluations (see Examples) and on policy reports such as the World Bank’s TIDES report. It also draws on established indicator manuals such as the OECD Oslo Manual for innovation and the OECD Frascati Manual for research and development. Drawing on these sources improves the quality of your data and makes findings easier to compare with evidence from other interventions and regions.

The indicator repository lists indicators for firm-level evaluations by topic, from firm performance and innovation to digitalisation, management practices, and energy efficiency. Each indicator comes with a plain-language definition and a metric. Use them as a starting point: pick the indicators that fit your ToC and learning questions, consult similar evaluations and reports, and adapt the indicators to your intervention.

title: Step 1: develop a Theory of Change
text:
Step 1Step 2Step 3Step 4Step 5Step 6Step 7Step 8
Before any data is collected and before any evaluation contract is signed, a managing authority needs to be clear about what the intervention is trying to achieve. It also needs to know how progress towards that goal will be measured, and what data will be needed to do so. A ToC makes this logic explicit and evaluation-ready.

title: Step 1: develop a Theory of Change
text:
Summary
This page covers what a Theory of Change (ToC) is and how it relates to the intervention logic required in cohesion policy programmes. It walks through each component of the causal chain, from inputs to goals, with examples, and explains why building one strengthens both evaluation design and policy lessons.

title: Step 1: develop a Theory of Change
section: What is a ToC, and how does it relate to your intervention logic?
text:
What is a ToC, and how does it relate to your intervention logic?
In cohesion policy programmes, managing authorities are already required to articulate an intervention logic: a structured account of how a policy instrument is expected to produce its intended results. A ToC builds on this familiar concept and makes it more explicit and evaluation-ready.
An intervention logic maps the pathway from inputs to outputs to results. A ToC adds two important elements: it specifies the assumptions that must hold at each step for the logic to work, and it makes clear which links in the chain are strong and which are uncertain. This is precisely the information a randomised controlled trial (RCT) is designed to test.
If your intervention already has a well-developed intervention logic in its programme document or partnership agreement, you have a strong starting point. The task of building a ToC is largely one of making that logic more precise, defining each step clearly enough that it can be measured.

title: Step 1: develop a Theory of Change
text:
Components of a ToC
A ToC follows a causal chain from resources invested to long-term change achieved, with assumptions sitting at every junction:


  
    
      
    
  

  
  
  
  
  
  

  
  
  INPUTS

  
  ACTIVITIES

Note: elements of a ToC.

Inputs are the resources, efforts, and actions invested in a policy. For cohesion policy programmes, inputs might include co-financing from the European Union, national co-financing, and the administrative capacity of the managing authority and intermediate bodies.

North‑East Romania: inputs

Number of staff involved in designing and implementing the digitalisation grants
Available budget to disburse digitalisation grants


Activities are the concrete actions undertaken to deliver the intervention. These are what the intervention actually does.

North‑East Romania: activities

Outreach and information campaign for potential applicants
Pre-assessment questionnaire to express interest in digitalisation grants
Call for proposals to deliver digitalisation grants


Outputs represent the direct and immediate products of the activities conducted within a policy. They are tangible and observable products or deliverables that demonstrate the completion of specific tasks. For cohesion policy programmes, these correspond closely to the output indicators that managing authorities are already required to report to the European Commission.

North‑East Romania: outputs

Digitalisation grants are awarded to selected companies


Short-term results refer to the immediate changes that occur as a direct result of the outputs. These outcomes are often related to changes in knowledge, attitudes, skills, and behaviours among the target population. Although short-term outcomes are not the intervention’s ultimate goals, they play a crucial role in achieving the larger objectives.

North‑East Romania: short-term results

Digital solution procured, installed, configured and tested
Digital solution is operationalised, used by employees, customers and others in the supply chain.​​


Medium-term results are the intermediate changes that occur due to sustained efforts and progress from short-term outcomes. These outcomes indicate progress towards the overall goal and often involve shifts in social norms, policies, or organisational practices. These correspond closely to the result indicators that cohesion policy programmes report on, though impact evaluations typically aim to go further by establishing a credible causal link between the intervention and the result.

North‑East Romania: medium-term results

Companies achieve advanced digital transformation
Improved time management and business efficiency


Impacts are a policy’s broad, long-term aspirations or objectives. They describe the ultimate impact or change that the policy aims to achieve. Goals are usually overarching and may require significant time and effort to accomplish.

North‑East Romania: impacts

Increase in sales, employment, productivity (Total Factor Productivity) and profitability
Higher resilience to economic shocks, due to the business versatility ensured though the digital solutions


Assumptions are the underlying beliefs, conditions, or factors that are considered to be true but have not yet been fully proven or tested. Assumptions may involve external factors, stakeholder behaviour, or contextual influences that must align for the theory to work as expected.

North‑East Romania: assumptions

Employees will possess, or will be able to acquire, the digital skills needed to effectively use the solution for advanced digital transformation
Companies have sufficient organisational flexibility to change internal processes
Companies have the organisational capacity
Companies’ customers and suppliers are sufficiently active in digital channels (online payments, e-commerce transactions, digital invoicing) to make adoption beneficial
Suppliers, partners, and customers will engage with and use digital links (communications, transactions, data exchange) established by companies, ensuring network effects and value creation.

title: Step 1: develop a Theory of Change
section: Why invest time in developing a ToC?
text:
Why invest time in developing a ToC?
Developing a ToC is well worth the effort for two important reasons. First, it sharpens the design of your evaluation. By mapping out the causal logic of an intervention, a ToC generates clear research questions and helps teams identify which results to measure and what data to collect.
It can be built collaboratively, starting from the intended long-term change and working backwards through the chain of events needed to get there. This process is particularly useful in a partnership context, where multiple stakeholders may have different views on how the policy is supposed to work. It also prompts a credibility check: is there actually evidence, from comparable interventions in other regions or member states, to support each step in the logic?
Second, a ToC produces richer and more transferable policy lessons. Measuring the right intermediate results reveals not just whether an intervention worked, but how and why it worked. Opening this “black box” transforms evaluation findings from a simple pass/fail verdict into actionable insight that can inform the next programming period. The knowledge gained also travels better: findings grounded in a clear causal logic are more readily applied by other managing authorities facing similar challenges in different regional contexts.

North‑East Romania: why investing time
In Romania, the World Bank supported the managing authority in developing a ToC and in applying systematic methods to quantify the managing authority’s own expectations about intervention impacts before the call launched. This exercise revealed gaps between what the intervention was designed to achieve and what its indicators actually measured. This allowed the design to be adjusted before implementation rather than after the evaluation.

title: Why and when to use a randomised controlled trial
section: What is the real impact of an intervention?
text:
What is the real impact of an intervention?
Definition. Impact is the difference between what happens after an intervention is introduced and what would have happened in its absence. What would have happened in its absence is called the counterfactual.
The dilemma. The counterfactual is a “what if” and cannot be observed. Ideally, the same participant would be observed twice, once with the intervention and once without it, and the two compared. That is impossible: each participant either takes part or does not. Every impact evaluation method is a way of approximating that missing second observation.
The solution. Impact evaluation methods differ in how they estimate the counterfactual. This page provides an overview of the main approaches and the role of RCTs among them.

Note: impact is the causal effect of the intervention: the gap between what happened with it and what would have happened in its absence.

title: Why and when to use a randomised controlled trial
section: What does impact evaluation measure exactly?
text:
What does impact evaluation measure exactly?
Monitoring tracks what an intervention delivers and how the situation of the target group develops, using output and result indicators. Impact evaluation goes one step further: it estimates how much of the change in results was caused by the intervention, by comparing what happened with the counterfactual.


Outputs
What an intervention delivers. For example, grants disbursed, participants enrolled, training sessions run.


Results
What changes for participants or the target group. For example, employment, skills, energy savings, firm growth.


Before implementation, the activities of an intervention can be mapped against the change they are expected to bring about. This mapping shows, in advance, why each step should lead to the next. That causal logic – the how and why behind each step – explains the intervention’s reason for existing. The mapping also shows what needs to be measured to test whether the expected change is actually happening.

  Inputs
  →
  Activities
  →
  Outputs
  →
  Results

But which results should be looked at exactly? An intervention can change many things, and not all of them can or should be measured. To know which results to look at, and when to expect them to change, the starting point is to spell out how the intervention is supposed to work: how its inputs and activities lead to outputs, and how those outputs are expected to lead to results.
This chain is the foundation of a theory of change, and having thought it through helps in designing a strong impact evaluation. There is more on this in Step 1: develop a Theory of Change.
Making the chain explicit also surfaces the assumptions behind each link, and shows which of them the intervention’s impact depends on most. If one of these assumptions does not hold (for example, that firms will take up the support they are offered), the intervention may fall short of its intended impact. Such weak links can be tested directly, as shown below under How can it be delivered better?

title: Why and when to use a randomised controlled trial
text:
Challenges in measuring impact
The value of an intervention lies in the change it causes: its additionality. Measuring additionality requires knowing what participants would have done without the intervention – the counterfactual.
Identifying the change an intervention has caused can be difficult when participants are not assigned at random but selected. Selected applicants may differ from those who were not selected; for example, they may be more motivated or have more resources. Most of these traits are never recorded in any database or questionnaire. When participants later do better on the results of interest than the applicants who were not selected, it is impossible to tell how much of that difference is due to the intervention.

Selection bias arises when the comparison group differs from the participants in ways that also affect results. In that case, the impact estimate is biased.

Consider an illustrative innovation-grant scheme: EUR 50,000 to each of 100 firms, where “success” means launching a new product. Compare two selection rules.



Strategy A: fund the top performers


Firms that succeed: 80 of 100
Would have succeeded anyway: 65
Succeeded because of the grant: 15
Additionality rate: 19%


Strategy A looks stronger at first glance, as it is associated with 80 successes, but only 15 of these succeeded because of the grant.




Strategy B: fund firms that need it


Firms that succeed: 55 of 100
Would have succeeded anyway: 20
Succeeded because of the grant: 35
Additionality rate: 64%


Strategy B shows fewer successes in total, but 35 of them happen because of the grant, more than twice as many as under A.



Raw success counts can be misleading: to assess effectiveness, interventions need to be judged on their impact. Which applicants to target remains a policy choice, set by the intervention’s objectives; cohesion policy may deliberately support those whose direct returns are lower, to reduce disparities. Whatever the target group, measuring additionality shows what the support actually changes.


Paying for what would have happened anyway
Support that pays for what would have happened anyway is often called deadweight. Top performers would likely have invested anyway, so public funds mostly substitute for money they would have spent regardless – generating little that is truly additional per euro.


Crediting the intervention with existing strengths
Comparing funded, stronger firms with unfunded, weaker ones credits the intervention with firms’ pre-existing quality, not with what the grant did.


Where support makes the most difference
Support changes behaviour most where it removes a real constraint: a good project that could not otherwise go ahead.


Can experts predict where support makes a difference?
Evidence suggests not reliably. In a business plan competition in Nigeria, judges’ scores did not predict which firms would survive or grow three years later (McKenzie and Sansone, 2019; see below Common questions about RCTs).

title: Why and when to use a randomised controlled trial
text:
Finding the counterfactual
The counterfactual can never be observed directly, so it has to be estimated.
Strategy. Find a group that, on average, looks like the participants would have looked without the intervention. This group is the comparison group.
Comparison groups can be formed in two ways, depending on how participants are assigned to the intervention:



Random assignment: randomised controlled trials


The comparison group is created before the intervention starts, by randomly assigning who receives it. Random assignment makes the two groups similar on average and so avoids the selection bias described above.




Non-random assignment: quasi-experimental methods


Participants are selected in another way, for example through applications, scores or eligibility rules, and the comparison group is drawn from those who did not take part. It can be identified before the intervention starts (for example, with baseline data and a known selection rule) or after it has been rolled out.

title: Why and when to use a randomised controlled trial
section: How an RCT creates a comparison group
text:
How an RCT creates a comparison group
Intuition. As explained on the home page, the intervention is assigned at random, so the treatment group and the comparison group are similar on average at the start. The comparison group’s results therefore show what would have happened to the treatment group without the intervention.

Note: treatment and comparison groups start at a similar level and diverge after the intervention starts; the gap between them is the impact of the intervention.

Because assignment is decided by chance, the two groups are similar on average, differing systematically only in whether they receive the intervention. Take applicants for a grant: randomising who receives the money means that, on average, the two groups are similar in observable characteristics such as size, sector or turnover, and also in unobservable ones such as management quality or motivation. That is why, in a well-implemented RCT, no statistical adjustment for applicant characteristics is needed to obtain a credible estimate: the difference in average results between the two groups can be interpreted as the causal effect of the intervention.

What “random” means here. Not randomly sampling a sub-population to study, but randomly deciding, among eligible applicants, who receives the intervention and who does not (or who receives another intervention).

Strengths and requirements. The Commission’s Better Regulation toolbox (Tool #68) describes randomised controlled trials as “the benchmark for scientific quantitative methods”. Their main strengths are:

They provide strong causal evidence: because assignment is random, a difference in results between the groups can be attributed to the intervention rather than to pre-existing differences
No assumptions about levels or trends between groups are needed, as long as randomisation is implemented correctly
The estimate is simple to calculate and to explain: it is the difference in average results between the groups

RCTs also have requirements. Random assignment has to be built into the selection process, usually before the intervention starts. Enough eligible participants are needed to detect an effect, and the assignment has to be respected during implementation. When an RCT may not be the right choice below discusses these further.

Running example: North‑East Romania
Throughout this site, one intervention supported by the EuroCOMP Lab illustrates these ideas in practice: a digitalisation grant scheme for micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) in North-East Romania, run by the Regional Development Agency with World Bank support.

Randomisation can support transparency and trust
When more applications are eligible than the budget can fund, a lottery among eligible applicants is a transparent way to decide who receives support. It gives every eligible applicant the same chance, and the selection rule can be explained and verified in advance.

text:
Quasi-experimental methods
When participants are not assigned at random, quasi-experimental methods estimate the counterfactual by comparing participants with non-participants under specific assumptions. They can be planned before an intervention starts – for example, around an existing scoring rule – or applied once it has been rolled out, using data that already exist. The overview below is not exhaustive: it presents some of the most common methods. The Commission’s Better Regulation toolbox (Tool #68) describes further ones, such as synthetic controls.

Quasi-experimental methods always rely on assumptions, some stronger than others. If those assumptions do not hold, the impact estimate is biased. Many of these assumptions are not testable directly, so they need to be stated and discussed. The credibility of the evaluation depends on the credibility of the assumptions made. RCTs also depend on conditions being met; see Strengths and requirements.




Pre-post (before and after)



Method

Compare participants before and after the intervention.

Identifying assumption

In the absence of the intervention, participants would have had the same measured results as before. That means no other factors or events, for example economic shocks, affect the result besides the intervention. This is a strong assumption that rarely holds in practice.



For example, sales might rise after a grant simply because the whole regional economy is recovering at the same time, not because of the intervention.

There is no difference between participants and non-participants besides participation in the intervention. The reason for participation must be unrelated to results. Again, this is unlikely to hold in practice.

Identifying assumption

Matching



Method

Participants are matched with non-participants who share the same observable characteristics. Matching tries to mimic an RCT. It can be done in different ways: a participant can be matched with one non-participant, or with a weighted average of all similar non-participants, where closer matches count more.

Identifying assumption

There are no differences between participants and matched non-participants in unobserved characteristics that affect the result.



For example, two firms matched on size and sector might still differ in the owner’s ambition or management quality, both of which would likely affect results.





Regression discontinuity design



Method

Compare participants who were just eligible with those who were just ineligible. This does not measure impact for all participants, only for those at the cut-off, which is why the estimate is called a local average treatment effect. The advantage is that unobservable characteristics stop being a concern.

Identifying assumption

the criteria determining who falls above or below are not manipulated
a large number of units sit around the cut-off
nothing else changes suddenly at the cut-off

Instrumental variables



Method

Use a variable – the instrument – that influences whether units take part in the intervention but is otherwise unrelated to the results of interest. The difference in results between units with different values of the instrument, divided by the difference in their participation rates, gives the effect of taking part for those whose participation the instrument changed. The Better Regulation toolbox (Tool #68) illustrates the approach with the Covenant of Mayors in Italy: the presence of a territorial coordinator offering technical support made municipalities more likely to join, and was assumed to be otherwise unrelated to the mayors’ re-election results (Martelli et al., 2018). A randomly assigned encouragement, such as an invitation or an information visit, can also serve as an instrument; the same logic is used in RCTs where not everyone offered support takes it up.

Identifying assumption

The instrument must clearly influence participation, and it must affect results only through participation – in the toolbox’s terms, the exclusion restriction. This condition cannot be tested and has to be argued. The estimate applies only to those whose participation was changed by the instrument, not to all participants, and data on the instrument are needed for both participants and non-participants.



For example, a local business adviser who promotes a grant may make firms more likely to apply. But if the same adviser also gives firms other help, the adviser’s presence affects results through more than the grant, and the exclusion restriction does not hold.

title: Why and when to use a randomised controlled trial
section: What can be learned from an RCT?
text:
What can be learned from an RCT?
Whether or not there is already good evidence that an intervention works, there can be a case for experimentation. The starting question is whether the intervention is working as well as it could be.



Does the intervention have an effect at all?


It is not yet known whether the intervention works, or who it reaches and how it should be designed. Answering this requires a credible comparison group, which for an RCT means randomising before the intervention launches. Example: in North-East Romania, a lottery decided which eligible firms were invited to apply for a digitalisation grant, and the others formed the comparison group (see above).




How can it be delivered better?


There is already evidence that the intervention works, and implementation may already be under way. The question is which version of the intervention works best. Example: the Digitrans pilot below compares a grant alone with a grant combined with technical assistance.



Comparing versions is also a way to address weak links in the theory of change. Where impact depends on an assumption that may not hold, for example that firms will take up the support they are offered, alternative ways of addressing it can be tested within the same evaluation.

Digitrans example The Digitrans pilot (see Examples for more details) tested and compared two alternative ways to increase digital adoption among MSMEs in Bulgaria, Poland and Slovakia. Firms were randomly assigned to either (i) a comparison group receiving no support, (ii) a financial subsidy alone, or (iii) the same subsidy paired with technical assistance.
The pilot found that money alone was not the most effective approach. Firms that also received technical assistance used digital tools 2.5 times more intensively than those with the subsidy alone. This is evidence that capability, not just cash, was a constraint to digitalisation.


North‑East Romania: testing outreach The North-East Romania intervention asked both questions. It used one experiment to find out whether the grants were effective and a second to study how best to conduct outreach. Before the digitalisation call, the regional development agency randomly selected 26 of 46 towns for in-person information visits, in which a consultant explained the call and helped firms complete the pre-assessment survey. The 26 visited towns produced 110 applications against 71 in the 20 towns without visits, about 4.2 per town against 3.6. Applicants from visited towns were also smaller firms (12.6 employees on average, compared with 19.6).


Colombia: group vs individual management support Iacovone et al. 2022 compared two ways to deliver management consulting to auto-parts firms: one-to-one (about USD 28,950 per firm) and in groups of 3–8 firms (about USD 10,500). Both raised management scores by around 9 percentage points, but only group consulting significantly raised sales and profits.

title: Why and when to use a randomised controlled trial
section: When an RCT may not be the right choice
text:
When an RCT may not be the right choice


01

Not the right tool
The question is excellent but is not about impact, for example satisfaction with services or cost per service. Monitoring and feedback data are easier and do not need a counterfactual.



02

Not yet
The theory of change is not clear, or implementation is unlikely to work because key conditions, such as functioning markets or delivery capacity, are not yet in place.



03

Statistically not feasible
Too few units or too little money. Large indirect or spillover effects that cannot be measured. (Spillovers alone are not a reason to drop an RCT: if expected, they can be designed for and measured; see Step 5: how to randomise.) Support that has to reach all eligible recipients at once, for example emergency aid after a natural disaster. Treatment assigned at too high a level, for example regional policy.



04

Maybe not worth it for learning
The answer is already known from credible existing studies, or there is no generalisable “why” because the intervention is one-off with little scale or replication potential.



If an RCT is the right tool in principle, Step 4: check whether an RCT is feasible checks whether it is feasible in practice: oversubscription, timing, legal basis, institutional buy-in and measurable results.

section: Learning through RCTs is a continuous process
text:
Learning through RCTs is a continuous process
Every RCT raises new questions along with the ones it answers, each round building on the last. That is how knowledge of what works, for whom and under what conditions grows, and how it feeds into better interventions. Exchange within a community of practice matters, so that managing authorities learn from each other, not just from their own findings.
But before adopting what worked elsewhere, questions of external validity need to be considered, as what worked in one place may not necessarily work in another. The key question is whether the conditions are comparable: is the target group similar, and are the conditions essential to that effect actually in place in the new setting?

Review Before considering how to embed an RCT, review the intervention’s theory of change, identify risks and the learning questions this round should answer, and the results most likely to change. Review lessons from other settings and countries and adapt them. Identify baseline needs of potential beneficiaries in the region.


Design Choose a credible comparison group and set the sample size needed to detect a meaningful effect. Turn the results identified in Review into measurable indicators using primary and secondary data, and set out the data collection plan, budget and timeline in terms of reference.


Test Test different intervention designs and delivery modes to identify what works best. Assess for whom the intervention works best. Address take-up challenges. Learn about mechanisms, unintended effects and crowding out.


Invest Get a quantitative and credible impact estimate that can guide future investments. Conduct cost-benefit analyses to avoid wasting money and to inform funding decisions. Scale up based on evidence.

title: Why and when to use a randomised controlled trial
text:
Common questions about RCTs



Are RCTs only for academics?

No. The basic idea is simple: who receives the intervention is decided by chance, like a coin toss, so the treatment and comparison groups are similar on average. The impact estimate is then the difference in average results between the two groups, which is straightforward to explain to non-specialists.
Designing and running an RCT does require careful planning and some technical support, for example for sample size calculations and for running the random draw – as do other rigorous evaluation methods, which in turn need their assumptions checked. With that support in place, RCTs are transparent and relatively easy to communicate.



Is random assignment allowed under EU rules, and does it contradict selection on merit?

Random assignment is allowed and can be a fair way to select among equally eligible applicants. The Directorate-General for Regional and Urban Policy (DG REGIO) has formally confirmed that randomisation is permissible under EU cohesion policy rules (for more information, see A legal basis for random selection).
Random assignment does not replace selection on merit but can supplement it. To illustrate this, imagine a two-stage process in which all applicants are first assessed against the call’s eligibility and quality criteria as usual. In the second stage, only those who pass enter the draw. Expert panels still decide who is eligible, but they do not rank or choose among equally eligible applicants. Interventions can also be designed to fund the strongest applicants outright and randomise only within a middle band of scores, as was done in Extremadura.
Randomisation is already used to select beneficiaries across Europe. Managing authorities and agencies in Spain, Czechia, Croatia and Romania have used random assignment to allocate EU-funded support, as has the European Commission itself for SME energy-efficiency grants across 34 countries, and interventions in Bulgaria and Poland are preparing to do the same (see Examples).



Why are RCTs often called the gold standard?

Because they provide robust causal evidence. Random assignment makes the treatment and comparison groups similar on average, in characteristics that can be measured as well as in those that cannot, so a difference in results between the groups can be attributed to the intervention rather than to pre-existing differences. No assumptions about how the groups would otherwise have evolved, such as parallel trends, are needed, as long as randomisation is implemented correctly. And the estimate is simple to calculate and to explain: it is the difference in average results between the groups. The Commission’s Better Regulation toolbox (Tool #68) accordingly describes randomised controlled trials as “the benchmark for scientific quantitative methods”.
This does not make an RCT the right choice in every case. It has to be feasible, ethical and well implemented, and some questions are better answered with other methods.



Are RCTs more expensive than other rigorous methods?

Randomisation is an allocation rule. It determines who is assigned to an intervention and who is not, but says nothing about how results are measured afterwards. Measuring results (for example, employment, energy savings or firm turnover) requires data, which costs money and takes time – not just for RCTs but for whichever evaluation method is used. RCTs usually plan a baseline survey from the design stage; with a large enough sample they do not strictly need one, though collecting one is good practice. Where results are already recorded in administrative registers, the cost of an RCT is similar to that of any other rigorous evaluation: legal and GDPR clearance to access and link the registers, and analytical time.
RCTs do come with additional staffing costs. Unlike a method applied retrospectively to data that already exists, randomisation must be run and monitored while the intervention is ongoing, so the managing authority needs staff assigned to it on an ongoing basis.



Can RCTs show why an intervention works?

Only to the extent that the design allows. A standard RCT shows whether an intervention made a difference, not through which channels. Specific pathways can be tested with a multi-arm design: participants are randomised across several treatment arms that receive different components or combinations of components (for example, a grant alone versus a grant combined with business advisory support), and results are compared across arms. Data on intermediate results and qualitative methods, such as interviews with participants, can help explain the mechanisms behind an estimated effect.



What exactly does an RCT measure?

The effect of whatever was randomised – most commonly, being assigned to (or offered) an intervention. That is why it matters to get the learning questions right at the design stage. To separate the effect of one component from another, those components need to be randomised separately too, for example through a multi-arm design.



Do RCT findings apply beyond the study population?

Every empirical method faces the question of whether findings hold beyond the sample they were estimated on, so external validity is not a concern unique to randomisation. A single RCT cannot show whether an intervention will work everywhere, but it can show a lot about the conditions under which it worked in that case. When a similar intervention is designed elsewhere, it is possible to assess how similar those conditions are and judge how far the original findings are likely to apply. The more similar RCTs are run across different regions and countries, the more confidently general conclusions can be drawn.



Can RCTs deliver findings within a programming period?

A staggered or phased roll-out combined with an RCT can be a source of continuous learning. Early waves of participants already generate short-term results while later waves are still being enrolled, so a managing authority can see early signals – take-up, engagement, first movements in results – well before the intervention is fully rolled out, and adjust design or targeting for later waves accordingly. Long-term results can, by construction, only be observed after a few years, which may come too late to change the current programming period. But similar interventions are likely to follow, in the same region or elsewhere in the EU, so knowing whether an intervention achieved its intended effect still helps allocate future funding more efficiently.



Do RCTs assume everyone responds the same way?

No. The effects an RCT most commonly measures – the average treatment effect or the intention-to-treat effect – compare average results between the treatment and comparison groups. Neither assumes that every member of these groups responds identically, only that the average difference is a meaningful summary of the intervention’s impact. With a large enough sample, effects can also be analysed by subgroup. Administrative registers often already record the characteristics on which effects may differ (for example, size, sector or region), which makes it relatively cheap to check whether an intervention works differently for different groups.



Is further analysis needed after randomisation?

Yes. If sample sizes are large enough and treatment is assigned randomly, the treatment and comparison groups will be similar on average – not that every participant has an identical match in the other group, only that characteristics balance on average. Good practice is to check this balance on observable characteristics at baseline, before the intervention starts. In practice, participants also do not always stay in the group they were originally assigned to. This happens when randomisation is on assignment to an intervention rather than on take-up: the assigned and non-assigned groups remain comparable, but those who actually participate may differ from those who do not. In this case, what is reported is the intention-to-treat effect – the average effect of being assigned to the intervention, rather than of participating in it.



How large does the sample need to be?

Detecting a given effect with confidence needs enough observations in each group – the smaller the expected effect, the larger the sample must be. This is why power calculations are carried out at the design stage.
A power calculation needs a few inputs: the smallest effect that would still be meaningful to detect, how much the result already varies across participants before the intervention runs, expected take-up of the intervention (as this affects the effective size of the treatment group), how much loss of observations to expect over time and whether assignment happens at the level of the individual applicant or of a group they belong to. Assigning by group generally needs a larger total sample to reach the same precision.
See Power calculations, part of Step 4, for a walkthrough of turning these inputs into an actual sample size calculation.



Is it difficult to get responses from the comparison group?

It can be, so it is worth planning for at the design stage. Often, though, results of interest are already captured in administrative registers rather than collected through a survey, so comparison group response rates are not a concern.
If data on results need to be collected through surveys, a group that received nothing may feel less invested in answering than a group that participated. Looking across dozens of studies, World Bank economist David McKenzie found that differential attrition between treatment and comparison groups averages only a few percentage points. The gap widens mainly when the treatment is large and highly visible, such as a sizeable cash grant. Examples on this site show both cases. In Extremadura, there was no evidence of selective attrition in follow-up survey responses. In the European Commission’s SME energy-efficiency grants, firms offered a grant of up to EUR 10,000 answered follow-up surveys far more often than the comparison group (91% against 65%), so the estimates rely on statistical corrections for who responded. Sustained follow-up – repeat calls, alternative contact channels, incentives for non-respondents – can help close such gaps, as in Czechia.



Is it unethical to have a comparison group?

Not necessarily. Where the budget does not allow all eligible applicants to be funded, some are turned away whatever the evaluation method; randomisation only determines how the available funds are allocated, giving every equally eligible applicant the same chance. Where funds would allow a wider roll-out, starting with part of the eligible population can still be justified if the aim is to learn whether the intervention works before scaling it up – for example through a phased roll-out in which the comparison group receives support later. Other ways of choosing among equally eligible applicants are not necessarily more accurate: in a business plan competition in Nigeria, expert judges’ scores had no relationship with which businesses went on to survive, hire staff or turn a profit three years later (McKenzie and Sansone, 2019).
Nor does a comparison group have to mean receiving nothing at all: RCTs can compare two different versions of an intervention, so every participant receives some form of support and the question becomes which version works better. What matters is that participants are properly informed about the study, their rights and how any data on them are processed and stored – which is why RCTs are often reviewed beforehand by a research ethics committee (an Institutional Review Board, or IRB, in some countries), which is also the body participants can turn to with complaints.



Do RCTs require ethical clearance?

Not always. Whether ethics review is legally mandatory depends on the country, the institution running the study, the type of intervention and whether personal data are involved. For example, an RCT studying an intervention’s effect on firms using administrative data to measure results often does not require ethical clearance. Seeking it anyway is still recommended: a research ethics committee helps ensure that participants are properly informed, that data handling complies with GDPR and that there is a body participants can turn to with complaints.

title: How to design a randomised controlled trial
text:
This page covers the internal team to assemble before starting, and eight sequential steps for designing a credible randomised controlled trial (RCT): Theory of Change (ToC), learning questions, indicators, feasibility, randomisation, data sources, data collection, and data quality.
A well-designed RCT does not begin with randomisation. It begins with a clear understanding of what an intervention is trying to achieve and why. The eight steps below set out the preparatory work that makes randomisation meaningful and the findings credible. They are numbered in a logical order, but their work overlaps in practice, and most of it is done before the first call for applications is launched.
Examples on these pages involve firms, because the EuroCOMP Lab’s experiments have so far focused on business support. The same steps apply to any intervention, whether it reaches people, households, schools, municipalities or other units.
The timeline below shows when the work of each step usually happens. Everything up to the random draw has to be in place before the intervention starts, which is what makes the comparison between the two groups valid.

title: How to design a randomised controlled trial
section: Eight steps for designing an RCT successfully
text:
Eight steps for designing an RCT successfully


Before you start: assemble your internal evaluation team
Identify who inside the managing authority will take on each role before working through the eight steps.


Step 1: develop a Theory of Change
Map the causal logic of your intervention, from inputs to long-term goals, and make the assumptions explicit.


Step 2: define learning questions
Formulate the specific questions the evaluation is designed to answer, grounded in the ToC.


Step 3: determine relevant indicators
Select the indicators that will be used to measure change at each level of the ToC.

Tool: Indicator repository



Step 4: check whether an RCT is feasible
Check whether the conditions for a valid RCT are in place: oversubscription, timing, legal basis, and political buy-in.

Choose a randomisation design, from a simple lottery to a phase-in or an encouragement design, decide how the draw is run, and pre-register the design before the intervention begins.

Step 6: identify available data sources
Decide whether to rely on primary data, administrative data, or a combination, and map what is already available.


Step 7: collect data

title: How to design a randomised controlled trial
section: Before you start: assemble your internal evaluation team
text:
Before you start: assemble your internal evaluation team
The managing authority brings knowledge that no outside expert can replicate: how the intervention works in practice, who the target beneficiaries are, what the political constraints are, and what a meaningful result would look like. External consultants and data collection firms are available to provide methodological and operational support, and many managing authorities will choose to work with them. But whether the RCT is implemented with external support or largely in-house, a core internal team needs to be in place from the start. Without it, key decisions get made by default rather than by design, and the evaluation risks being shaped by what is convenient rather than what matters.
Before working through the eight steps, identify who inside the managing authority will take on each of the following roles:


An evaluation focal point
The person who leads the process, coordinates across the other roles, and serves as the primary contact for the external evaluation team. Ideally someone with some familiarity with impact evaluation methods, or who has been through the EuroCOMP Lab training.


A project manager
Someone with detailed knowledge of the intervention: eligibility criteria, selection process, implementation timeline, and the population of applicants. This is the person who can answer the policy questions that drive the evaluation design, particularly what effect size would be meaningful and what the intervention is realistically expected to achieve.


Where possible, it is also helpful to involve:


A legal or procurement officer
Involved early, to confirm that the national legal framework permits randomisation and to manage the procurement process.


A data protection officer
To ensure that data-sharing agreements and General Data Protection Regulation compliance are in place before fieldwork begins.



The internal team does not need to be large: in smaller managing authorities, one or two people may cover several roles. What matters is that the responsibilities are clearly assigned and that the evaluation focal point has the authority to make decisions and the access to intervention information they need.
Where internal capacity or methodological expertise is limited, external experts can be hired to support evaluation design, data collection, or both.

title: Step 2: define learning questions
text:
Summary
This page covers why learning questions must come first, what makes a good learning question, the four types of question (primary, heterogeneity, mechanism, and implementation), and how to link them to the Theory of Change (ToC).

title: Step 2: define learning questions
text:
Why evaluation questions come first
The ToC developed in Step 1 sets out the causal logic of the intervention. Evaluation questions translate that logic into a concrete analytical agenda: they specify which links in the causal chain will be tested, which results will be measured, and what the evaluation can credibly claim to have shown at the end.
Getting this step right matters more than it might appear. Vague or poorly scoped evaluation questions lead to data collection that is too broad, analysis that is unfocused, and findings that cannot be clearly attributed to the intervention. Conversely, well-formulated questions make every subsequent decision easier: they tell you which indicators to select (Step 3), which data sources to prioritise (Step 6), and what the evaluation team will need to deliver.

title: Step 2: define learning questions
section: What makes a good learning question?
text:
What makes a good learning question?
A well-formulated learning question has four characteristics:
Specific. It names the intervention, the target population, the result of interest, and the time horizon. Generic questions such as “did the intervention work?” are not answerable. A specific question might be: does receiving a research and development (R&D) grant increase a firm’s total R&D expenditure within two years of the award?
Causal. For a randomised controlled trial (RCT), the central question is always about causation, not correlation. The question should be framed in terms of the effect of the intervention, not merely whether change occurred. This means the question implicitly requires a comparison: between supported units and comparable units that did not receive support.
Answerable. The question must be answerable with the data and methods available. An evaluation that asks about 10-year productivity effects but only has a two-year window will not be able to answer its own primary question. Scope questions to what the evaluation can credibly deliver.
Decided in advance. Evaluation questions must be set before data collection begins, not after. Questions formulated after seeing the data are prone to selective reporting and undermine the credibility of the findings. Pre-registration on a public registry (see Step 5) locks in the questions publicly before any findings are seen.

title: Step 2: define learning questions
text:
Types of learning questions
A well-structured evaluation typically includes a primary question and a set of secondary questions. These serve different purposes and should be clearly distinguished.
The primary question focuses on the main effect of the intervention on the most important result. This is the question the evaluation is powered to answer: the sample size and data collection plan are designed around it. For most competitiveness and innovation interventions, the primary question concerns a key result such as R&D expenditure, product innovation, or labour productivity.

North‑East Romania: primary question
Does receiving a digitalisation grant increases business performance (e.g. sales) and productivity?

Heterogeneity questions ask whether effects differ across subgroups, for example by size, sector, location or prior experience with public support. These questions are important for understanding for whom the intervention works best and informing targeting decisions in future programming rounds.

North‑East Romania: heterogeneity question
How do impacts of receiving a digitalisation grant vary across firm size, location, sector, and initial level of digitalisation?

Mechanism questions probe how the intervention produces its effects: which links in the ToC are activated. By measuring intermediate results, these questions open the “black box” and generate richer policy lessons than a simple estimate of the final effect.

North‑East Romania: mechanism question
Does the digitalisation grant increase investments in digitalisation and technology adoption?

Implementation questions assess whether the intervention was delivered as intended and what barriers affected take-up or compliance. These are particularly important for interpreting null results: an evaluation that finds no effect needs to establish whether the intervention was actually delivered.

North‑East Romania: implementation question
What share of companies in the treatment group, that were invited to apply, were actually contracted?

title: Step 2: define learning questions
section: Linking learning questions to the ToC
text:
Linking learning questions to the ToC
Every learning question should map to a specific link in the ToC. A useful discipline is to write out the ToC and, for each arrow connecting two levels, ask: do we have a question that tests this link? If a link is left untested, either the evaluation is under-powered to examine it, or the link is assumed to hold without evidence.

title: Step 2: define learning questions
text:
Scoping and realism
Evaluation questions must be scoped to what the evaluation can credibly deliver. Two common pitfalls are worth flagging:
Over-ambition. An evaluation that promises to answer questions about long-term productivity effects, regional spillovers, and mechanisms simultaneously may not be powered to answer any of them well. Prioritise the primary question and be selective about secondary questions.
Attribution. Learning questions should be scoped to what can be attributed to the intervention, not to broader trends. If a question asks whether firms in the region became more innovative, the answer will reflect macroeconomic conditions and parallel policies as much as the intervention itself. A well-scoped causal question asks about the difference between the treatment and comparison groups, not about levels.
