text:
Step 1Step 2Step 3Step 4Step 5Step 6Step 7Step 8
By this point you have mapped your intervention’s causal logic, defined what you want to find out, and chosen the indicators you will use to measure it. The question this step answers is whether you can actually run a randomised evaluation to get those answers. How to design it follows in Step 5.
An RCT is not always possible. Before investing time and resources in a randomised design, a managing authority needs to check whether the basic conditions are in place, and whether enough units will take part.

title: Step 4: check whether an RCT is feasible
text:
Summary
This page covers five feasibility conditions that must be in place before committing to a randomised controlled trial (RCT), why randomisation must be designed in from the start, and how to reach enough units for a credible evaluation.

title: Step 4: check whether an RCT is feasible
section: Five conditions for a feasible RCT
text:
Five conditions for a feasible RCT
Work through these five questions before committing to a randomised design. If the answer to the first three is not yes, an RCT is unlikely to be feasible and you should explore alternative approaches with your evaluation team.


1. Is the intervention oversubscribed?
An RCT requires more eligible applicants than available funding slots. If you can support everyone who qualifies, there is no basis for a lottery, and no credible comparison group. Oversubscription is the single most important precondition.


2. Is there enough time?
Randomisation must happen before the first grant is awarded. If the intervention has already launched, it is too late. Planning must ideally begin at the intervention design stage.


3. Is there a legal basis?
Most national frameworks were designed around ranking or first-come-first-served selection and say nothing about random assignment. Explicit permission, either in existing regulations or through an intervention-specific instrument, must be confirmed before proceeding.


4. Is there political and institutional buy-in?
An RCT requires sustained commitment from the managing authority and any intermediate bodies involved in delivery. If key stakeholders are not on board, or if political changes could interrupt the evaluation midway, the investment may not be recoverable.


5. Can the results actually be measured?
The indicators selected in Step 3 must be observable through administrative records, a survey, or both. If the main result indicator cannot be reliably measured for both treatment and comparison groups, the evaluation will not produce credible findings even if the design is sound.



Is randomisation permitted under your national legal framework?
Before designing the lottery or scoring mechanism, confirm that your national legal framework, and the specific legislation governing your intervention, either explicitly permits randomisation as a selection method or is flexible enough to accommodate it.
Most national frameworks were designed around ranking or first-come-first-served selection and say nothing about random assignment. A clear legal basis is the precondition for experimental evaluation to happen at all. See the legal framework page for country examples, key legal elements, and practical steps.

title: Step 4: check whether an RCT is feasible
section: Randomisation must be designed in from the start
text:
Randomisation must be designed in from the start
The most common mistake is treating randomisation as something that can be added once the intervention is already running. It cannot. By the time the first grant is awarded, the comparison group must already be defined, the eligibility rules must be locked in, and the baseline data should have been collected.

North‑East Romania: building the eligibility pool

  OutreachSocial media, radio, and events in 20+ cities
  Online applicationsAbout one hour to complete
  Automatic screeningStops as soon as a criterion fails
  1,038 eligible firmsScreened from over 1,500 applicants by September 2023

North-East Romania combined three steps that are usually separate (application, eligibility check, and baseline data collection) into a single online survey. This meant that by the time the eligibility pool was confirmed, the baseline data was already in hand. In October 2023, 519 of the 1,038 eligible firms were randomly selected to receive a grant. The other 519 became the comparison group.

title: Step 4: check whether an RCT is feasible
text:
Do you have enough units?
To detect the impact of an intervention, you need enough units in both the treatment and comparison groups. Too few units and even a real effect may be invisible: ordinary variation between units drowns out the signal. The technical term for this is statistical power, but the practical question is simple: is your eligible pool large enough?
The answer depends on how large an effect you expect, how much units vary on the main result indicator, and how confident you want to be in the findings. An evaluator will run a power calculation to translate these inputs into a minimum required sample. More details on power calculations
Lessons from EuroCOMP Lab projects point to several ways of reaching large enough numbers.



Invest heavily in outreach, especially to reach new beneficiaries

Standard outreach channels might fail to reach the units that the interventions are designed to serve. It is therefore worth investing in outreach and in testing different outreach approaches. Measuring which ones work can significantly expand the eligible pool and improve the quality of applications.
For interventions targeted to firms, standard outreach channels (newsletters, social media posts, agency websites) consistently fail to reach the firms that the interventions are designed to serve. Firms without prior experience of EU funding, smaller firms, and firms in rural or remote areas are systematically less likely to apply. This is not because they are ineligible, but because they do not know the intervention exists or lack the resources to navigate the application process. In this case, effective outreach might require direct, personalised engagement: in-person events, road trips to municipalities, collaboration with mayors and local business associations, and hands-on application support.

North‑East Romania
In North-East Romania, the World Bank randomised outreach activities across 46 cities, selecting 26 for road-trips where a consultant explained the call and helped firms complete the pre-assessment survey. The 26 cities that received road-trips produced 110 applications, against 71 in the 20 cities that did not: about 4.2 per city against 3.6. Applications from road-trip cities also came from significantly smaller firms (12.6 employees on average, compared to 19.6 in comparison cities). Compared to previous calls, the total number of applicants tripled and the number of eligible firms more than doubled. This small experiment demonstrated both the effectiveness of in-person mobilisation and the value of embedding experimentation into intervention implementation.




Eligibility criteria should remain broad enough

Eligibility criteria should not be so restrictive that too few units qualify, but they should remain specific enough to identify the units with the highest potential to benefit. Linking the criteria to the intervention’s Theory of Change keeps the wrong units out of the pool.

Romania (South-Muntenia)
In South-Muntenia (Romania), the World Bank found that eligibility criteria for an innovation support intervention were quite restrictive given the region’s firm landscape. The World Bank worked with the managing authority to adjust the criteria to target a higher number of firms.




Base intervention design on evidence of need

Interventions that are designed without a prior assessment of beneficiary needs frequently suffer from misalignment: either too few units apply (under-subscription), or the intervention attracts units that are not its intended target. Both problems are expensive, leading to repeated calls, unused funds, or support that reaches units that would have done well without it.
A baseline needs assessment, conducted before the intervention launches, allows the managing authority to understand the regional landscape, calibrate grant sizes and eligibility thresholds, and anticipate demand more accurately. Where uncertainty about demand remains, piloting different intervention elements before full-scale rollout can reduce the risk of costly mismatches.

Italy
In Italy, a minibond intervention pre-identified 289 eligible firms, of which only 30 applied: a hit rate of 10.3%. Of the 19 firms that ultimately issued a minibond, most had access to alternative financing and may not have needed the intervention at all. A prior needs assessment could have revealed that the intervention’s terms were less attractive than alternative instruments already available in the region, including zero-interest loans and non-repayable grants from earlier interventions. The design could then have been adjusted before launch.




Simplify the application process

Complex, document-heavy application processes disproportionately burden units that are least familiar with EU funding: the very units that interventions are often designed to reach. For example, when compliance requirements are similar regardless of grant size, small firms face the same administrative burden as large ones, often pushing them to hire consultants and creating a market for intermediaries that adds cost without adding value.
Application requirements should be proportionate to the amount of funding requested. Processes should be fully digital, integrated with existing administrative databases wherever possible, and capable of providing real-time eligibility feedback so that units can assess their likelihood of success before investing significant time in an application.

North‑East Romania
In Romania, the pre-assessment survey was designed to do three jobs at once, in approximately 40 minutes. It collected baseline data for the evaluation, assessed firm eligibility in real time, and gave firms enough information to decide whether to proceed. Survey responses were automatically cross-referenced with official firm data, enabling instant verification of core eligibility criteria. Firms that did not meet the requirements were informed immediately, saving them from investing further time in a formal application that would have been rejected.
Eligible firms received individualised benchmark reports comparing their digitalisation levels to similar firms in their region, providing added value to participants whether or not they were eventually selected.




Use the application process to exchange information

The application process is usually treated as a one-way flow of information, with applicants submitting data to the managing authority. In practice, it can also deliver useful information and tools back to applicants. Doing so can make applicants more engaged during the process and help selected units make better decisions about which activities to prioritise. It can also improve the experience of units that are not selected, who are more likely to view the process positively even without being selected.
For interventions targeted to firms, the application process can raise awareness of a specific topic (e.g. digitalisation, innovation, energy efficiency). It can also help firms identify investment needs and provide benchmarks that inform business decisions, whether or not the firm is selected for support.

Croatia
In the Scinergy pilot in Croatia, the World Bank supported an extensive outreach and information campaign. It included a dedicated project website, a LinkedIn campaign with paid promotions, appearances in television and online media, presentations at industry events and scientific institutions, and webinars targeting thousands of firms. The campaign was structured around a business-science matchmaking concept, providing firms with substantive information about how to collaborate with research institutions, not just how to apply for a grant. The initiative attracted widespread media coverage and generated strong interest in applications well before the call officially opened.

title: A legal basis for random selection
text:
Step 1Step 2Step 3Step 4Step 5Step 6Step 7Step 8
For a managing authority to use randomisation as part of its beneficiary selection process, the legal framework governing that intervention must either explicitly permit it or be flexible enough to accommodate it without ambiguity. Most national frameworks were designed around two conventional selection methods (ranking proposals by score, or first-come-first-served) and say nothing about random assignment. A clear legal basis is the precondition for experimental evaluation to happen at all.
Given the strict European regulatory framework, Member States needed assurance that randomisation was permissible under EU cohesion policy funding. The European Commission’s Directorate-General for Regional and Urban Policy (DG REGIO) issued letters confirming that RCTs are allowable under EU cohesion policy rules and emphasising the need for counterfactual approaches to estimate causal impacts. These letters were instrumental in encouraging the cultural change needed to adopt experimental evaluation methods.
The key regulatory anchor is Article 44 of the Common Provisions Regulation (EU) 2021/1060, which requires managing authorities to evaluate the effectiveness of their interventions but does not prescribe the method. This leaves room for RCTs as one of the methods managing authorities can choose.

title: A legal basis for random selection
text:
Summary
This page covers the legal preconditions for using randomisation under European Union (EU) cohesion policy and the key elements any national legal framework must address. Country examples from Spain and France show how randomised controlled trials (RCTs) have been embedded in law.

title: A legal basis for random selection
section: Key elements any legal framework must address
text:
Key elements any legal framework must address
Regardless of the legislative level (national law, implementing regulation, or intervention-specific instrument), the following elements should be covered.

Explicit permission to randomise, with a two-stage process. Randomisation must be framed as applying after eligibility assessment, not instead of it. Stage 1 assesses all applicants against pre-defined competence-based criteria. Stage 2 randomly assigns equally eligible applicants to treatment and control groups. This makes clear that the lottery does not replace merit-based selection: it determines who among equally deserving applicants receives support when the intervention is oversubscribed.
Conditions for use. The legal text should specify when randomisation is permissible. There must be a clear research question, measurable results, genuine oversubscription, and a sufficient sample size confirmed by a power analysis. There must also be a pre-registered evaluation protocol and informed consent from all applicants at the point of application.
Transparency and documentation. The randomisation algorithm, software, and results of the draw must be documented, stored, and publicly communicated. Notarial certification of the draw is recommended. All applicants, selected and non-selected, must be told whether they were selected and why.
Protection of the control group. Non-selected eligible applicants must retain the right to apply to future calls. Providing equivalent support to control group members through parallel instruments during the evaluation period should be avoided wherever possible, to prevent contamination.
Role of expert panels. Expert evaluation panels assess eligibility in Stage 1. Their role ends once the eligible pool is defined. The randomised algorithm determines selection from that point: panels do not rank or choose among eligible applicants.
Data access and independence. The evaluation must be conducted by an independent team. Data-sharing agreements with administrative data holders (tax authorities, business registries) must be in place before the evaluation begins, with General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) compliance addressed explicitly.

title: A legal basis for random selection
text:
Country examples

Spain: royal decrees as legal foundation
Spain provides the most developed example of embedding RCTs in a national legal framework for public funding. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the Spanish government established its Inclusion Policy Lab as part of the Minimum Income Scheme and Social Shield policy. The lab ran 32 RCTs with €200 million in funding, partnering with leading researchers and institutions, including Nobel laureate Abhijit Banerjee and J-PAL Europe, the European office of the Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab. Evaluated interventions, including personalised employment services for the homeless and digital skills training, showed significant improvements in employment rates and life satisfaction.
The legal foundation was provided by two royal decrees: Royal Decree 938/2021 (Real Decreto 938/2021, de 26 de octubre) and Royal Decree 378/2022 (Real Decreto 378/2022, de 17 de mayo). They funded the pilots under Spain’s Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan and required each one to include an impact evaluation using an RCT. The decrees outlined the responsibilities of subsidy recipients participating in pilot evaluations, mandated coordination with beneficiary entities, and promoted evidence-based policymaking, transparency, and accountability as explicit legal objectives.
In July 2024, Spain’s Supreme Court annulled Royal Decree 378/2022 after a challenge by Castilla y León, a region that had been left out of the grants. As reported, the ruling concerned how the grants were allocated between regions, not the use of RCTs.
Two factors were critical to the Spanish success. First, the initiative was framed as a social investment rather than an administrative requirement. This framing secured the political backing needed to pass the legislation and maintain it through a change of government. Second, when the May 2023 elections brought a new administration, a Memorandum of Understanding signed between the World Bank and the regional government of Extremadura prior to the elections ensured continuity in the evaluation process. The MoU covered technical advice on evaluation design, scoring mechanisms, randomisation of applicant selection, and independent outsourcing of the evaluation to prevent political influence.


France: constitutional amendment as enabling legislation
France adopted a higher-level approach, embedding the right to conduct policy experiments directly in the 2003 constitutional amendment, which added provisions under Articles 37-1 and 72 of the French Constitution allowing local and national authorities to run policy experiments. This constitutional foundation enabled 300 policy experiments by 2019, including the Youth Policy Lab (€150 million in public funding, supported by economists Esther Duflo and Marc Gurgand), which led directly to legislative reforms in education and health insurance.

title: Balance checks: are the groups comparable?
text:
Step 1Step 2Step 3Step 4Step 5Step 6Step 7Step 8
A randomised lottery is designed to produce two groups, treatment and comparison, that look alike before the intervention starts. This comparability is the foundation on which the entire evaluation rests. If the groups are similar at baseline, any difference in results at endline can be attributed to the intervention. If they are not, that attribution falls apart.
This page explains what balance means in practice, how to verify it, and what to do when the groups turn out to be different on some characteristic, because no lottery produces perfect balance every time.

title: Balance checks: are the groups comparable?
text:
Summary
This page explains what balance means, why it matters, how to check it, and what to do if the groups turn out not to be comparable after the lottery.

title: Balance checks: are the groups comparable?
text:
Why comparability matters so much
The logic of a randomised controlled trial (RCT) is simple: take two groups of similar units, give one group the intervention and withhold it from the other, then compare results. The comparison is only meaningful if the two groups were genuinely similar to begin with. For example, if the treatment group happened to contain more high-performing firms before the intervention started, any difference in results at endline may simply reflect that head start rather than the intervention’s effect.
Randomisation is the mechanism that makes comparability likely, but it does not guarantee it, especially with smaller samples. A random draw can, by chance, produce a treatment group that is slightly different (e.g. older, larger, or more export-oriented firms) from the comparison group. With enough units, these chance differences average out. With fewer units, they can be large enough to matter.
This is why the balance check is one of the first things an evaluator does after the baseline survey is complete. It is not a formality: it is a quality control on the randomisation itself.

title: Balance checks: are the groups comparable?
text:
What a balance check involves
A balance check compares the two groups on a set of characteristics measured at baseline, before the intervention has begun and before either group knows whether they have been selected. For firm-level evaluations, these characteristics typically include:

Firm size (number of employees, in full-time equivalents)
Firm age (years since establishment)
Revenue or turnover
Sector or industry classification
Prior research and development (R&D) or innovation activity
Export participation
The result indicators themselves, above all the main one, measured before the intervention

For interventions that reach people, typical characteristics include age, gender, education, employment status and income, plus the baseline values of the result indicators.
For each characteristic, the evaluator calculates the average value in the treatment group and the average value in the comparison group, and tests whether the difference between them is larger than you would expect by chance from a random draw.

title: Balance checks: are the groups comparable?
section: How to read the balance table
text:
How to read the balance table
The evaluator will present the balance check as a table showing the average value of each characteristic in each group, the difference between them, and a statistical test of whether that difference is larger than chance would produce. The result of that test is usually expressed as a p-value.



What the table typically shows


In a well-executed randomisation with a reasonably large sample, most characteristics will show no statistically significant difference between the groups. The few that do are usually the result of chance: out of twenty variables tested, you would expect one to appear imbalanced simply because of how probability works, even in a perfectly conducted lottery.




What raises a concern


A concern arises when many variables show imbalance simultaneously, or when the main result indicator itself differs significantly at baseline. This suggests the randomisation may have been compromised, perhaps because some units were selectively excluded, or because the draw was not conducted as described.




One or two imbalanced variables in a balance table is almost always chance. Imbalance on many variables, or on the main result indicator, is a signal worth investigating.

title: Balance checks: are the groups comparable?
section: What to do if the groups are not perfectly balanced
text:
What to do if the groups are not perfectly balanced
Perfect balance is the goal, not a guarantee. When the balance check reveals a meaningful difference on one or more characteristics, there are two main responses. Importantly, neither involves re-running the lottery.
Control for the imbalanced variable in the analysis. The most common and appropriate response is to include the imbalanced characteristic as a control variable in the statistical model used to estimate the intervention’s impact. This adjusts the comparison to account for the pre-existing difference, producing a more accurate estimate of the intervention’s effect. The evaluator handles this. The managing authority simply needs to know that it is standard practice, not a workaround.
Do not re-randomise. Once units know their assignment, or once the intervention has begun, re-running the lottery is not an option. It would undermine the integrity of the design and the trust of participants. If a significant imbalance is discovered before the intervention launches and before units have been notified, the evaluation team should be consulted immediately. In rare cases, a new draw may be possible, but this is the exception.

Never drop units from the analysis because they appear to be outliers or because their inclusion makes the findings less clean. Dropping units selectively, even for apparently good reasons, can introduce bias and undermines the integrity of the evaluation.

title: Step 7: collect data
text:
Step 1Step 2Step 3Step 4Step 5Step 6Step 7Step 8
Step 6 determined where the data will come from. This step is about how and when to collect it. For most randomised controlled trial (RCT) evaluations of competitiveness interventions, this means planning at least one round of primary survey data collection: a baseline before the intervention. It also means coordinating access to the administrative data sources identified in Step 6. Whether a primary follow-up survey (midline/endline survey) is also needed depends on the availability of administrative data, as described below.

title: Step 7: collect data
text:
Summary
This page covers when and how many data collection rounds to plan, why surveys are used, which method to choose, and who to collect from. It also covers the role of external data collection firms, how to design and pilot the questionnaire, how to minimise attrition, and General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) compliance requirements.

title: Step 7: collect data
text:
Plan the data collection rounds
An RCT evaluation requires data at multiple points in time. The exact rounds depend on the Theory of Change (ToC) and the data sources available.
Baseline survey: conducted before the intervention begins and might be used as the basis for randomising units into treatment and comparison groups. It captures pre-treatment characteristics, enables balance checks after randomisation, and provides the benchmark against which post-intervention results are compared. It must be completed before randomisation is revealed. A baseline primary survey is almost always needed, since administrative data rarely contains the intermediate results and mechanism variables required by the evaluation.

North‑East Romania: baseline survey
A baseline survey (pre-application data) was administered: the primary objective of the baseline survey was to conduct an initial evaluation of the business’s digital tool requirements and help determine their intervention eligibility. The survey questions covered topics such as firm location, sector, financial considerations (e.g. profits, capital, assets, liabilities), and legal prerequisites. The survey required approximately an hour to complete and was completed online by each firm between June and the end of September 2023.

Follow-up survey: collects data from units after the intervention has started, to measure results once effects can realistically be expected to have materialised.
Follow-up rounds are usually named by their position in time. A follow-up conducted while effects are still unfolding is called a midline. It typically captures shorter-term results. The final follow-up, conducted when longer-term effects can be expected, is called the endline. The rounds to include depend on when the ToC expects effects to emerge and on the evaluation questions, bearing in mind that each additional round adds cost and respondent burden and can increase attrition. For example, in an evaluation of business support, a midline might capture changes in management practices or technology adoption, while the endline might capture changes in turnover, employment, or productivity.
In the European Union (EU) context, a dedicated follow-up survey is not always necessary. Administrative data, consistently available across member states, can cover many of the core results indicators without placing any additional burden on participants. Where administrative data provides sufficient time, unit, and indicator coverage, it could be considered as the main data source for follow-up. For example, for firms, administrative records typically include turnover, employment, exports, and labor costs.
A primary follow-up survey, at midline or endline, becomes necessary when the evaluation requires results or mechanisms that administrative records do not contain. For example, in an evaluation of business support, these might include management practices, innovation behaviour, digital technology adoption, or respondent-reported perceptions of the intervention.

North‑East Romania: follow-up data collection
A follow-up survey was administered: the 1,038 firms surveyed at baseline were contacted for a follow-up survey conducted between March and May 2025. Interviews took approximately 60 minutes to complete and covered nine key topics:

general administrative details about the business
background information on the business manager
an overview of the business
details on products/services, market presence, revenue, and customers
the use of telecommunications and internet across business locations
relevant digital indicators for the business
methods and processes used for routine business operations
key factors influencing technology adoption, such as investments and management decisions
financial information for the business in 2024


Administrative data timing: access to administrative records should be requested and negotiated well in advance of the baseline. These sources typically come with a reporting lag of one to two years, which must be factored into the evaluation timeline. The advantage is coverage: administrative data tracks all units in the sample, including those who do not respond to surveys, making it a more complete picture of results than a survey endline alone.
In the EU, the consistent availability of administrative data means that a primary follow-up survey can often be avoided. Prioritise administrative data for core financial and employment results; reserve primary survey rounds for the results and mechanisms that only participants themselves can report on.

title: Step 7: collect data
text:
Why surveys?
Surveys are the most widely used tool for collecting primary data in impact evaluations of public support interventions. They make it possible to gather structured, comparable information directly from the units that an intervention is designed to benefit, capturing precisely the results and mechanisms that administrative records do not contain.
A particular strength of surveys is their scalability. Rather than collecting information from every single unit in a target population, a well-designed survey can be conducted on a carefully selected subset: a sample. Provided that sample is representative, the findings can be generalised with confidence to the full population.
Evaluations of business support often measure competitiveness and innovation results, such as changes in firm-level Research and Development (R&D) investment, technology adoption, or management practices. For these, surveys are often the only way to capture the intermediate results that sit between a grant payment and a long-term productivity gain visible in national statistics. They are also essential for understanding why an intervention worked or did not, by measuring the mechanisms that link the intervention’s activities to its results.

title: Step 7: collect data
text:
Paper vs. electronic surveys
While paper-based surveys remain in use in some contexts, electronic surveys are the clear standard for evaluations today and should be the default choice. Digital surveys offer built-in data validation (mandatory fields, range checks, and logical skip patterns), catching errors at the point of entry rather than during analysis. They eliminate manual transcription entirely, are faster to deploy, easier to monitor in real time, and simpler to adapt if pilot testing reveals problems.

title: Step 7: collect data
text:
Choose a collection method
There is no single best method. The right choice depends on who the respondents are, what the questions require, and the available budget. Three methods are in common use:
Computer-Assisted Telephone Interviewing (CATI) involves trained interviewers conducting structured surveys over the phone. CATI reaches a broad range of respondents quickly and is well-suited when response rates need to be actively managed: interviewers can follow up with non-respondents and clarify questions in real time. It is also practical when beneficiary contact details are already held in project management systems. Surveys must be kept short enough to hold respondents’ attention on the phone.
Computer-Assisted Personal Interviewing (CAPI) takes the form of face-to-face interviews conducted with a tablet or laptop loaded with survey software. The personal interaction tends to produce more nuanced and accurate answers, particularly on sensitive topics such as firm finances or employment decisions. CAPI is best reserved for complex questionnaires and small, geographically concentrated samples: it is the most expensive method and carries a risk that the interviewer’s presence influences responses.
Web surveys are sent to respondents via email or embedded in an online platform, inviting them to complete the survey at their own pace. They are the least expensive method and can be deployed quickly to large samples, making them well-suited to digitally comfortable populations such as small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and technology firms. Response rates for unsolicited web surveys are often low, so active follow-up is essential.
In practice, methods can be combined: begin with a web survey, follow up with CATI for non-respondents, and use CAPI selectively for subgroups where richer detail is needed.

North‑East Romania: primary respondents
Data in North-East Romania was collected using a web survey (baseline survey) and involved CAPI and CATI methods for the follow-up survey, depending on respondents’ availability.

title: Step 7: collect data
section: Who to collect from, and when
text:
Who to collect from, and when
Choosing the right respondent. In surveys of people, participants usually answer for themselves. For firm-level surveys, the ideal respondent is a senior decision-maker, such as the Chief Executive Officer (CEO), Chief Financial Officer (CFO), or equivalent, who has oversight of the firm’s strategic and financial decisions. The respondent should ideally be the same person at baseline and endline to ensure that differences reflect real changes rather than differences between respondents. Where the intervention targets a specific group within the firm, such as R&D personnel, those individuals may be more appropriate for certain questions.

North‑East Romania: primary respondents
The primary respondents were CEOs and/or firm owners, with additional input from senior representatives of relevant departments when necessary.

Timing within the year and the day. Choose survey timing that fits when respondents are actually available, both within the year and within the day. Avoid periods when people are away or under pressure, offer a choice of times, and allow respondents to reschedule or to complete the survey in more than one sitting. Be mindful of survey fatigue: respondents who are contacted repeatedly for monitoring and reporting purposes may become less willing to participate over time.
For firms, surveys are best conducted during standard working hours, but offer a choice of times, for example early morning, lunchtime, or late afternoon. A respondent can also start the survey at one point and finish it on another day. Within the year, August might be a poor time to survey firms in most European countries due to summer holidays. The end of the financial year is also problematic, as finance teams are occupied with closing accounts.

title: Step 7: collect data
section: The role of data collection firms and evaluation consultants
text:
The role of data collection firms and evaluation consultants
Managing authorities can implement RCTs in-house including conducting surveys and data analysis. However, implementing RCTs comes with many specificities and challenges. The technical expertise needed can be contracted in. Having the right expert team on board makes all the difference.
What managing authorities need is a well-crafted Terms of Reference (ToR): the document that attracts the right teams, sets the methodological bar, and defines the conditions for a credible, policy-relevant evaluation. A strong ToR is therefore not a procurement formality: it is the managing authority’s most important contribution to the quality of the evaluation. For more on ToRs, see Writing terms of reference for an RCT.
The division of responsibilities between the managing authority, the evaluation consultant and/or the data collection firm should be made explicit in procurement. Close collaboration is key for a successfully conducted RCT.
Depending on which activities the managing authorities conduct in-house, the evaluation consultant or data collection firm supports or conducts the following activities:

designing the survey instrument
translating and piloting the questionnaire
determining the sample
setting up the digital survey platform
recruiting and training enumerators
managing fieldwork
monitoring response rates
implementing quality controls
delivering a clean dataset
carrying out the statistical analysis once data has been collected


North‑East Romania: primary respondents
The survey implementation was undertaken by a team of 30 enumerators hired by Romanian-based data collection firms.

title: Step 7: collect data
text:
Designing the questionnaire

Start with what already exists
Before writing a single question, review existing, validated survey instruments. Using questions that have already been tested in comparable evaluations and surveys saves time, improves data quality, and makes findings comparable with evidence from other interventions and regions. For firm-level surveys, key reference sources include:

Community Innovation Survey (CIS): the standard EU framework for measuring innovation activity in firms
Firm Adoption of Technology (FAT) Survey: World Bank instrument on technology adoption across sectors
World Bank Enterprise Surveys (WBES): firm-level data on investment, productivity, and the business environment
World Management Survey (WMS): management practices across firms and countries
Flash Eurobarometer on SME Digitalisation: digital technology adoption and skills across EU member states
ECB Survey on Access to Finance of Enterprises (SAFE): financing conditions and constraints for SMEs


The survey question repository collects questions from the firm-level surveys listed above, organised by topic, from company details and financial performance to innovation, digitalisation, and management practices. Use them as a starting point: pick the questions that match your indicators, consult similar evaluations and underlying survey instruments, and adapt the questions to your intervention.
Browse the survey question repository



Questionnaire design
A good questionnaire is clear, concise, and purposeful. Every question should map to an indicator in the ToC. Questions included for general interest add respondent burden without adding analytical value and should be removed.
Questions should address only one idea at a time. Double-barrelled questions, which ask about two things simultaneously (such as “Did the grant improve your firm’s R&D capacity and export performance?”), make it impossible for respondents to give an accurate answer and should always be avoided. Wording should be neutral: leading questions undermine the reliability of the data.
Response scales, such as Likert scales or numerical ratings, should be consistent across the questionnaire and clearly labelled. Questions should flow in a logical sequence, moving from general topics to more specific ones. Sensitive questions, such as those about turnover, profitability, or employment figures, are best placed towards the end, once some rapport has been established.
Questions that ask about quantities, values, or periods of time should always specify the unit and reference period explicitly. State the currency (e.g. €), the unit of magnitude (e.g. full-time equivalents, thousands of euros), and the exact time reference (e.g. “in the last financial year, ending [month]”) directly in the question text or as a visible instruction above the response field.
Where surveys are conducted in multiple languages, the questionnaire should be professionally translated and then back-translated to verify that meaning has been preserved accurately.


Piloting the questionnaire
No questionnaire should go into the field without first being tested. A pilot survey is conducted with a small group representative of the target population. It reveals problems invisible on paper: ambiguous wording, questions that take too long to answer, response options that do not cover the full range of experiences, and technical glitches in digital forms. The questionnaire should be revised based on pilot findings before full deployment. Skipping the pilot almost always costs more in the long run through lower data quality and analytical workarounds.

title: Step 7: collect data
text:
Minimising attrition
Attrition (units that cannot be reached or refuse to take part at follow-up) is one of the most common threats to the validity of an RCT. Even modest attrition becomes a serious problem if it is higher in one group than the other, since differential attrition can bias the impact estimates. Prevention is far easier than correction, and the groundwork must be laid at baseline.
Collect robust contact information at baseline. Record multiple contact points for each participant: the primary respondent’s name, direct phone number, and email; a backup contact; and a postal address (for firms, also the website). Ask respondents explicitly for permission to follow up at in subsequent survey rounds and to contact them via alternative channels if the primary contact changes.
Maintain a tracking database throughout the intervention period. Do not wait until the follow-up survey to discover that contact details have gone stale. Update the database periodically using public registries, project monitoring data, and any contact made for compliance or monitoring purposes.
Make re-contact as easy as possible at follow-up. Send advance notices before the follow-up fieldwork begins. Use the same survey mode as the baseline where possible, as familiarity reduces refusal rates. Keep the follow-up survey as short as the evaluation objectives allow: respondent fatigue is a leading cause of non-response in follow-up rounds.
Document and report all non-response. Record the reason for every non-response using standardised codes (refused; could not be reached; closed or moved away; no longer eligible). This documentation is essential for the attrition analysis in Step 8.

title: Step 7: collect data
text:
Data protection and GDPR compliance
For EU managing authorities, compliance with the GDPR is a legal obligation that applies to any data collection exercise involving personal data. Before any survey goes into the field, the following must be in place:

A clear legal basis for processing personal data, typically the performance of a task carried out in the public interest, such as evaluating public spending (GDPR Article 6(1)(e)), or the explicit consent of respondents
An informed consent process: respondents must be told how their data will be used, how long it will be retained, and who will have access, before they agree to participate. More information on informed consent
Anonymisation or pseudonymisation of responses wherever possible
Appropriate data security measures, including restricted access to identifiable data

Managing authorities should involve their Data Protection Officer or the responsible person within the organization early in the design process: not as a final approval step, but as part of initial planning. Data sharing agreements with third-party survey firms or external evaluators must address GDPR requirements explicitly.

text:
Step 1Step 2Step 3Step 4Step 5Step 6Step 7Step 8
Data collection for an RCT often involves collecting sensible data from participants who have a right to know what that data will be used for, who will have access to it, and what their choices are. Informed consent is the mechanism through which those rights are exercised. Getting it right is a legal requirement under GDPR and a precondition for ethical evaluation practice.
The GDPR is the central legal reference for any collection of personal data in the EU, and its requirements should be consulted carefully when designing the consent form and the wider data-handling arrangements. This page offers practical guidance, not legal advice. The applicable legal bases and national rules depend on the intervention and the member state, so involve your Data Protection Officer or another responbible person from the start and consider bringing in legal consultants to review the consent form and any data-sharing agreements.

title: Informed consent in RCT data collection
text:
Summary
This page explains what informed consent means in a European Union (EU) randomised controlled trial (RCT) and what a consent form must contain. It also covers how to handle the distinction between mandatory and voluntary participation, and how to ensure General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) compliance throughout.

title: Informed consent in RCT data collection
section: What informed consent means in this context
text:
What informed consent means in this context
Informed consent is a participant’s freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous agreement to the processing of their data for a defined purpose. In the context of an RCT, it covers two distinct activities that must be kept clearly separate:
Intervention participation: applying for a grant, entering an eligibility process, and being subject to randomised selection. This is governed by the legal basis for the intervention, not by consent. Applicants cannot meaningfully consent to or refuse the administrative processing that is required to run the intervention.
Evaluation data collection: providing information for research purposes beyond what is required for the intervention: extended administrative data tracking, AI-assisted data quality checks, or follow-up interviews. This is where genuine informed consent applies. Participants must be able to choose whether to take part in each optional activity without any consequence for their intervention eligibility.

Never bundle consent to evaluation data collection with consent to intervention participation. Applicants who must tick a consent box to submit an application are not giving free consent: they are being coerced. Under the GDPR, consent is not freely given if participation in an intervention is conditional on agreeing to data processing that is not necessary for that intervention.

title: Informed consent in RCT data collection
section: What a consent form must contain
text:
What a consent form must contain
A consent form for RCT data collection should cover the following elements.

1. Identity and purpose
State clearly who is conducting the research, who the data controller is, and what the evaluation is designed to find out. Name and provide contact details for:

The managing authority (data controller and primary contact)
Any research partners with access to the data (e.g. World Bank, university)
The Data Protection Officer of each data-processing party

The purpose statement should be broad enough to cover the full range of anticipated uses, including future policy reports and academic publications, without being so vague that participants cannot understand what they are agreeing to.

Illustrarive example
“This survey is being conducted by the [NAME OF AGENCY] and it’s [NAME OF PARTNER(S)]. The goal of the evaluation study is to assess the effectiveness of innovation grants on the creation of successful innovation projects by small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and SMEs’ business outcomes and competitiveness.”



2. What data will be collected and why
Describe each category of data that will be collected, clearly distinguishing between:


Mandatory data
Required for intervention administration and collected under a legal basis other than consent.


Optional data
Collected solely for research purposes and requiring explicit consent.


For each optional category, explain what it is, why it is useful to the research, and what happens if the participant declines.


3. The randomisation
Explain clearly that the evaluation uses a randomised design: all eligible applicants have an equal chance of being assigned to the treatment group (offered the support) or the comparison group (not offered it). Participants must understand this before they enter the process. The explanation should be plain and non-technical.

Illustrarive example
“To achieve a rigorous and unbiased evaluation, the selection of eligible firms invited to submit a formal application is randomised. Information from this form will be used to establish a baseline list of eligible firms. A random sample will then be assigned to the treatment group (invited to fill out the formal application) and the remaining firms will be assigned to the control group (not invited to formally apply).”



4. Who will have access to the data
Name every party that will have access to the data, in what capacity, and under what safeguards. If data will be transferred outside the European Union (for example, to the World Bank as an international organisation), state this explicitly. Specify the transfer mechanism: Standard Contractual Clauses, an adequacy decision, or the organisation’s own data protection framework.


5. How long data will be retained
State the retention period for each category of data. For extended administrative data tracking, such as access to tax and registry records, the retention period specified from the date of submission should be long enough.


6. Confidentiality and anonymisation
Explain how the data will be protected and confirm that no individual unit (e.g. firm or person) can be identified from published results. Publications, reports, and academic studies must present findings exclusively in aggregate, anonymised, or statistical form.


7. Voluntary participation and the right to withdraw
State explicitly that:

Participation in optional data collection activities is voluntary
Declining or withdrawing consent carries no penalty and does not affect intervention eligibility
Withdrawal of consent can be exercised at any time, in writing, and does not affect the lawfulness of processing that already took place
Upon withdrawal, the participant may also request deletion of their data



8. Participant rights under GDPR
Inform participants of their rights: access to stored data (including a free copy), rectification of inaccurate data, data portability, restriction of processing, and the right to lodge a complaint with the national supervisory authority. Provide the contact details of both the managing authority’s Data Protection Officer and the relevant national supervisory authority.


9. Duration of participation and follow-up
State how long the initial form will take and whether participants may be contacted for follow-up purposes. Where follow-up surveys or subsequent evaluation rounds are planned, participants should know at baseline that they may be contacted again and for how long this may continue.


10. Signature and confirmation
The form must be signed by the participant or, for a firm, by an authorised representative: founder, owner, Chief Executive Officer, or other legal representative. Record the signatory’s first and last name, and obtain a signature (electronic or physical). Confirm that the choices were made freely and without coercion.

title: Informed consent in RCT data collection
section: Structuring the consent: mandatory core and optional modules
text:
Structuring the consent: mandatory core and optional modules
A best practice is to structure the consent document as a short checklist of distinct processing activities, each with its own tick box. This makes the mandatory/optional distinction visible and enforceable, and creates a clear audit trail of what each participant agreed to.
Example:

  
    Box 1: Randomised intervention participation (required)
    Covers participation in the evaluation study, acknowledgement of the randomised selection methodology, data sharing with partners (e.g. for monitoring and research purposes), and consent to be contacted for follow-up questions for up to six years. This box is required to proceed with the application.
  
  
    Box 2: Direct institutional access to transactional data (optional, but important for evaluation quality)
    Authorises the managing authority (and its partners) to access historical, current, and future firm data from national fiscal and corporate registries, including tax authority, trade registry, and the Ministry of Finance. Valid for up to ten years from form submission.
  
  
    Box 3: Document quality control via secure AI tools (optional, but important for evaluation quality)
    Permits the use of secure AI tools to cross-check the consistency of submitted textual descriptions and financial statements (such as balance sheets). The AI tools do not retain or store data; all information remains under the sole control of the survey provider.
  


Box 1 is required. Boxes 2 and 3 are optional but described as important for the quality of the evaluation. Participants must be able to tick Box 1 without ticking Boxes 2 or 3, and the intervention must function correctly regardless of which optional boxes are selected.

title: Informed consent in RCT data collection
text:
Special considerations for EU RCTs
Ethical approval. For research involving human subjects, including firm-level surveys, it is recommended to seek ethical approval from an Institutional Review Board (IRB) or equivalent body. Managing authorities working with a university or international research partner should confirm that ethical approval has been obtained and that the consent form has been reviewed as part of that process.
Data transfers to international organisations. If the research partner is based outside the EU, the data transfer must be covered by an appropriate GDPR mechanism. Each partner might process personal data under its own institutional Privacy Policy. This must be stated in the consent form and in the data-sharing agreement between the managing authority and the research partner.
Control group consent. Participants in the comparison group are also research subjects: they are surveyed, tracked in administrative data, and their data are used in the analysis. They must receive the same information notice and consent form as the treatment group. The only difference is that they are not offered the support.
Plain language. The consent form will be read by participants (for firms, owners and managers), not lawyers. Legal citations are required for completeness but must be accompanied by plain-language explanations.
Multilingual forms. Where the intervention operates in a non-English-speaking member state, the consent form should be available in the local language.

title: Examples of RCTs in public interventions
text:
Spain: financial support to innovate

Extremadura, SpainBin-ranking RCT56 firms in the middle band2024–2025



The problem
Market failures keep research and development (R&D) investment in Extremadura below its optimal level. Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the region under-invest in innovation, particularly in agriculture and the ecological transition.


What was done
The Regional Government of Extremadura (JUNTA) and the Extremadura Science and Technology Park Foundation (FUNDECYT-PCTEx) created an EU-funded matching grant scheme for small and medium firms.
Each cycle awards EUR 3.5 million in grants, up to EUR 250,000 per firm (EUR 138,000 on average), financing 35% to 80% of a firm’s proposed R&D investment.



What experimentation sought to answer

“What is the impact of R&D grants on SMEs’ business performance?”



The intervention

  The interventionMatching grants of up to EUR 250,000 per firm (average EUR 138,000) for R&D projects
  WhereExtremadura, Spain; regional government (JUNTA) with FUNDECYT-PCTEx, EU-funded
  Who is randomisedFirms: SME applicants, mainly agriculture and ecological transition, scored on 11 criteria
  The designBin-ranking RCT: the middle bin randomised, 22 funded vs. 34 not funded
  Outcomes trackedPrivate R&D investment, implementation success, expected sales growth
  Starting pointMarket failures keep regional R&D investment below its optimal level



Key steps and dates


ApplicationsDeadline May 2024

→

External scoringJul–Oct 2024

→

Middle-bin lotteryDec 2024

→

R&D grantsAwarded Dec 2024

→

Follow-up surveyMar–Apr 2025




How the intervention was tested
Extremadura ran an advertising campaign to attract at least 100 applicants. External reviewers scored every application on 11 objective criteria and grouped proposals into low, medium and high quality.


  Quality score

  
  High quality
  accepted and funded automatically

  
  Medium quality: 56 firms
  equally eligible, randomised by lottery
  22 funded · 34 not funded
  this band is the sample for study

  
  Low quality
  rejected automatically

  
  
  Only the middle band is randomised
  The strongest/weakest applicants
  are accepted/rejected automatically

  This design works well when eligibility criteria are clear and resources are limited.

Note: Extremadura's bin-ranking design: only medium-quality applicants, the bin where expected returns are least certain, are randomised.


Why this design. Strength: it leverages investment-return uncertainty for applications with unclear returns. Limitation: it requires a large sample size in the middle range.

Randomisation successfully balanced key firm characteristics: the comparison group and the treatment group looked the same on average. There was no evidence of firms with certain characteristics dropping out of the study more than others (selective attrition) in follow-up survey responses.


What the intervention achieved
Three months after receiving the grant, firms in the treatment group reported higher planned R&D investment and stronger confidence in their projects than the comparison group.


+48%
More planned R&D investment for 2025
EUR 65,000 above the comparison-group average.


67%
Probability of successful implementation
Up from 16% without funding, according to expert priors.


×2
Expected sales growth, conditional on success
From 8% to 16% after receiving the grant, according to expert priors.



Over half of the comparison-group firms planned to continue their R&D projects using other funding or their own resources. Public R&D subsidies can significantly boost private investment, but careful targeting is needed to avoid simply displacing money firms would have spent anyway.

title: Examples of RCTs in public interventions
text:
Czechia (Moravian-Silesian): scientific decision-making for entrepreneurs

Moravian-Silesian region, CzechiaSimple lottery246 firms2024–2026



The problem
The Moravian-Silesian region is moving away from an economy built on coal mining and heavy industry. Despite a relatively educated population and considerable public support, it has long had one of the lowest rates of active entrepreneurship in Czechia.
World Bank fieldwork found two constraints. Ability: entrepreneurs had strong technical skills but struggled to validate a business model, understand customers and test their assumptions. Ambition: many could start a business but struggled to win more customers and grow.


What was done
In September 2022, the European Commission approved the Just Transition Programme (JTP): EUR 1.641 billion for Czech coal regions, including vouchers of up to EUR 21,100 for business development, EUR 42,200 for innovation and EUR 21,100 for digital transformation.
The World Bank and the Moravian-Silesian Innovation Centre (MSIC) designed Smart Start to complement these vouchers with skills support. Across seven workshops, entrepreneurs worked on the Business Model Canvas, customer journeys, business hypotheses, customer interviews and testing a minimum viable product, ending with a pitch.



What experimentation sought to answer

“Can building business capabilities and a more experimental, evidence-based mindset improve business decisions, customer acquisition and firm performance?”



The intervention

  The interventionSmart Start: seven 3-hour workshops on scientific decision-making, plus individual consultations and feedback from trainers and peers
  WhereOstrava, Moravian-Silesian region; Just Transition Programme with MSIC
  Who is randomisedFirms: 246 interested entrepreneurs, voucher applicants and others from the region
  The designSimple lottery with unequal shares: 163 invited to the training vs. 83 with no support
  Outcomes trackedLearning and mindset, business changes, motivations for change, sales, profits and employment
  Starting pointOne of the lowest rates of active entrepreneurship in Czechia



Key steps and dates

  Diagnostic and design2022–2023
  →
  Outreach in two batchesJan–Aug 2024
  →
  Random selection
  →
  Seven workshopsSep–Nov 2024
  →
  Midline surveyNov–Dec 2024
  →
  Endline surveyJul–Sep 2026



How the intervention was tested
Smart Start was first meant only for firms applying for Just Transition vouchers. When the voucher scheme was delayed, the team widened recruitment to entrepreneurs across the region through advertising, networks and social media. Firms were therefore recruited in two batches: voucher applicants and an extra sample from the general public.
Eligible firms that completed a baseline survey were randomly assigned within each batch: about two in three were invited to Smart Start and the rest formed the comparison group.


  
  246
  interested firms

  

  
  RANDOM SELECTION
  same chance for every firm

  
  

  
  163 invited (~2/3)
  Smart Start workshops

  
  83 no support (~1/3)
  comparison group

Note: The 246 firms were randomly assigned within each recruitment batch (voucher applicants and an extra sample from the general public); comparison firms did not receive any intervention during the study period.


Why this design. Strength: demand exceeded the places available, so a lottery gave every eligible applicant an equal and transparent chance instead of a subjective selection. Inviting two in three let more entrepreneurs receive support while keeping a comparison group large enough for causal evaluation. Limitation: not every invited firm took part, so the study reports both the effect of being offered the intervention (intention to treat) and the effect on firms that actually attended.

Of the 163 invited firms, 81% attended at least one session and about 60% completed the training. About 70% of firms answered the midline survey (120 invited and 52 comparison firms), and their baseline characteristics remained balanced between the two groups.
Implementation brought several challenges:

Recruitment was resource-intensive. Voucher applicants could be contacted directly, but the extra sample needed advertising and outreach. The first round took about eight weeks; lessons from it shortened later rounds.
Entrepreneurs had little time. Many found it hard to set aside several hours for repeated sessions, and some more advanced voucher applicants saw less value in the training.
Floods. Severe flooding in September 2024 disrupted the planned start of several groups and forced rapid rescheduling. The training was nevertheless completed.
Noisy financial data. Self-reported sales and profits are noisy for small, young firms, so the midline used paper and online questionnaires, incentives for non-respondents and direct follow-up by the field team.


What worked in practice: plain Czech and concrete business benefits rather than academic terms; active outreach (applications dropped sharply when promotion stopped); peer recommendations and testimonials; repeated feedback and practical assignments; and personalised feedback from trainers, which entrepreneurs valued most.



What the intervention achieved
At midline, Smart Start had changed how firms went to market and raised their sales, and entrepreneurs linked these changes to what they had learned in the training.


+47%
Go-to-market change intensity
Change intensity was 47% higher than in the comparison group, and 42% of invited firms made moderate or larger changes, for example to customer targeting and sales channels, versus 19% of comparison firms.


+98%
Training-related reasons for change
Invited firms cited 2.10 training-related reasons for their business changes on average, versus 1.06 in the comparison group.


+64%
Monthly sales
CZK 103,325 above the comparison-group average of CZK 160,271. Effects were larger among firms that actually attended.



There was no significant effect yet on profits or on internal production and operations management. Firms may have been investing in customer acquisition and growth, so profits may take longer to show, but this is an interpretation, not a demonstrated mechanism. Results were measured soon after the training, rely on self-reported financial data and come from one post-industrial region.

Smart Start cost about EUR 450 per participating company to deliver. Because the curriculum now exists and partners can use their own facilities, this could fall to around EUR 250 when scaled through local partners.


What happened next

Smart Selling (June 2025 – February 2026): a second course on turning customer understanding into systematic sales, covering sales funnels, customer acquisition and retention, direct selling, objection handling, CRM and sales targets, through six one-to-one sessions and a workshop.
Access for the comparison group: firms left out by the lottery were offered the training in September–October 2026.
Continued delivery: MSIC is set to deliver Smart Start to five groups in 2027, with financing close to being secured.

Croatia, national programmeSimple lottery210 firms2023–2025



The problem

Matched firms and scientists took part in a two-day matchmaking event in February 2024: “speed-dating” sessions followed by joint workshops, plus legal and communication support to help pairs plan R&D projects together.

text:
Romania (North-East): financial support to digitalise

North-East region, RomaniaLottery with encouragement to apply1,038 firms2023–2025



The problem
Romanian SMEs lag behind the EU average in digital performance. Key barriers to digital transformation include a lack of financing, awareness, and capacity to capitalise on digital investments.
Among the 1,038 likely eligible firms in North-East Romania, firms met 4.3 of 12 digital indicators on average, and 67% named lack of finance as their main obstacle.


What was done
The North-East Regional Development Agency (RDA) offers non-refundable grants of EUR 15,000 to 100,000 for digital tools, equipment and services, covering 90% of eligible project costs. The first call had EUR 31 million: EUR 26.35 million from the European Regional Development Fund and EUR 4.65 million from the state budget.
The RDA and the World Bank formed a learning partnership, announced publicly at the launch of the grant scheme. The first call was non-competitive and framed as a pilot to generate learning.



What experimentation sought to answer

“What is the impact of digitalisation support on Romanian SMEs’ performance?”



The intervention

  The interventionNon-refundable grants of EUR 15,000–100,000 for digital tools, equipment and services, covering 90% of eligible costs
  WhereNorth-East Romania; North-East Regional Development Agency (RDA), co-funded by EU cohesion policy
  Who is randomised1,038 likely eligible SMEs, identified by a pre-assessment survey from over 1,500 applicants
  The designLottery among pre-identified applicants, with encouragement to apply: 519 selected and invited to apply vs. 519 not selected
  Outcomes trackedDigital investments, use of digital tools, firm performance
  Starting pointFirms met 4.3 of 12 digital indicators on average; 67% named lack of finance as their main obstacle



Key steps and dates

  Pre-assessment surveyMay–Sep 2023
  →
  Lottery before a notaryOct 2023
  →
  Full proposalsMostly by end of winter 2024
  →
  Contracts signedMar 2024–Mar 2025
  →
  Follow-up survey



How the intervention was tested
Firms first completed a pre-assessment survey that assessed their digital maturity, recorded their interest in applying and gave them an automated, simplified check of their eligibility. Piloted in May 2023 and closed in September 2023, it identified 1,038 likely eligible SMEs from over 1,500 applicants. In October 2023, 519 of them were selected at random, in front of a notary, and invited to submit full proposals; the other 519 formed the comparison group.


  
  1,038
  likely eligible firms

  

  
  LOTTERY
  in front of a notary

  
  

  
  519 invited to apply
  393 submitted full proposals · 333 contracted

  
  519 not selected
  comparison group

Note: Only firms identified as likely eligible entered the lottery. Of the 519 selected firms, 76% submitted a full proposal and 64% had signed a contract by March 2025.


Why this design. Strength: it requires, and so ensures, wide outreach, thanks to a simple application process. Limitation: firms may drop out after they apply, which affects statistical power.



What the intervention achieved
The short-term results compare the firms selected in the lottery with the comparison group, whether or not they went on to sign a contract, only a few months after contracts were signed. They are therefore conservative estimates, based on firms’ self-reported survey data.


+101%
Investment in digital tools
Selected firms invested about twice as much in digital tools as the comparison group.


+291%
Spending on digital tools for business administration
Software spending rose by 167% and production-related digital investment by 352%.


+5.6 pp
Firms using ERP software
Against 26% in the comparison group. The share using CRM software was 3.1 percentage points higher than the comparison group’s 11.7%.



No significant short-term effect on profits or sales has been observed yet. Selected firms showed slightly higher sales and labour productivity, but the differences were not statistically significant, likely because implementation was at an early stage. Tailored support and continued monitoring will be essential to ensure inclusive and sustained digital transformation.


Outreach was tested too. Before the call, the agency randomly selected 26 of 46 towns for in-person information visits. The visited towns produced more applications, and the additional applicants were smaller firms (see What do you want to learn?).

section: Bulgaria: human-led versus AI-led business consulting
text:
Bulgaria: human-led versus AI-led business consulting

Northern BulgariaFour-arm RCT600 firms2026–2027 (planned)



The problem
Northern Bulgaria’s micro and small enterprises (MSEs) - over 98% of firms in the region - lag far behind southern Bulgaria and the EU average. Depopulation and ageing have left “ghost towns” with shrinking labour pools and declining customer bases, and managerial skills, often picked up informally, limit the uptake of modern business practices. AI adoption is strikingly low: just 6.5% of firms in the region use AI, against an EU average of 13.5%.


What is being tested
The Bulgarian Small and Medium Enterprises Promotion Agency (BSMEPA) is launching an intervention that pairs group training in managerial skills with one of three ways of delivering further support: one-to-one human-led consulting, a subscription to an off-the-shelf AI platform such as ChatGPT Premium, or a customised AI tool that proactively nudges managers towards it. The aim is to find out whether AI-led alternatives can match costly human consulting at a fraction of the price.



What the evaluation aims to answer

“Can lower-cost, AI-led consulting match the effectiveness of traditional human-led consulting for small firms?”



The intervention

  The interventionGroup training in managerial skills, then one of three support modes: human-led consulting, an AI subscription, or a customised AI-led consulting tool
  WhereNorthern Bulgaria; Bulgarian Small and Medium Enterprises Promotion Agency (BSMEPA)
  Who is randomised600 MSEs (fewer than 50 employees) in retail, agricultural processing, services and manufacturing, stratified by sector, region and owner gender
  The designFour-arm RCT: pure control, training + human consulting, training + AI subscription, training + AI-led consulting tool (150 firms per arm)
  Outcomes trackedFirm sales, sales per worker, profits and exports; management practices, foreign-market knowledge, access to suppliers, finance and customers
  Starting pointMSEs report 88% lower sales per worker than larger firms on average, and only 6.5% of regional firms use AI, against an EU average of 13.5%



Key steps and dates

  Recruitment and applicationsBaseline Jan–Mar 2026 (planned)
  →
  Random assignment
  →
  Training and consulting rolloutMar–Sep 2026 (planned)
  →
  Endline surveyOct–Dec 2026 (planned)
  →
  Follow-up surveyOct–Dec 2027 (planned)



How the intervention is designed
The Agency will mobilise applicants directly across northern Bulgaria; up to 450 eligible firms will be offered business support, with no applicant guaranteed a place. Once 600 eligible firms have applied, firms are randomly allocated, stratified by sector, region and owner gender, to a pure control group or one of three treatment arms.


  
  600
  eligible MSEs

  
  
  
  
  

  
  150 control
  no training or consulting

  
  150 training + human-led consulting
  one-to-one, in person

  
  150 training + AI subscription
  e.g. ChatGPT Premium

  
  150 training + AI-led consulting tool
  proactive nudges

Note: 600 eligible MSEs are randomly assigned in equal shares to a control group and three treatment arms, so each AI-based alternative can be compared directly to human-led consulting.


Why this design. Strength: putting human-led consulting and two AI-based alternatives in the same trial, against the same control group, lets the evaluation rank all three by cost-effectiveness rather than comparing each in isolation. Limitation: with 150 firms per arm, the study is powered to detect a change in sales of around 26% or more, so more modest effects could go undetected.



What the evaluation will answer


Human-led vs AI-led
Whether a customised, proactively nudging AI tool can approach the effectiveness of costly one-to-one human consulting, at a lower marginal cost.


Off-the-shelf vs custom AI
Whether simply subscribing managers to an existing tool like ChatGPT Premium is enough, or whether a tailored, proactive AI platform is needed to change business practices.


How durable are the gains?
Whether improvements from AI-enabled consulting persist for longer than from human-led consulting, since managers keep the ability to self-serve after the support ends.



The main risks to the evaluation are insufficient take-up of consulting or AI services, and non-random attrition between the baseline and the two follow-up rounds. The team is mitigating these with in-person mobilisation to build the applicant pool, and by collecting detailed contact and backup information from every participant to support tracking through autumn 2027.
