title: Examples of RCTs in public interventions
section: Poland: AI assistance for smarter Horizon Europe applications
text:
Poland: AI assistance for smarter Horizon Europe applications

Poland, national programmeThree nested RCTs~120,000 SMEs reached



The problem
Polish SMEs underperform in Horizon Europe, the EU’s flagship innovation funding programme: a 16.5% success rate, against an EU-27 average of 20.3%. Funding is also highly concentrated - just 11 SMEs account for roughly a third of all Polish projects. A previous support scheme, “Grants for Eurogrants”, converted only 400 of about 1,700 applications into signed contracts, and just 19 firms ultimately secured EU funding. Only 20.1% of firms report knowing PARP, the agency responsible for this support.


What is being tested
The Polish Agency for Enterprise Development (PARP) is testing a three-stage pilot: behavioural messaging to raise awareness of its support; a machine-learning model that scores firms’ likelihood of Horizon Europe success, used to target encouragement calls; and an AI-based advisory tool paired with a human “technology scout” for firms that express interest in applying.



What the evaluation aims to answer

“Can behavioural messaging, algorithmic targeting and AI-assisted advice raise the number and quality of Polish Horizon Europe applications?”



The intervention

  The interventionA three-stage pilot: behavioural outreach messaging, machine-learning targeting with encouragement calls, and AI-tool-plus-technology-scout application support
  WherePoland; Polish Agency for Enterprise Development (PARP)
  Who is randomised~120,000 SMEs reached with outreach messages; ~11,000 Horizon-eligible firms in the targeting stage; up to ~500 interested firms in the support stage
  The designThree nested RCTs: a messaging A/B/C test, ranked-vs-random encouragement calls, and AI-tool-and-scout support (~200 firms) vs. a waitlist
  Outcomes trackedEmail/ad engagement, applications to PARP and Horizon Europe, blind-rated application quality, funding success, and firm employment, revenue and survival
  Starting pointJust 16.5% of Polish Horizon Europe applications succeed, against an EU-27 average of 20.3%, and only 20.1% of firms report knowing PARP



Key steps and dates

  Outreach messaging
  →
  ML targeting
  →
  Encouragement calls
  →
  Support sign-up
  →
  AI tool and scout support



How the intervention is designed
Three experiments are nested inside PARP’s own application funnel. First, roughly 120,000 SMEs are randomly shown one of three outreach messages, from a plain fact-based announcement to versions adding behavioural nudges and information about the new AI-powered support. Second, from a pool of about 11,000 Horizon-eligible firms, one half is ranked by a machine-learning model trained on past Horizon winners; the top 500 ranked firms and 500 randomly selected firms then both receive an encouragement call. Third, among the roughly 400–500 firms that register interest in extra support, 200 are randomly selected for immediate access to an AI advisory tool and a technology scout, while the remainder are waitlisted.


  
  Stage 1: Outreach
  ~120,000 SMEs
  3 randomised messages (A/B/C)

  
  Stage 2: Targeting
  ~11,000 eligible firms
  ranked (500 called) vs. not-ranked (500 called)

  
  Stage 3: Support
  ~400–500 interested firms
  ~200 AI tool + scout vs. waitlist

  
  

  Each stage is a separate randomisation, feeding firms forward into PARP's existing application funnel.

Note: Three nested experiments track firms from broad outreach through algorithmic targeting to intensive AI-and-scout application support.


Why this design. Strength: nesting three experiments inside PARP’s own application funnel means each stage’s estimate is drawn from firms who arrive naturally through that funnel, not an artificial sample. Limitation: because later stages depend on take-up from earlier ones, the sample shrinks at each step, leaving less statistical power for the innermost support experiment.



What the evaluation will answer


Does messaging move firms?
Whether behavioural nudges - social proof, urgency framing, expected-value framing - raise click-throughs and registrations more than PARP’s standard, fact-based messaging.


Can an algorithm find promising firms?
Whether a machine-learning “Horizon potential score”, trained on past winners, identifies firms more likely to submit competitive applications than outreach targeted at random.


Does AI-assisted support raise quality?
Whether pairing an AI advisory tool with a human technology scout increases application rates, application quality and ultimately funding success, compared with PARP’s standard waitlist resources.



The clearest risk to implementation is legal: whether informing firms that a machine-learning model identified them as “high-potential” is compatible with EU data-protection law is still under review, and may limit how the targeting stage can be communicated. The team is also tracking whether firms treat encouragement phone calls as credible outreach from PARP rather than as spam.

section: Romania (North-East): AI assistance for smarter grant reviews
text:
Romania (North-East): AI assistance for smarter grant reviews

North-East region, RomaniaMulti-phase RCT~800 proposals2026–2027 (planned)



The problem
At Romania’s Regional Development Agencies, grant application reviews are slow and inconsistent. The 2023 Microenterprise call at the North-East RDA took roughly seven months from submission to contract, generated 50 technical-financial appeals and 19 contracting appeals, and disadvantaged smaller firms: enterprises under two years old, with no employees or turnover below RON 250,000, succeeded only 14% of the time, against over 90% for firms with turnover of RON 1.5–2 million. Many applicants turn to a large consultancy industry - an estimated EUR 527 million in annual turnover across 1,500 firms - just to navigate the process.


What is being tested
The North-East Regional Development Agency (RDA), with the automation company UiPath, has built an AI decision-support tool that benchmarks proposed budgets, flags risks, and supports reviewers on eligibility and quality criteria. It is being embedded in the 2026 Microenterprise Growth Grant Call (about EUR 30 million), with reviewers randomly assigned to work with or without the tool, and funded projects randomly assigned to AI-assisted or standard monitoring.



What the evaluation aims to answer

“Can an AI decision-support tool make public grant reviews faster, more consistent and better targeted, without compromising fairness?”



The intervention

  The interventionAn AI decision-support tool, co-developed with UiPath, that benchmarks budgets, flags risks and supports eligibility and quality scoring for grant reviewers
  WhereNorth-East Romania; Regional Development Agency (RDA), embedded in the 2026 Microenterprise Growth Grant Call (~EUR 30 million)
  Who is randomised~1,000 expressions of interest and ~800 full proposals, reviewed by 30–40 trained reviewers; ~150 funded projects
  The designMulti-phase RCT: reviewers randomised to AI-assisted or human-only review at each stage; ~150 grants allocated by lottery within score bands; funded projects randomised to AI-assisted or standard monitoring
  Outcomes trackedReview time and scores, clarification requests and appeals, on-time disbursement, and funded-firm survival, employment, revenue and investment
  Starting pointThe 2023 call took roughly seven months from submission to contract; firms under two years old or with no employees had a 14% success rate, against over 90% for the highest-turnover firms



Key steps and dates

  Expression of interest2026 call (planned)
  →
  AI-assisted or human review
  →
  Full proposal and review
  →
  Funding lottery
  →
  AI-assisted or standard monitoringUntil Q2 2027 (planned)



How the intervention is designed
Around 1,000 expressions of interest are expected, each assigned to one of 30–40 trained reviewers who are randomly given, or not given, access to the AI tool; reviewers cycle between AI-assisted and unassisted batches so the comparison is not confounded by reviewer ability. Roughly 800 full proposals then go through the same randomised review process. Of the approximately 600 proposals that clear eligibility checks, about 150 are funded through a lottery run separately within AI-assisted and human-only score bands, so funding decisions stay comparable across review modes. Funded projects are then randomly assigned to AI-assisted or standard monitoring during implementation.


  
  1,000
  expressions of interest

  

  
  800
  full proposals

  

  
  600 eligible
  funding lottery, by score band

  
  
  

  
  75 funded: AI monitoring
  automated risk flags

  
  75 funded: standard monitoring
  human oversight only

Note: Reviewers are randomly assigned to work with or without the AI tool at each review stage (not shown); funded projects are then randomly split between AI-assisted and standard monitoring.


Why this design. Strength: randomising AI access at the reviewer-proposal level, with each reviewer cycling between AI-assisted and unassisted batches, isolates the effect of the tool from differences between reviewers. Limitation: because a reviewer with AI access can choose how much to rely on it, the design measures the effect of being offered AI support (intention-to-treat), not of using it, though usage telemetry will help distinguish the two.



What the evaluation will answer


Faster, more consistent reviews
Whether AI-assisted reviewers complete assessments faster, and with fewer clarification requests or appeals, than reviewers working without AI support.


Sharper targeting of promising firms
Whether the relationship between evaluation scores and firms’ later performance is stronger when those scores were produced with AI assistance.


Fair treatment across firm types
Whether AI assistance changes the pattern of scores and funding by owner gender, firm age and sector, as part of a pre-registered bias audit.



The central safeguard against biased AI outputs is a systematic audit of scoring patterns across firm groups after the expression-of-interest phase; if the audit finds significant disparities, the underlying prompts and models will be reviewed and adjusted before the full-proposal stage goes ahead.

title: Examples of RCTs in public interventions
section: Romania (South-Muntenia): the returns to innovation subsidies
text:
Romania (South-Muntenia): the returns to innovation subsidies

South-Muntenia region, RomaniaTwo-stage cluster RCT~900 SMEs2026–2028 (planned)



The problem
South-Muntenia is a lagging EU region, ranked 243rd of EU regions on the Regional Innovation Scoreboard, with an Innovation Readiness Index of just 28. Only 6.3% of firms are classified as innovative, and just 1.4% of the workforce works in high-tech sectors. Between 2014 and 2020, Romania allocated EUR 1.6 billion to public research institutes but only EUR 74 million to private firms, and the region hosts just 3% of the country’s research infrastructure.


What is being tested
The South-Muntenia Regional Development Agency (SM-RDA) is allocating EUR 24.8 million in innovation subsidies to SMEs, cross-randomised with management training on change and innovation culture. Grants are assigned through a two-stage design: geographic or sectoral clusters are randomly assigned different shares of funded firms, and firms within each cluster are then randomly selected to receive funding - allowing the evaluation to separate a firm’s own private return from spillovers onto its neighbours.



What the evaluation aims to answer

“Do the private returns to innovation subsidies for SMEs exceed their social returns, once spillovers to other firms are taken into account?”



The intervention

  The interventionInnovation subsidy grants (50–70% co-financed by firms) for R&D projects, cross-randomised with management training on change and innovation culture
  WhereSouth-Muntenia, Romania; South-Muntenia Regional Development Agency (SM-RDA), EUR 24.8 million SME innovation grant allocation
  Who is randomised~900 SMEs across 100 geographic or sectoral clusters (~9 firms per cluster), excluding agricultural firms
  The designTwo-stage RCT: clusters randomised to 0%, 33%, 66% or 100% funding intensity, then firms randomised to funding within each cluster; management training cross-randomised at firm level
  Outcomes trackedShort-run revenue, inputs, profit, productivity, investment, pricing and product variety; medium- to long-run technology adoption, new products, licensing and patenting
  Starting pointOnly 6.3% of firms in the region are classified as innovative and just 1.4% of the workforce works in high-tech sectors, with an Innovation Readiness Index of 28



Key steps and dates

  Call for proposalsJun–Sep 2026 (planned)
  →
  Cluster formation
  →
  Cluster-level intensityOct 2026 (planned)
  →
  Firm-level lotteryOct 2026 (planned)
  →
  Grant and monitoringTo Q1 2028; endline Q1–Q2 2028 (planned)



How the intervention is designed
After the call for proposals closes, applicant firms are grouped into roughly 100 clusters based on geographic or sectoral proximity. Each cluster is then randomly assigned a funding intensity - the share of its firms that will receive a subsidy, set at 0%, 33%, 66% or 100% - and firms within the cluster are randomly selected for funding up to that share. Comparing outcomes across clusters with different intensities isolates spillover effects, while comparing funded and unfunded firms within the same cluster isolates each firm’s own private return.


  Cluster-level intensity (randomised across ~100 clusters)

  
  0% funded

  
  33% funded

  
  66% funded

  
  100% funded

  
  Example cluster at 33% intensity: 9 firms, 3 randomly funded

  
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
  
  funded
  funded
  funded

  Comparing across clusters isolates spillovers; comparing within a cluster isolates each firm's own private return.

Note: Clusters are randomly assigned a funding intensity; within each cluster, firms are then randomly selected for funding up to that share.


Why this design. Strength: varying funding intensity across clusters, on top of randomising which firms within a cluster are funded, lets the evaluation separate a firm’s private return from spillovers onto its neighbours and competitors. Limitation: the design captures spillovers within a cluster but not across cluster boundaries, which the team plans to approximate separately with a structural, network-based model.



What the evaluation will answer


Do subsidies pay off for the firm?
Whether receiving an innovation subsidy raises a firm’s revenue, profits, productivity and investment in the short run, and its technology adoption and patenting over the longer run.


Do the gains spread, or just shift?
Whether firms in higher-intensity clusters see larger productivity gains through knowledge diffusion, or whether funded firms instead grow at competitors’ expense.


Does training make subsidies work harder?
Whether pairing the grant with training on change management and innovation culture strengthens firms’ ability to absorb and use the funding.



The main risk to the spillover analysis is statistical power: if spillovers turn out to be smaller than about 8 percentage points (roughly a third of the expected direct subsidy effect), that part of the analysis will be underpowered. Even so, the team notes the resulting estimates will still provide useful benchmarks for calibrating models of innovation diffusion, an area where experimental evidence remains scarce.

section: Europe: grants for SME energy efficiency
text:
Europe: grants for SME energy efficiency

34 European countriesSimple lottery1,964 SMEs2024–2026



The problem
Energy efficiency is one of the cheapest ways for a firm to cut energy use and costs, yet most European SMEs invest little in it. Among the firms that applied to this pilot, only 22% had invested in energy efficiency in the year before applying, even though 62% already monitored their energy use and almost all planned some form of capital investment. Advice on its own was not turning plans into purchases.


What was done
The European Commission (DG GROW and EISMEA), the Enterprise Europe Network (EEN) and the World Bank ran the EENergy pilot, funded by the EU Single Market Programme.
On top of the advisory support EEN advisors already provide, the pilot offered a reimbursement grant of up to EUR 10,000 for energy-efficiency measures: equipment and installations, consultancy, or staff training. The evaluation was designed into the pilot from the start, before the first call opened.



What experimentation sought to answer

“Does money on top of advice change what small firms invest in, and does it cut their energy use?”



The intervention

  TimelineCall 1 opened February 2024 (1,406 firms); lottery June 2024; activities from July 2024; Call 2 December 2024 to February 2025 (558 firms); follow-up surveys Q1 2025 and Q1 2026; findings September 2026
  The interventionEENergy: a reimbursement grant of up to EUR 10,000 for equipment, consultancy or training, on top of standard EEN advisory services
  Where34 European countries; European Commission (DG GROW, EISMEA) and Enterprise Europe Network with the World Bank, funded by the EU Single Market Programme
  Who is randomised1,964 eligible SMEs across two open calls: 54% micro, 36% small, 9% medium-sized; 36% in manufacturing
  The designSimple lottery among eligible applicants, run separately for each call and stratified by consortium and advisor: 986 offered the grant vs. 978 receiving advisory services only
  Outcomes trackedEnergy-efficiency and renewable investment, energy use and spending, energy management practices, revenue, profits and employment
  Starting pointOnly 22% of applicant firms had invested in energy efficiency in the year before the pilot, although 62% already monitored their energy use



Key steps and dates

  Two open calls
  →
  Eligibility check
  →
  Lottery
  →
  Grants and advisory services
  →
  Follow-up surveys



How the intervention was tested
Firms applied in two open calls, from February to May 2024 and from December 2024 to February 2025. Applications were screened against the EU definition of an SME and against the pilot’s requirements, including an energy-efficiency action plan agreed with an EEN advisor and a target of at least 5% lower energy consumption. Eligible firms then entered a lottery, run separately for each call and stratified by consortium and advisor characteristics, so that funded and unfunded firms came from the same pool and worked with comparable advisors.


  
  1,964
  eligible firms

  

  
  LOTTERY
  every firm, the same chance

  
  

  
  986 offered a grant
  up to EUR 10,000, plus advice

  
  978 standard group
  advisory services only

Note: Every firm in the study had already cleared eligibility and was working with an EEN advisor, so the lottery isolates the effect of the money rather than the advice.


Why this design. Strength: because the grant was drawn by lottery among firms that all received the same advisory service, the comparison separates the effect of the cash from the effect of the advice, across 34 countries at once. Limitation: firms offered the grant answered follow-up surveys far more often than the standard group (91% against 65%), so the estimates depend on statistical corrections for who responded.



What the intervention achieved
One year on, the grant had changed what firms bought and how they managed energy. Total energy-related investment was about EUR 9,700 higher per firm in the grant group, almost all of it capital spending, with renewable-energy installations the single largest category.


+26 pp
Firms investing in energy efficiency
43% of firms offered the grant made an energy-efficiency investment, against 17% of the standard group.


×3
Firms investing in renewables
The share investing in renewable energy rose from 10% to about 30%.


+31 pp
Firms setting energy-reduction goals
83% of the grant group set energy-reduction goals, against 52% of the standard group, alongside more regular energy monitoring.


The response was strongest among the smallest firms. Renewable-energy investment rose by 22 percentage points among micro and small firms, against 5 points among medium-sized firms. The fixed EUR 10,000 was worth roughly 5% of annual revenue for the median micro firm, but only 0.1% for the median medium-sized firm, which is the clearest explanation on offer for the gap.

Averaged across all firms, no reduction in electricity consumption or total energy spending was detectable one year after the grants, and there was no detectable effect on revenue, profits or employment. Savings did appear for particular groups: electricity consumption fell by about 10% among micro and small firms, and electricity spending by about 20% among firms in the second call. The practical lesson for the design of similar grants is to scale a fixed grant to firm size, or to target smaller firms, and to justify it on investment and management change rather than on short-run business performance.


  Further reading

section: Bulgaria, Poland and Slovakia: Digitrans, digital adoption support for MSMEs
text:
Bulgaria, Poland and Slovakia: Digitrans, digital adoption support for MSMEs

Bulgaria, Poland and SlovakiaThree-arm RCT629 MSMEs2024–2025



The problem
Small businesses in Bulgaria, Poland and Slovakia show limited adoption of digital tools beyond what regulation or the financial sector requires. The 2022 Digital Economy and Society Index places all three countries in the bottom quartile of EU members for business digitalisation.
Current public support schemes in the region largely overlook this: MSMEs account for 98% of businesses and two-thirds of employment, yet most schemes still emphasise technology adoption and financial assistance, leaving the managerial and organisational capabilities firms need to make use of new tools unaddressed.


What was done
The World Bank designed Digitrans, a standardised support instrument tested across Bulgaria, Poland and Slovakia, integrating a financial subsidy with technical assistance to address both resource and capability constraints.
The financial subsidy provides up to EUR 2,000 per firm towards the cost of adopting digital business tools. The technical assistance component adds 10 weeks of diagnostic assessment, group training and one-to-one advisory support.



What experimentation sought to answer

“Does pairing technical assistance with a financial subsidy improve MSME digitalisation outcomes more than a subsidy alone?”



The intervention

  The interventionA financial subsidy of up to EUR 2,000 per firm, with a subset of firms also receiving 10 weeks of technical assistance
  WhereBulgaria, Poland and Slovakia; World Bank Digitrans pilot, EU-funded
  Who is randomised629 MSMEs with 5–35 employees and at least 12 months trading, drawn from over 1,600 applications
  The designThree-arm RCT, stratified by country, firm size and digital sophistication: comparison (209), subsidy only (210), subsidy plus technical assistance (210)
  Outcomes trackedDigital tool adoption and usage, managerial and organisational change, firm performance
  Starting pointSmall businesses show limited digital adoption beyond what regulation or banks require



Key steps and dates

  ApplicationsMay–Jul 2024
  →
  Eligibility and interview
  →
  Random assignment
  →
  Subsidy and supportQ3–Q4 2024
  →
  Follow-up surveyFrom Q4 2024



How the intervention was tested
Firms applied through an open call across Bulgaria, Poland and Slovakia in 2024, and those meeting the eligibility criteria completed a baseline interview. Eligible firms were then randomly assigned by the World Bank into one of three groups, with randomisation stratified within each country by firm size and digital sophistication so that groups were balanced from the outset.


  
  629
  randomised firms

  

  
  STRATIFIED LOTTERY
  by country, size and
  digital sophistication

  
  
  
  

  
  209 comparison group
  benchmarking report only

  
  210 financial subsidy
  subsidy plus benchmarking report

  
  210 subsidy + technical assistance
  the full support package

Note: Randomisation was stratified within each country by firm size and digital sophistication, splitting 629 eligible firms into a comparison group and two support groups of about 210 firms each.


Why this design. Strength: a three-arm design separates the effect of money from the effect of capability-building support, rather than only comparing supported firms to unsupported ones. Limitation: it needs a larger sample than a simple two-arm trial to detect the same effect size, since firms are split three ways.


Allocation resulted in balanced groups across a broad range of firm characteristics, creating a solid foundation for rigorous impact evaluation. There was no evidence of systematic differences between groups at baseline, so later changes can be reliably attributed to the support received rather than to pre-existing differences.



What the intervention achieved


×2.5
Digital tool usage is 2.5 times higher with combined support
Firms that received both types of support increased their digital tool usage intensity more than twice as much as those with a subsidy alone.


×2
Managerial changes are more common with technical assistance
Firms in the combined support group were twice as likely to introduce internal organisational and managerial changes.


82% vs 67%
Combined support leads to deeper use of digital tools
Firms with technical assistance made better use of advanced software functions: 82% used CRM systems for client communication, against 67% in the subsidy-only group.



Firms receiving only a financial subsidy typically limited their spending to the subsidy value, with no meaningful increase in the sophistication of tools available to them. Effective digitalisation support needs to go beyond subsidising technology purchases: the benefits of combined support were especially strong among smaller firms, firms with low initial digital capabilities, service-sector firms and women-led businesses.


  Further reading
  
  Campos, F., Iacovone, L., Iwanowski, D., and Reichenbach, A. W. 2025. “Bridging the Digital Gap: Evidence from a Multi-Country Pilot on Supporting MSME Digitalization in the EU.” World Bank, Washington, DC.

title: Examples of RCTs in public interventions
text:
Colombia: scaling up management consulting

Antioquia, Cundinamarca, Valle del Cauca and Eje CafeteroThree-arm RCT159 firms2012–2018



The problem
Colombian auto parts manufacturers show wide variation in management practices, and weaker practices are closely tied to lower productivity. Structured, hands-on management consulting can improve how firms are run, but delivering it in a resource-intensive, one-to-one format is costly - a cost that can be prohibitive for small and medium firms to finance on their own, and for governments seeking to support large numbers of firms at once.


What was done
The World Bank, in partnership with the Government of Colombia, tested two lower-cost ways to deliver management consulting to small and medium manufacturers: individual, firm-by-firm consulting delivered by local teams, and a more novel group-based model that works with several firms together to bring costs down further.
Every participating firm, including the comparison group, first received a diagnostic assessment of its management practices across five areas - logistics, human resources, finance, marketing and sales, and production - carried out by a team of specialist consultants.



What experimentation sought to answer

“Can lower-cost individual or group-based consulting improve small and medium firms’ management practices and performance?”



The intervention

  The interventionA diagnostic for every firm, followed by individual or group-based management consulting
  WhereColombia; auto parts manufacturing sector
  Who is randomised159 eligible firms (manufacturers, tier 1/2 suppliers, 2+ years old, 10+ workers), in 53 matched triplets
  The designThree-arm RCT: comparison, individual consulting (~USD 28,950/firm), group consulting (~USD 10,500/firm)
  Outcomes trackedManagement practices; employment, sales, value-added and profits via administrative records
  Starting pointBaseline management scores ranged from 43 to 51 out of 100 across practice areas



Key steps and dates

  ApplicationsAnnounced Apr 2012
  →
  Diagnostic phaseJun–Oct 2013
  →
  Matched-triplet lotteryNov 2013
  →
  Consulting deliveredIndividual Mar–Nov 2014; group Sep 2015–May 2016
  →
  Outcome tracking2014–2018



How the intervention was tested
218 firms applied to Colombia’s Programa de Extensionismo Tecnológico. After screening for eligibility - established auto parts manufacturers that were tier 1 or 2 suppliers, at least two years old, with at least ten employees, and located in Antioquia, Cundinamarca, Valle del Cauca or the Eje Cafetero - 159 firms formed the final sample.
Firms were then grouped into 53 matched triplets, formed to minimise differences in location, size, labour productivity and management practices between the three firms in each triplet. Within each triplet, firms were randomly allocated to a comparison group, individual consulting, or group consulting.


  
  159
  eligible firms

  

  
  53 MATCHED TRIPLETS
  by location, size,
  productivity, practices

  
  
  
  

  
  53 comparison group
  diagnostic only, no consulting

  
  53 individual consulting
  ~USD 28,950/firm, over 6 months

  
  53 group consulting
  ~USD 10,500/firm, in groups of 3–8

Note: Firms were matched into triplets before randomisation, then randomly allocated within each triplet to a comparison group, individual consulting, or group consulting.


Why this design. Strength: matching firms into triplets before randomising keeps the three groups closely balanced on size, productivity and starting management practices, even with a modest overall sample. Limitation: with only 53 firms in each arm, the design has less statistical power to detect small effects than a larger, simple two-arm trial.



What the intervention achieved


+9 pp
Management practices improved in both groups
Individual and group consulting each raised firms’ management practice scores by around 9 percentage points on average, relative to a baseline of 56%.


+28% to +33%
Sales and profits rose for group-consulting firms
Firms receiving group-based consulting saw significant gains in sales, value-added and profits; the effects of individual consulting on firm performance were smaller and not statistically significant.


USD 273,000
Estimated average annual profit increase, group consulting
At a cost of about USD 10,500 per firm, the estimated profit gains from group consulting paid back its cost within about a month.



Group-consulting firms reported far more contact with each other after the consulting than before it: business links between study firms were almost non-existent at baseline, but around half of group participants said they still communicated with other group members roughly a year later, and firms whose management practices changed the most tended to be grouped with others who also improved the most - evidence that peer learning, not just lower delivery cost, contributed to group consulting’s stronger results on firm performance.


The rollout of group consulting was delayed by more than a year due to a budgetary payment delay, and only 68% of group-assigned firms completed the intervention, compared with 87% for individual consulting. Delays like this are a practical risk to weigh when comparing the cost-effectiveness of different delivery models.


  Further reading
  
  Iacovone, L., Maloney, W. F., and McKenzie, D. 2022. Improving management with individual and group-based consulting: Results from a randomized experiment in Colombia. Review of Economic Studies, 89(1), 346–371.

section: Yemen: testing whether internships help youth find work
text:
Yemen: testing whether internships help youth find work

Sanaa and Aden, YemenStratified RCT583 young graduates2013–2015



The problem
Young jobseekers in Yemen often face a catch-22: firms are reluctant to hire someone without prior work experience, yet that experience is hard to gain without first being hired. Early jobs matter because they build both job-specific and soft skills, but firms may under-invest in providing them - a reluctance that can be sharper still in a fragile, conflict-affected setting. Job opportunities for young graduates were also increasingly scarce following Yemen’s 2011–12 political crisis.


What was done
The Enterprise Revitalization and Employment Pilot (EREP) tested a subsidised-internship model: the pilot paid half the cost of a six-month internship, with the host firm covering the rest, and matched applicants to firms based on the firm’s stated requirements. Recent graduates in Sanaa and Aden applied online and were screened for eligibility before being considered.



What experimentation sought to answer

“Can a subsidised matchmaking scheme help young jobseekers gain their first work experience, and does that experience translate into better employment outcomes afterwards?”



The intervention

  The interventionEnterprise Revitalization and Employment Pilot (EREP), internship component: matching grants covering half the cost of a six-month internship, plus matchmaking between graduates and firms
  WhereRepublic of Yemen; Sanaa and Aden
  Who is randomised583 eligible youth (Yemeni, Sanaa/Aden residents, graduated within 2 years), to treatment (430) or control (153)
  The designStratified RCT: treatment group offered matchmaking to internships subsidised at 50% of cost, for up to six months
  Outcomes trackedEmployment, months worked and earnings, via a follow-up phone survey
  Starting point3,487 eligible youth applied; 500 were randomly invited to a two-day basic skills training (477 attended)



Key steps and dates

  ApplicationsOct–Dec 2013
  →
  Skills-training invitationJan 2014; training Feb–Mar 2014
  →
  Random assignment
  →
  MatchmakingMar–May 2014
  →
  Follow-up surveyMar 2015



How the intervention was tested
The pilot launched in August 2013 through a project website, media events and campus outreach. Applications ran from October to December 2013, closing with 3,487 eligible applicants. Of these, 500 were randomly invited to a two-day basic skills training - chosen with probability proportional to the demand for their specialisation - and 477 attended.
The resulting experimental sample of 583 individuals was randomly assigned, within strata defined by specialisation and city, to a treatment group of 430 (offered matchmaking to a subsidised internship) or a control group of 153. Eleven human resource advisors then matched treatment-group applicants to firms based on the firm’s requirements, sending CVs for firms to interview and decide whether to offer a placement.


  
  3,487
  eligible applicants

  

  
  500 invited to training
  477 attended

  

  
  583 experimental sample
  assigned within 39 strata

  
  
  

  
  430 treatment
  offered matchmaking

  
  153 control
  no internship match

Note: Applicants were randomly invited to basic skills training, then the resulting sample was randomly assigned, within specialisation-and-city strata, to a treatment group offered internship matchmaking or a control group.


Why this design. Strength: randomising within strata defined by specialisation and city, among applicants who had already been invited to training, helps ensure the treatment and control groups started out comparable in skills and local job-market conditions. Limitation: more applicants were assigned to treatment than there were internship placements available, so actual take-up (36.7%) fell well below the treatment assignment rate - which is why the study reports both an intention-to-treat effect and a larger effect scaled up for those who actually took up an internship.



What the intervention achieved


+17 pp / +42 pp
More likely to have worked at all in 2014
Being offered internship matchmaking raised the chance of having worked at all during 2014 by 17 percentage points on an intention-to-treat basis, from a 61% employment rate in the control group, and by 42 percentage points among those who actually took up an internship.


+0.35 s.d. / +0.85 s.d.
Employment gains persisted months after the internship ended
On a standardised index of employment outcomes measured three to five months after internships ended, effects remained statistically significant: 0.35 standard deviations on an intention-to-treat basis, and 0.85 standard deviations for those who took up an internship.


36.7%
Take-up among those assigned to treatment
Only 158 of the 430 people assigned to treatment were actually matched to and completed an internship placement, reflecting how binding capacity constraints were relative to demand for internship positions.



The internship raised employment more for male applicants than for female applicants, so the pilot did not close the pre-existing gender gap in employment outcomes. Because the evaluation covers only one year of the pilot rather than the two originally planned, the study had limited statistical power to say precisely how much smaller the effect was for women.


Conflict escalated partway through the pilot: Houthi forces took control of Sanaa in September 2014, and the second year of the pilot was cancelled, roughly halving the intended sample and reducing statistical power. The follow-up survey was also fielded earlier and more narrowly than planned, amid displacement and shortages of fuel, electricity and water. It also remains possible that some of the employment gains for treated youth came partly at the expense of other jobseekers in the economy - a general equilibrium effect this study could not measure.


  Further reading
  
  McKenzie, D., Assaf, N., and Cusolito, A. P. 2016. The demand for, and impact of, youth internships: Evidence from a randomized experiment in Yemen. IZA Journal of Labor & Development, 5(1), 1–15.

title: What is the EuroCOMP Lab?
text:
See it in action
A short introduction to the EuroCOMP Lab, how impact evaluations can make public support more efficient and effective, and how it is already being used to improve programmes across Europe.

title: What is the EuroCOMP Lab?
text:
What the EuroCOMP Lab does
DG REGIO and the World Bank are expanding their partnership on learning about the competitiveness agenda through the development of the EuroCOMP Lab. Its objective is to embed innovative experimental approaches in Member States’ investments in competitiveness programmes, with a focus on regional impacts. This second round of investment in rigorous policy experimentation supports cohesion policy’s competitiveness agenda, with a focus on new strategic and nimble innovations, as well as further institutional strengthening and cross-regional learning.
The EuroCOMP Lab finances three types of activities:

new (nimble and strategic) randomised controlled trials (RCTs) in competitiveness programmes across Europe
improved mechanisms and platforms for learning between networks of researchers, policymakers, and implementers in the EU
knowledge generation about what works in the medium to long term, including through the use of administrative data

By embedding innovative experimental approaches in Member States’ investments in competitiveness programmes, the project supports institutional strengthening and cross-regional learning, which will be critical for future competitiveness operations in Europe. The work generates innovative and rigorous policy experiments in areas such as green and digital transformation, setting the framework for future coordination and improvement of the policy mix in competitiveness programmes and interventions over time.
The studies designed in this project also contribute to a larger, global body of evidence on how to foster competitive markets, address market failures such as information asymmetries and behavioural biases, and adequately support and target private sector investment. The knowledge gained is intended for use in other regions too, enabling the World Bank to apply findings and lessons learned to enhance the effectiveness and impact of its operations globally.

title: What is the EuroCOMP Lab?
text:
Building on earlier work
An important first step towards embedding experimentation within cohesion policy funds was made through the cooperation between DG REGIO and the World Bank.
An open call for interested managing authorities in EU Member States working on the competitiveness agenda drew a strong response. The Strengthening of Monitoring and Evaluation of EU Innovation Programmes project, informally known as ‘Smart M&E’, then provided technical assistance for designing and setting up five innovative policy experiments in four Member States. This was possible thanks to considerable investment in building local and institutional capacities.
DG REGIO also supported policy experimentation on mechanisms to increase digitalisation among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in three further Member States, under the ‘Digitrans’ project. Together, these projects initiated an ambitious, strategic agenda that is helping managing authorities learn through policy experiments about the impact of competitiveness programmes.
The Examples page describes several of these experiments.

title: What is the EuroCOMP Lab?
text:
How it works
The programme runs for four years. All EU Member States are invited to take part, with a focus on lagging countries and regions.
Work with Member States includes technical assistance for better programming: reviewing theories of change, bringing good global practices to the EU, and supporting the design of outreach, targeting, and actionable, informative monitoring systems. The project works closely with external researchers, with a clear emphasis on capacity building, leveraging the existing evaluation network developed by DG REGIO, and offering on-demand support to regional authorities on introducing experimental learning into policymaking.
The World Bank focuses on analytical and advisory work, while implementation remains the responsibility of Member States. Wherever possible, impacts are assessed at sub-regional level, for example comparing capital cities with other regions, reflecting a clear mandate of DG REGIO’s focus under cohesion policy.

title: What is the EuroCOMP Lab?
text:
The programme’s four workstreams
The project follows a programmatic approach, given the complexity of the task and the need to sequence support to Member States. The work is organised into four workstreams. Across both phases, the first three will generate policy lessons and insights from 13 RCTs:

Workstream 1 generates new rigorous evidence on how to design cohesion policy programmes more effectively and efficiently.
Workstream 2 fosters new connections and improved mechanisms and platforms for learning between networks of researchers, policymakers, and implementers in the EU.
Workstream 3 follows up on the medium- to long-term impacts of ongoing RCTs under the Smart M&E and Digitrans projects.
Workstream 4 aims to enhance the understanding and measurement of competition levels, providing insights to support evidence-based decision-making. By identifying key influencing factors and analysing barriers to market competition, it focuses on the case study of EU public procurement.

title: What is the EuroCOMP Lab?
section: The EU must become more competitive
text:
The EU must become more competitive
To achieve greater productivity and to address a growing competitiveness gap with other leading economies, Europe must undergo a radical transformation. This gap, particularly compared with the United States and China, has been increasingly evident. In 2021, for instance, EU companies spent about half as much on Research and Innovation (R&I) as a share of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) as US companies. Increased funding alone will not close this gap.
For the past two decades, the EU’s top three investors in R&I have consistently been automotive companies, which mirrors the early 2000s in the US. While top investors in the US have recently shifted to the tech sector, EU companies continue to cite regulatory burden as an obstacle to investing in this sector.
Recent EU reports point to the need for a significant acceleration in technological and scientific innovation: enhancing commercialisation, and removing obstacles that hinder the growth, competitiveness, and financing of innovative companies. They highlight the need for policies that are better tailored to regional needs, implemented more quickly, simplified, and more strongly linked to performance.
Alongside the EU’s shrinking workforce, stagnant productivity growth, and rising public debt, its GDP growth is otherwise predicted to stall by 2050. This could force Europe to abandon key goals such as decarbonisation, digitalisation, or defence, leaving many regions struggling to progress further towards high-income status.

title: What is the EuroCOMP Lab?
section: Why more funding for cohesion policy alone is not enough
text:
Why more funding for cohesion policy alone is not enough
Substantial funds are already allocated to support the EU’s competitiveness and innovation objectives, but these investments are expected to be insufficient to address the EU’s rising needs and challenges.
Cohesion policy is one of the EU’s largest investments. It aims to foster balanced growth, reduce disparities, and enhance economic stability and competitiveness by supporting digitalisation, innovation, and competitiveness in less developed regions.

  Cohesion policy budget€361 billion for 2021–2027, through the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF), the Cohesion Fund, and the European Social Fund Plus (ESF+), as part of the EU's Multiannual Financial Framework (European Court of Auditors, 2023a)
  Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF)A temporary instrument established in the same period to support recovery from the COVID-19 economic crisis
  Future needA minimum additional investment of €750–800 billion a year, or 4.4–4.7% of EU GDP in 2023 (European Commission, 2024a)

Increased funding alone will not be enough: smarter policymaking is needed to drive higher returns on EU investments and strengthen Europe’s competitiveness. Innovation and learning in policymaking are key to increasing returns on European investments, and to improving Europe’s competitiveness and readiness to address global and regional challenges.
Turning funds into results also takes time: almost halfway through the RRF implementation period, by the end of 2023, the European Commission had disbursed around a third of the funds, €213 billion of the €723.8 billion, to Member States.
For the EU to compete globally, it must ensure that the funding invested by Member States reaches those in need while yielding substantial returns. This implies continuous policy improvements and their agile adaptation to changing circumstances. Evidence-based decision-making is essential for enhancing competition, economic growth, and social cohesion in the EU, with areas such as bureaucratic simplification and more effective public procurement serving as key examples.

title: What is the EuroCOMP Lab?
section: The case for more causal evidence
text:
The case for more causal evidence
Cohesion policy has a long record of evaluation, using a wide range of methods. Counterfactual evidence on the causal impact of specific interventions and implementation approaches is still comparatively scarce, however, and often arrives after the investments have been made. Recent systematic reviews call for more counterfactual evaluations of cohesion policy investments.

About 3% of the 2,940 EU evaluations to date use counterfactual analysis to estimate the return on investment.

In this context, lessons from past programmes and investments are not always easy to apply to future ones. Interviews with managing authority representatives show that evaluations are often experienced as a reporting obligation rather than a tool for learning, which experimentation aims to change.

title: What is the EuroCOMP Lab?
section: Increasing competitiveness through learning what works
text:
Increasing competitiveness through learning what works
Increasing competitiveness in the EU requires improving the effectiveness of investments under cohesion policy through learning what works better. The challenges faced by lagging regions require policy experimentation, trial-and-error, learning, and course-correcting when it matters most.
Experimental policy learning that relies on RCTs and other rigorous evaluation methods, followed by adequate stock-taking of what works, can help fill the current learning and policy innovation gap in cohesion policy’s competitiveness programmes. In the same way that companies invest in Research and Development (R&D) to identify the most successful products to scale up, evaluations can help identify novel interventions and the conditions under which the returns to current investments can be maximised.

title: What is the EuroCOMP Lab?
text:
EuroCOMP Lab at EURegionsWeek 2026
Few places bring Europe’s regional policy community together at this scale. EURegionsWeek 2026 gathered nearly 5,000 participants in Brussels, from policymakers and managing authorities to researchers and EU institutions, all asking: how can regional policy deliver more impact?
The EuroCOMP Lab, a partnership between the European Commission (DG REGIO) and the World Bank, organised a workshop on how to credibly measure what policies achieve. Instead of assuming a policy will work, regions shared how, together with the Lab, they test approaches, learn fast, and plan to use this evidence to improve programmes and implementation at scale.
Pioneering partners from Romania and Spain, who ran the very first experiments in their own multi-million programmes, shared what they learned. In Romania, a digital grant led to more sales and jobs for supported firms, with positive spillovers to neighbouring firms.
The timing matters: as Europe shapes the 2028–2034 budget, the decisions taken now will define how billions in cohesion policy funding are delivered.

Summary
This website offers the concepts, examples and practical resources needed to get started with RCTs, both for those considering one for the first time and for those who already have experience with experimentation. This page explains what RCTs are, how they fit among other impact evaluation methods, which questions they can answer and why they matter for cohesion policy. title: Randomised trials for EU-funded interventions
text:
What is an RCT?
Experimentation, or experimental evaluation, means testing an intervention by assigning eligible participants at random either to receive it (or one version of it) or to a comparison group (also called a control group) that does not receive it, or receives a different version or another intervention. This is called a randomised controlled trial (RCT). On this website, the terms “experimentation” and “RCT” are used interchangeably.
Randomisation can be used, for example, when there are more eligible applicants than available places, or when an intervention is rolled out in phases and the order in which participants receive it is decided at random. Comparing average results between the groups shows whether the intervention – and not something else going on at the same time – is the reason for the observed changes.
Who ends up in which group is decided by a random draw. It is not decided by who applied first, who looked most promising or whom the reviewer favoured. Because assignment is random, the groups are similar on average before the intervention starts, and any remaining differences between them are due only to chance. That is true not just for characteristics that can be measured, but also for those that cannot be observed. So when a difference between the groups shows up later, it can be attributed to the intervention, provided the trial is implemented as planned and results are measured in the same way for both groups.

title: Randomised trials for EU-funded interventions
section: What is impact evaluation – and where do RCTs fit in?
text:
What is impact evaluation – and where do RCTs fit in?

Impact evaluation answers the question: what causal effect did this intervention have on results such as employment, skills or firm growth – for whom did it work best, and under which conditions?

An impact evaluation compares what happened after an intervention was introduced with what would have happened in its absence: the counterfactual. Unlike monitoring, which tracks whether an intervention is implemented as planned, it tests whether the intervention caused a real difference. It is one of several types of evaluation, alongside implementation evaluation, that managing authorities can include in their evaluation plans.
There is more than one credible way to conduct an impact evaluation, and the right choice depends on the intervention, the available data and the timing. Quasi-experimental methods, such as matching, difference-in-differences or regression discontinuity design, compare participants with non-participants. Because participation is not decided by chance, the two groups may differ in ways that also affect results, so the credibility of the estimate rests on assumptions that need to be stated and discussed.
In an RCT, the comparison group is created by random assignment before the intervention starts, so the comparability of the groups does not depend on such assumptions. The Commission’s Better Regulation toolbox (Tool #68) describes randomised controlled trials as “the benchmark for scientific quantitative methods”, with quasi-experimental methods as the option when randomised trials are not possible. As an RCT requires random assignment to the intervention, it has to be planned before or during implementation. See more on how RCTs differ from quasi-experimental methods and when an RCT is the right choice on the RCTs: why and when page.

title: Randomised trials for EU-funded interventions
section: What questions can an RCT answer?
text:
What questions can an RCT answer?
An RCT can answer several kinds of questions, depending on how it is designed:


How effective is a given intervention?
Whether the intervention works, and for whom it works best.


Which version of an intervention is most effective?
How different versions of an intervention compare – which parts of an intervention work, which do not and how they work together.


How should an intervention be delivered?
How different delivery mechanisms change results, including how to target beneficiaries accurately and increase take-up.


Is it worth the cost?
How cost-effective the intervention is, and how it compares to other interventions.


The question one wants answered decides when, how and for whom the RCT has to be planned. To find out whether an intervention works at all, randomisation must be built in before launch, from the call for proposals. To find out which version works better (a grant alone versus a grant plus advisory support, for instance), an RCT can still be added after the intervention has started. Randomisation then shifts from who gets funded at all to which version each participant receives. See Choosing an evaluation design on the RCTs: why and when page.

title: Randomised trials for EU-funded interventions
text:
Why experiment in cohesion policy?
Cohesion policy supports all EU regions, investing in areas ranging from innovation and the green transition to transport, social inclusion and local development. To design and adjust these interventions well, managing authorities need robust evidence on what they achieve, for whom and under which conditions.
Experimentation is one way to obtain such evidence. Because an RCT creates the comparison group by random assignment, it provides robust causal evidence on whether an intervention made a difference.
Experimentation also supports evidence-based policymaking and adaptive learning. Testing different versions of an intervention, or rolling it out in phases, lets managing authorities learn while delivery is under way and adjust the design, targeting or delivery of later rounds. Findings from one region can inform similar interventions in other regions and in future programming periods.

Experimentation allows for testing, learning and adjusting during delivery.
